questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: In a patient with maxillofacial trauma, airway protection is a critical priority because facial injuries can compromise airway patency. Among the various options available for airway control in this setting, which technique is considered the most appropriate for securing the airway?
questions.explanation: In severe maxillofacial trauma, airway management becomes extremely challenging due to bleeding, edema, disrupted anatomy, and possible obstruction by fractured bones or soft tissue. In such cases, conventional airway methods like orotracheal intubation may be difficult or even impossible, especially if: 1. The mouth cannot be opened (trismus/fracture) 2. There is profuse bleeding or debris 3. There is a risk of worsening injury Under these conditions, tracheostomy provides a definitive and secure airway by bypassing the upper airway entirely. It ensures direct access to the trachea, making ventilation reliable even in distorted facial anatomy. Why other options are wrong: (C) Orotracheal intubation : May not be feasible in severe facial trauma (B) Laryngeal mask airway : Not a definitive airway; poor seal, aspiration risk (D) Mask ventilation : Ineffective due to facial disruption
questions.learning: In severe maxillofacial trauma, airway management becomes extremely challenging due to bleeding, edema, disrupted anatomy, and possible obstruction by fractured bones or soft tissue.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A pediatrician is counseling new mothers about breastfeeding. Which of the following situations is considered an absolute contraindication to breastfeeding?
options: Infants born to an HbsAg-positive mother
questions.explanation: Breast milk is almost always the ideal nutrition, but classic galactosemia in the infant (Option B) is one of the few absolute contraindications. These infants lack the enzyme to metabolize galactose, a component of the lactose in breast milk. Continued exposure leads to liver failure, cataracts, and intellectual disability. HIV infection (Option C) is a contraindication in developed nations, but in many developing countries, the WHO recommends breastfeeding if safe formula alternatives are unavailable. Alcohol consumption (Option A) is a relative contraindication; mothers are advised to limit intake and timing. Infants of HbsAg-positive mothers (Option D) can safely breastfeed once they receive the Hepatitis B vaccine and immunoglobulin at birth. Therefore, because galactosemia represents a life-threatening metabolic inability to process any human milk, it is the definitive absolute contraindication listed. These infants must be fed specialized lactose-free formula
questions.learning: Breast milk is almost always the ideal nutrition, but classic galactosemia in the infant (Option B) is one of the few absolute contraindications. These infants lack the enzyme to metabolize galactose, a component of the lactose in breast milk.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Transcutaneous electric nerve stimulation is used to reduce pain. What is the mechanism behind this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Gate control theory

Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) used for pain relief is based on the gate theory of pain. This method uses electrodes to activate Aα and Aβ fibers near the injury to relieve pain.

Gate control theory is based on the inhibition of pain pathway in the spinal cord. Various sensory inputs from a particular dermatome reach the dorsal horn of the spinal cord. The pain is transmitted via A-delta and C fibers, whereas, A-beta fibers carry tactile sensations (touch, pressure) and A-alpha fibers carry proprioception.

When these large-diameter A-beta/A-alpha fibers are stimulated, they inhibit the pain pathway in the spinal cord. This inhibition is thought to result from the local lateral inhibition of interneurons in the spinal cord.

Gate control theory operates at the substantia gelatinosa of the dorsal horn of the spinal cord.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A mother presents on day 8 of normal vaginal delivery with painful left breast, fever with chills. On examination, her left breast is tender and red with raised local temperature. What should be the line of management?
options: Analgesics and antibiotics, plenty of fluids, breastfeeding continued from right breast
Hot fomentation, analgesics, restricted fluids, avoid breastfeeding from either breast
Antibiotics, incision and drainage, avoid breastfeeding from either breast
Antibiotics, analgesics, restricted fluids, breastfeeding continued from right breast
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Analgesics and antibiotics, plenty of fluids, breastfeeding continued from right breast

The presentation is most consistent with acute puerperal mastitis:

• Day 8 postpartum
• Fever with chills
• Painful, tender breast
• Redness and increased local temperature

Management includes:

• Antibiotics → Treat bacterial mastitis, commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus.
• Analgesics → Relieve pain and inflammation.
• Adequate fluids → Maintain hydration.
• Continue breastfeeding → Breastfeeding should generally be continued because milk stasis worsens mastitis. Feeding/pumping from the affected breast is also usually encouraged if tolerated.

Why not the other options?

• (b) Restricted fluids and stopping breastfeeding are incorrect; both can worsen milk stasis.
• (c) Incision and drainage is indicated for a breast abscess, not uncomplicated mastitis. Breastfeeding usually does not need to be stopped.
• (d) Restricted fluids are inappropriate.

questions.text: The incidence of a disease is 4 per 1000 of the population with an average duration of 2 years. What is the prevalence?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 8/1000

The prevelance in the given situation is 8/1000 population.

Prevalence is given by the formula :

Prevalance = Incidence x Mean Duration

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is the mechanism of action of Rivaroxaban ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Factor Xa inhibition

Rivaroxaban is an oral direct factor Xa inhibitor. They represent a new class of oral anticoagulant drugs that do not require monitoring.

This group of drugs inhibit factor Xa in the final common pathway of clotting [conversion of Prothrombin (Factor II) to thrombin (Factor IIa)]. They are given as fixed doses and have a rapid onset of action.

Oral direct factor Xa inhibitors are indicated in:

* Prevention of embolic stroke in patients with atrial fibrillation (without valvular heart disease)

* Venous thromboembolic disease (VTE)

* Postoperative thromboprophylaxis in patients undergoing hip and knee arthroplasty

Direct factor Xa inhibitors:

* Rivaroxaban

* Apixaban

* Edoxaban

* Betrixaban

Parenteral direct thrombin inhibitors:

* Bivalirudin

* Argatroban

* Desirud

Note: The FDA recently approved the drug Apixaban for a new indication. The drug is now used to reduce the risk of stroke and systemic embolism in patients with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation.

Pearl PF0414: Classification of Anticoagulants

Classification of Anticoagulants

1) Vitamin K antagonist

Warfarin

2) Direct thrombin inhibitors (DTI)
Oral DTI

Dabigatran

Parenteral DTI

Monovalent DTI- Argatroban

Bivalent DTI- Lepirudin, Desirudin, Bivalirudin

3) Indirect thrombin inhibitors
Unfractionated heparin

Low molecular weight heparins

Enoxaparin, Dalteparin, Tinzaparin

Fondaparinux

4) Direct Oral Factor Xa Inhibitors
Rivaroxaban, Apixaban, Edoxaban, Betrixaban

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 15-year-old boy undergoes bilateral adrenalectomy for phaeochromocytoma. On the third postoperative day, the boy feels lethargic and tired. Blood pressure is 80/60 mm Hg, there is no sign of bleed. What could be the cause of this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Addisonian crisis

The given clinical scenario of hypotension with no presence of bleeding and bilateral adrenalectomy is suggestive of an Addisonian crisis. It is a life-threatening condition caused due to sudden insufficiency of adrenal hormones.

Acute adrenal insufficiency (adrenal or addisonian's crisis) is a medical emergency caused due to a precipitating illness unmasking insufficiency or trauma or severe sepsis causing adrenal hemorrhage (Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome) or surgical removal of the glands. It presents with non-specific symptoms such as shock with fever, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, hypocalcemia and electrolyte imbalances. It may be often misdiagnosed as an acute abdominal emergency.

Adrenal insufficiency can be primary (due to adrenal pathology), secondary (due to pituitary pathology- lack of ACTH) or tertiary (due to hypothalamus pathology- lack of CRH).

Autoimmune adrenalitis is the most common cause of primary adrenal insufficiency worldwide.

Tuberculosis is the most common cause of primary adrenal insufficiency in India.

Adrenal crisis requires immediate intervention owing to its high mortality rate. Immediate rehydration is initiated with a saline infusion at 1 litre/hr with continuous cardiac monitoring. Glucocorticoid replacement is initiated with an initial bolus injection of hydrocortisone 100 mg followed by 200 mg over 24 hours, preferably by continuous infusion or alternatively by IV or IM injections. Mineralocorticoid replacement is initiated once the daily dose of hydrocortisone has been reduced to <50 mg, since hydrocortisone at higher doses provides sufficient stimulation of mineralocorticoids.
questions.learning: Addisonian crisis — The given clinical scenario of hypotension with no presence of bleeding and bilateral adrenalectomy is suggestive of an Addisonian crisis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is shown in the given image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sebaceous cyst

The image shows a dark-colored summit over a swelling, usually seen in a sebaceous cyst.

Sebaceous cysts are the retention cysts of the sebaceous gland that are usually present on the face, scalp, or scrotum. They contain yellowish-white cheesy material with fat and epithelium.

Clinical features:

• The swelling is painless, soft, and freely mobile.
• Though non-transilluminating, they are Paget's test positive (fluctuant).
• Punctum is seen in 70% of the patients with sebaceous cysts. They are dark in color due to the accumulation of denuded epithelium.
• They also have an unpleasant sebum odor.
• The swelling can ulcerate and become painful (Cock’s peculiar tumor).
• Some cysts over the scalp may also harden over time (Sebaceous horn).
• Many may get infected and lead to abscess formation.

Treatment:

• Excision including skin adjacent to punctum using elliptical incision-dissection method.
• Incision and avulsion of cyst wall.
• In the presence of an abscess, an initial treatment with an incision later followed by excision of the cyst

Other options:

Option A: Dermoid cysts present as firm painless subcutaneous nodules and are of 4 types:

1. Sequestration dermoid - sequestration of epithelium during embryological development
2. Tubulodermoid - accumulation of secretions from ectodermal tube/duct
3. Implantation dermoid - implantation of the epidermis due to trauma
4. Teratomatous dermoid - having all 3 germ layers (ecto, meso, and endoderm)

Option C: Meningiomas are benign tumors arising from the meningothelial cells of the dura. They present with headaches, seizures, or focal neurological deficits.

Option D: Postauricular cutaneous mastoid fistula is a rare complication of chronic otitis media that heals very slowly and needs surgical closure.
questions.learning: Sebaceous cyst — The image shows a dark-colored summit over a swelling, usually seen in a sebaceous cyst. Sebaceous cysts are the retention cysts of the sebaceous gland that are usually present on the face, scalp, or scrotum.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn child is having respiratory difficulty. The doctor evaluated and the child was found to have a posterolateral defect as shown in the CT image below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bochdalek hernia

The clinical presentation of a newborn with respiratory distress and a posterolateral defect, as seen on the CT scan, suggests a diagnosis of Bochdalek hernia.

A diaphragmatic hernia occurs due to intrathoracic movement of the abdominal contents through a diaphragmatic defect. The types include:

* Bochdalek hernia (posterior): Most common type. Herniation occurs through the pleuroperitoneal foramen.

* Morgagni hernia (anterior): Herniation occurs through the foramen of Morgagni.

Clinical features :

* Respiratory distress is a cardinal sign in infants with a congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH). Early respiratory distress, within 6 hr after birth, is thought to be a poor prognostic sign.

* Children with CDH may also have a scaphoid abdomen and increased chest wall diameter.

* Bowel sounds may also be heard in the chest, with a bilateral decrease in breath sounds.

* The point of maximal cardiac impulse may be displaced away from the side of a hernia if a mediastinal shift has occurred.

* Retroperitoneal fat, left kidney, spleen or only the omentum commonly herniates through the defect. If the defect is large, most abdominal contents including the stomach may herniate.

Diagnosis:

* Chest radiography and passage of a nasal gastric tube confirm the diagnosis.

* CDH can be diagnosed on prenatal ultrasonography (between 16 and 24 weeks of gestation)

* High-speed fetal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can further define the lesion.

Treatment:

Variable period of time (24-72 hours) to allow for stabilization before surgical repair. Immediate respiratory support should be provided, including rapid endotracheal intubation and sedation.

Bag and Mask Ventilation is contraindicated in newborns with congenital diaphragmatic hernia because it causes distension of the stomach which in turn may limit the expansion of the already hypoplastic lung.

Other options:

Option B: A traumatic hernia occurs when an injury to the abdominal wall or diaphragm results in the protrusion of internal organs. It often develops after blunt or penetrating trauma and may require surgical repair depending on the severity.

Option C: Morgagni hernia is the defect at the anteromedial location. It is rarer than Bochdalek hernia and accounts for only 2-5% of CDH. About 90% of the cases occur on the right side. It is less symptomatic and the diagnosis is usually delayed until childhood. The patient presents with respiratory or upper GI symptoms. Respiratory symptoms like distress, tachypnea, and recurrent pulmonary infections are common in children. Other symptoms are abdominal pain, dyspnea, flatulence, and indigestion.

Radiographic findings

* Radiolucent para cardiac shadow may be seen retrosternal on lateral chest x-ray if there is bowel herniation.

* Rounded opacity in the right cardiophrenic angle may be seen if there is herniation of the omentum or solid organs. (Shown below)

Option D: A hiatal hernia occurs when a portion of the stomach pushes through the diaphragm into the chest cavity. It can cause symptoms such as heartburn, regurgitation, and chest pain, and may require medical or surgical treatment.
questions.learning: Bochdalek hernia — The clinical presentation of a newborn with respiratory distress and a posterolateral defect, as seen on the CT scan, suggests a diagnosis of Bochdalek hernia.

questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All of the following are examples of primary active transport except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. SGLT

Primary active transport directly utilizes energy from ATP hydrolysis to move substances against their electrochemical gradient. In contrast, secondary active transport uses the energy stored in an ion gradient (usually Na⁺) that was generated by primary active transport.

• SGLT (Sodium-Glucose Linked Transporter) does not directly use ATP.
• It transports glucose against its concentration gradient by utilizing the Na⁺ gradient created by the Na⁺-K⁺-ATPase.
• Therefore, SGLT is a secondary active transporter, not a primary active transporter.

| Primary Active Transport | Secondary Active Transport

| ------------------------ | --------------------------

| Direct ATP use | Indirect ATP use

| Na⁺-K⁺-ATPase | SGLT

| H⁺-K⁺-ATPase | Na⁺-amino acid cotransporter

| Ca²⁺-ATPase | Na⁺-Ca²⁺ exchanger

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text:
True regarding POAG:

A. Abnormality of the trabecular meshwork is seen on gonioscopy
B. Family members are likely to develop steroid responsiveness.
C. Dilatation of the pupil is associated with exacerbation of IOP
D. First degree relatives are at 1% increased risk of POAG
E. Visual field defect can exist with normal C:D ratio
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. B and E only

In primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG), family members are likely to develop steroid responsiveness (statement B) and visual field defect can exist with a normal C:D ratio (statement E).

Statement A: Gonioscopy cannot visualize the specific abnormalities that occur in the trabecular meshwork in POAG. Gonioscopy diagnoses POAG because of the visibility of all the structures of the angle of the anterior chamber in contrast to the non-visibility of different structures in angle closure glaucoma.

Statement C: Primary angle-closure glaucoma is associated with exacerbation of IOP with pupillary dilatation and not POAG.

Statement D: There is a 10% increased risk of POAG in siblings and a 4% increased risk in children of patients with POAG.

POAG also known as chronic simple glaucoma of adult-onset is characterized by the presence of any 2 of the following 3 categories of changes:

• Increased intraocular pressure:

• IOP >21mmHg on more than one occasion, and/or
• Circadian variation in IOP of >8 mmHg, or
• Asymmetry in IOP > 5 mmHg between both eyes

• Optic nerve head changes suggestive of glaucomatous damage. These may include one or more of the following changes:

• Vertically oval cup
• Cup-disc (C:D) ratio > 0.6 (average cup: disc ratio 0.3-0.4)
• Asymmetry in C:D ratio > 0.2 between both eyes.
• Narrowing, notching, or pallor of the neuroretinal rim.
• Disc haemorrhages
• Nasal shifting of retinal vessels-Bayonetting sign
• Lamellar dot sign

• Visual field changes - isopter contraction, barring of blind spot, paracentral scotoma, Seidel's scotoma, Bjerrum's scotoma, double arcuate scotoma, and Roenne's central nasal step.

A patient presenting with just raised IOP and visual field defects with normal optic nerve head findings such as a normal C:D ratio can still be diagnosed as POAG (statement E).
questions.learning: B and E only — In primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG), family members are likely to develop steroid responsiveness (statement B) and visual field defect can exist with a normal C:D ratio (statement E).

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Give the diagnosis of the condition shown in the image given below.
questions.explanation: The provided clinical image shows a child with an abnormally high-riding, undescended scapula on one side. This congenital condition is known as Sprengel's deformity (Option D). It occurs due to the failure of the scapula to descend from its embryonic cervical position to its final thoracic position. It is often associated with a bony or fibrous "omovertebral" bar and limited shoulder abduction. Ankylosing spondylitis (Option A) is a systemic inflammatory disease of the spine and SI joints. Facioscapulohumeral dystrophy (Option B) is a muscular dystrophy that would show scapular "winging" due to muscle weakness rather than a high-riding bone. Cervical fracture (Option C) would present with acute pain and trauma history. Sprengel's deformity is often part of the Klippel-Feil syndrome. Surgical intervention (like the Woodward or Green procedure) is used to improve both cosmetics and function. Thus, the undescended scapula is diagnostic
questions.learning: The provided clinical image shows a child with an abnormally high-riding, undescended scapula on one side. This congenital condition is known as Sprengel's deformity (Option D).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 51-year-old woman reports a palpable lump in her right breast discovered during a routine examination. The mass measures more than 5 cm, and ipsilateral axillary lymph nodes are palpable. If the lesion is confirmed to be malignant, what is the most likely stage of the disease?
questions.explanation: Breast cancer staging follows the TNM (Tumor, Node, Metastasis) system. In this clinical scenario, a tumor mass measuring over 5 cm is classified as T3. The presence of "palpable lymph nodes" in the "ipsilateral axilla" that are clinically suspicious signifies N1 status. The prefix "c" denotes "clinical" staging based on examination and imaging before surgery. Therefore, the likely clinical stage is cT3N1M0. Option C (cT4) is incorrect because T4 requires invasion into the chest wall or skin (e.g., ulceration, peau d'orange) regardless of size. Options B and D use the prefix "y," which denotes staging after neoadjuvant therapy (post-treatment staging), which has not occurred in this patient yet. Assuming no evidence of distant metastasis (M0), the findings of size >5cm and positive axillary nodes lead directly to the cT3N1M0 classification, placing the patient in Stage IIIA
questions.learning: Breast cancer staging follows the TNM (Tumor, Node, Metastasis) system. In this clinical scenario, a tumor mass measuring over 5 cm is classified as T3.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Identify the histopathological image.
questions.explanation: The histology shows islands and nests of small, dark-blue basaloid cells invading the dermis. The diagnostic feature present is peripheral palisading, where the nuclei of the outermost layer of cells in the nest are arranged in a neat, parallel row. This appearance is the hallmark of Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC), the most common type of skin cancer. Squamous cell carcinoma (Option B) is characterized by keratin pearls and intercellular bridges. Adenocarcinoma (Option C) would demonstrate glandular structures and mucin production. Malignant melanoma (Option D) would show highly atypical melanocytes with prominent nucleoli, often containing melanin pigment. BCC is slow-growing and rarely metastasizes but can be locally destructive, earning it the name "rodent ulcer." It most commonly occurs on sun-exposed areas of the face, particularly the nose. Identifying these discrete microscopic patterns is fundamental for pathology and the clinical management of common cutaneous tumors

questions.text: Identify the correct statements regarding HPV vaccination: 1. Primary target group = girls 9– 14 years 2. It is recommended to give single dose by both WHO and national guidelines in targeted age group 3. Target coverage is 90% of eligible girls 4. Provides complete protection
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 3 only

1. Primary target group = girls 9– 14 years: Correct.

• WHO target: Girls aged 9– 14 years

2. It is recommended to give single dose by both WHO and national guidelines in targeted age group: Correct.

• Current WHO recommendations and GOI guidelines support: single-dose HPV vaccination in males and females upto 21 years, and 2 doses following that.

3. Target coverage is 90% of eligible girls: Correct.

• WHO cervical cancer elimination target: 90% - 70% - 90%
•

Pillar 1: 90% HPV Vaccination

•

WHO's updated single-dose recommendation (2022):

• WHO SAGE (Strategic Advisory Group of Experts) reviewed evidence and concluded that one dose provides comparable efficacy to 2– 3 doses in girls aged 9– 14
• This simplifies logistics and reduces cost, critical for low-middle income countries (LMICs)

•

Pillar 2: 70% Screening

• 70% of women screened with a high-performance test by age 35, and again by age 45

Screening Intervals

| Strategy | Interval

| -------- | --------

| Co-testing | Every 5 years

questions.text: A 6-year-old boy has recently started telling his full name, although he cannot recite a poem. His Developmental Quotient (DQ) in the language sphere is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 50%

Developmental Quotient (DQ) is used to assess a child’s developmental progress and is calculated as:

DQ = (Developmental Age ÷ Chronological Age) × 100

A 6-year-old child (72 months) who has just started telling his full name has a language developmental age of approximately 3 years (36 months). Therefore:

DQ = (3 ÷ 6) × 100 = 50%

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient who sustained blunt abdominal trauma after a road accident is admitted to the ICU overnight. He is hemodynamically stable. On abdominal examination, he now has tenderness, rigidity, and rebound tenderness. Which is the next best step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Laparotomy

• In blunt abdominal trauma, management is guided primarily by hemodynamic status and the presence or absence of peritonitis.
• Although stable patients are often observed or evaluated with imaging, the development of tenderness with rigidity and rebound tenderness indicates peritonitis, strongly suggesting a hollow viscus injury (eg, bowel perforation) or ongoing intra-abdominal contamination/bleeding.
• Investigations like eFAST or diagnostic peritoneal lavage (DPL) are used when the diagnosis is unclear, especially in unstable patients.
• However, in a patient who has clear peritoneal signs, imaging tests should not delay definitive treatment.
• Therefore, the next best step is immediate exploratory laparotomy (Option A).

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: The following findings were noted during the autopsy of a patient with a gunshot injury. What is the likely range of the gunshot?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Close range

The likely range of the gunshot injury shown above is close range, characterized by a circular wound with blackening and tattooing.

To determine the range of firing, the following parameters are used:

• The entry wound size and shape
• Blast effect – Muzzle end imprint and edge eversion
• Blackening, Tattooing, Singeing of hair, Abrasion collar, and Grease collar
• Hair should be preserved to determine the range of firing which can be examined for carbonization/desiccation in close range, also from lead deposition around the wound to assess the range of firing.

Blackening occurs due to the deposit of smoke and can be removed with a wet cloth. This can be seen up to around 15 cm of firing. Whereas, tattooing occurs due to the deposition of unburnt powder particles and are difficult to remove. They are also called stippling or peppering. This is seen up to 50 cm of firing.

Abrasion collar: Gyroscopic movement of the bullet, the skin's elasticity, and the grease and dirt particles on the bullet's surface are the major causative factors of abrasion and grease collar. They are seen on the skin around the wound of entry at all ranges. Depending on the angle of entry made by the bullet, i.e.

• A perpendicular entry of the bullet develops the abrasion collar of a rounded shape.
• An acute angular entry of the bullet develops the abrasion collar of an oblique or oval shape.
• Some contusion present in the abraded collar is known as contusion collar

Grease collar: Mostly seen on the clothing and is seen as a black deposit, sharply outlined as if printed (better seen on light colour clothes and fair-skinned individuals). Its medicolegal importance is that it helps derive information such as entry wound and direction of firing.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the structure marked in the CT scan ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cribriform plate

The structure marked in the image is the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone. The image shown is a coronal section of paranasal sinuses at the level of anterior ethmoidal cells.

The cribriform plate is identified as a bony structure that separates the nasal cavity from the anterior cranial fossa. It is part of the ethmoid bone and is a sieve-like structure as it is pierced by the olfactory nerve fibers.

Crista Galli is also a part of ethmoid bone that projects superiorly from the cribriform plate. It provides attachment for the falx cerebri.

The anterior ethmoidal canal is identified by its location below the roof of ethmoidal air cells. The anterior ethmoidal artery passes through this canal and it is important to identify this to avoid bleeding from this vessel during sinus surgeries.

The posterior ethmoid canal/foramen is an opening in the ethmoid bone through which the posterior ethmoidal artery, vein, and nerve traverse. It is not visualized in this image as it is a coronal section at the level of anterior ethmoidal cells.

The optic nerve can be identified as an oval intraorbital structure in the coronal sections.
questions.learning: Cribriform plate — The structure marked in the image is the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone. The image shown is a coronal section of paranasal sinuses at the level of anterior ethmoidal cells.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the artery marked by blue arrow.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Superior mesenteric artery

The artery marked by the blue arrow is the superior mesenteric artery (SMA), which gives rise to various branches that supply the small intestines, cecum, ascending, and part of the transverse colon.

The CT also depicts nutcracker syndrome, a left renal vein entrapment syndrome characterized by extrinsic compression of the left renal vein (marked by a red arrow), most commonly between the abdominal aorta and superior mesenteric artery. This syndrome is one of the postulated reasons for left-sided varicoceles being more common than the right side.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An elderly male who presented with the following lesion as shown, is diagnosed with stage T3 carcinoma with no clinically palpable inguinal lymph nodes. What is the management strategy for this patient?
options: Penectomy + Superficial inguinal lymph node dissection
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Penectomy + Superficial inguinal lymph node dissection

The most appropriate management for this patient with stage T3 carcinoma of the penis with no clinically palpable inguinal lymph nodes is penectomy with superficial inguinal lymph node dissection.

In penile carcinoma, total amputation of the penis is done if the stump is < 2cm after resection of the tumour and partial penectomy is done if the stump is >2cm. Carcinoma of the penis is commonly a squamous cell carcinoma. It arises from the skin of the glans penis or the prepuce. The lesion can be flat or warty in appearance.

• T1- confined to the skin
• T2- invades the corpus spongiosum or cavernosum.
• T3- invades the urethra
• T4- invades adjacent structures.

The first lymph node to be involved is the superficial inguinal lymph node and thus, superficial inguinal lymph node dissection or sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) helps evaluate the spread of penile cancer.

Tumours of low-grade and low-stage are managed by Mohs’ surgery. Tumors involving the glans penis require glansectomy, and in advanced cases require partial penectomy.
questions.learning: Penectomy + Superficial inguinal lymph node dissection The most appropriate management for this patient with stage T3 carcinoma of the penis with no clinically palpable inguinal lymph nodes is penectomy with superficial inguinal lymph node dissection.

Thus cadmium 0.3 mg/L exceeds the safe limit by \~100 times.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50-year-old male presents to the emergency with a BP of 160/100 mmHg and a heart rate of 120. CECT done reveals a Stanford A aortic dissection. What is the initial management of this given condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Beta blocker medication

The initial management of patients with all types of aortic dissection is beta blocker medication to control hypertension along with pain management. Patients with Stanford Type A (DeBakey Types I and II) will require surgical intervention once the patient's blood pressure is stabilized.

Aortic dissection occurs when a defect or flap occurs in the intima of the aorta.

Predisposing factors:

1. Age
2. Hypertension
3. Marfan syndrome
4. Pregnancy
5. Other connective tissue disorders, for example, Ehlers–Danlos syndrome, giant cell arteritis, systemic lupus erythematosus
6. Coarctation of the aorta
7. Turner or Noonan syndromes
8. Aortic cannulation site (iatrogenic).

The most typical presentation of aortic dissection is a tearing interscapular pain. The dissection may also result in aortic wall rupture into the pericardium (cardiac tamponade) or mediastinum (left haemothorax).

Contrast-enhanced CT is currently the most preferred imaging modality for aortic dissection. Double-lumen aorta is seen on CECT. Transesophageal echocardiography is preferred for patients who are unstable for transportation.

Acute aortic dissection can be classified by the original DeBakey system, based on the location of the proximal tear and distal extent of the dissection flap, or the Stanford system which uses the location of the proximal tear alone.

Management of aortic dissection:

The initial management of patients with all types of aortic dissection is beta-blocker medication to control hypertension along with pain management. The preferred beta-blocker drug is esmolol. Hemodynamic stability is an important consideration.

• Stanford Type A (DeBakey Types I and II) requires surgical intervention once the patient's blood pressure is stabilized.
• Stanford Type B (DeBakey type III) is best managed by antihypertensive drugs. For patients with complicated type B dissection, percutaneously placed endovascular stents are currently preferred. Surgery is reserved for the rare patients not suitable for stenting.

Other options:

Options B and D: Low molecular weight heparin and vitamin K inhibitors are contraindicated in aortic dissection as they can worsen the risk of bleeding.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following is correctly matched regarding classification of portal hypertension according to site of vascular obstruction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pre-hepatic presinusoidal – Portal vein thrombosis

Portal hypertension is defined as an increase in the hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) >5 mmHg (clinically significant when ≥10 mmHg). It is classified according to the site of vascular obstruction into pre-hepatic, intrahepatic (presinusoidal, sinusoidal, postsinusoidal), and post-hepatic causes.

Portal vein thrombosis is the classic example of pre-hepatic presinusoidal portal hypertension.

Why not the other options?

• A. Sinusoidal – Veno-occlusive disease: Veno-occlusive disease (sinusoidal obstruction syndrome) is a postsinusoidal intrahepatic cause, not sinusoidal.
• C. Intrahepatic presinusoidal – Cirrhosis: Cirrhosis is the most common cause of sinusoidal portal hypertension, not presinusoidal.
• D. Post-hepatic postsinusoidal – Schistosomiasis:

• Schistosomiasis causes intrahepatic presinusoidal portal hypertension due to periportal fibrosis.
• Post-hepatic causes include Budd-Chiari syndrome, inferior vena cava obstruction, and constrictive pericarditis.
questions.learning: Pre-hepatic presinusoidal – Portal vein thrombosis Portal hypertension is defined as an increase in the hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) >5 mmHg (clinically significant when ≥10 mmHg).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A female patient presents with complaints of pain over the anterolateral aspect of thigh after normal vaginal delivery. Which is the nerve injured in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lateral cutaneous nerve

The given clinical scenario of a patient with symptoms of pain over the anterolateral aspect of the thigh is suggestive of meralgia paresthetica. It is due to compression neuropathy or neuroma of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve of the thigh.

The lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh arises from the posterior divisions of the ventral rami of L2 and L3, and it supplies the skin of the anterior and lateral surfaces of the thigh up to the knee.

It is prone to injury especially as it leaves the pelvis deep to the inguinal ligament just medial to the anterior superior iliac spine. The angulation of the nerve as it crosses the iliac crest makes it vulnerable to compression during hip extension which may increase angulation and tension on the nerve. This leads to impaired sensation, pain and paraesthesia on the anterolateral aspect of thigh, in the distal end of the cutaneous distribution of this nerve. The symptoms don't cross the midline, nor extend below knee or behind hamstrings laterally

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which among the following instruments is not used in the Sahli's method of hemoglobin estimation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. D

Option D is RBC pipette, it is not used in Sahli's method of hemoglobin estimation. The instruments used are comparator with brown glass standard(Option A), graduated hemoglobin tube(Option B), Sahli's pipette (Option C)and stirrer.

Sahli's method of estimation of hemoglobin is based on colorimetric measurement of the intensity of color developed on the addition of dilute hydrochloric acid (N/10 HCl) reagent to the blood.

In Sahli's method, hemoglobin is converted to acid hematin with the action of dilute hydrochloric acid (N/10 HCl). The brown color of the acid hematin is matched to its intensity with a standard brown glass comparator in a visual colorimeter called Sahli’s colorimeter. It can be used to estimate oxyHb and reduced Hb.

Sahli's method is a simple bedside test and is cost-effective. However, it has some disadvantages, which include visual errors, the inability to measure other forms of hemoglobin like carboxyhemoglobin, methemoglobin, and sulfhemoglobin, fading of the comparator over time, and the color of acid hematin fading quickly.

The visual error can be reduced by taking the average of three readings; first, when the color is slightly darker than the standard; second, when the color exactly matches the standard; and third, when the color is slightly lighter than the standard.
questions.learning: D Option D is RBC pipette, it is not used in Sahli's method of hemoglobin estimation. The instruments used are comparator with brown glass standard(Option A), graduated hemoglobin tube(Option B), Sahli's pipette (Option C)and stirrer.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A deceased male was posted for a post-mortem examination. His relatives reported that he had a tattoo over his skin, which was not found during the autopsy. Which of the following would you examine to determine the absence of his tattoo?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lymph nodes

The lymph nodes should be examined in this case.

Some amount of material or dye used for creating tattoo marks is transported through lymph to the regional lymph nodes.

A faded tattoo mark can be visualized by:

* Ultraviolet light

* Infrared photography

* Rubbing the part and examining it with a magnifying lens

In decomposed bodies, the tattoo marks can be visualized by removing the epidermis with a moist cloth. The lymph nodes near a tattoo mark also show a deposit of the pigment.

Hence in cases where a tattoo mark has disappeared naturally or has been removed, the lymph nodes must be examined before making any conclusions.
questions.learning: Lymph nodes — The lymph nodes should be examined in this case. Some amount of material or dye used for creating tattoo marks is transported through lymph to the regional lymph nodes.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 76 year-old female presented with a non-healing ulcer on the labia majora for a period of 6 months, measuring 2 cm x 3 cm. No lymph nodes were palpable. Biopsy shows squamous cell carcinoma. How do you manage this case?
options: Total vulvectomy with unilateral LN dissection
Partial vulvectomy with ipsilateral inguinofemoral LN dissection
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Partial vulvectomy with ipsilateral inguinofemoral LN dissection

According to the recent FIGO guidelines,the patient’s lesion measuring 2 cm x 3 cm with no palpable lymph nodes falls under stage Ib vulval cancer and it's management is partial vulvectomy with ipsilateral inguinofemoral lymph node dissection.

For stage IB cancers, radical partial vulvectomy is recommended for the primary tumor and as the women with stage IB cancer can have diseased lymph nodes even without palpable enlargement of nodes, Sentinel Lymph Node Biopsy (SLNB) and/ inguinofemoral lymphadenectomy is performed.

Ipsilateral dissection of lymph nodes is performed if the vulvar lesion is present laterally, >2cm beyond the midline. In cases where the vulvar lesion lies within 2 cm from the midline, bilateral inguinofemoral Lymph Node dissection will be performed.

In this patient, the best management would be to perform Partial vulvectomy with ipsilateral inguinofemoral LN dissection among the given options.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which neurotransmitter is responsible for anterograde dilatation of the small intestine?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. VIP

VIP is responsible for anterograde dilatation of the small intestine.

Peristalsis involves the contraction of a segment of intestine behind the bolus of food and relaxation of a segment of the intestine in front of the bolus of food.

Cholinergic neurons passing in anterograde direction produce NO and VIP which cause relaxation of a segment of the intestine in front of the bolus.

Cholinergic neurons passing in retrograde direction produce substance P and acetylcholine which cause contraction of a segment of the intestine behind the bolus.

Note: In achalasia cardia, there is decreased release of NO and VIP in the distal part of the esophagus.
questions.learning: VIP VIP is responsible for anterograde dilatation of the small intestine. Peristalsis involves the contraction of a segment of intestine behind the bolus of food and relaxation of a segment of the intestine in front of the bolus of food.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presented with complaints of itching and discharges on flexure aspect of elbow and the lesions were red as shown below. What is your diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Atopic dermatitis

The presence of diffuse, erythematous, itchy plaques on the flexural aspects of the elbow of a child is suggestive of atopic dermatitis.

Atopic dermatitis is the cutaneous manifestation of atopy, characterized by a family history of asthma, allergic rhinitis, or eczema.

There is a clear genetic predisposition. A characteristic defect is an impaired epidermal barrier. In many patients a mutation in the gene encoding filaggrin (a structural protein in the stratum granulosum) is responsible.

Patients may display many immunoregulatory abnormalities, including increased IgE synthesis, increased serum IgE levels, and delayed-type hypersensitivity reactions.

The disease progresses in three phases: Infantile, childhood, and adult.

In infants, the lesions of atopic eczema most frequently start on the face but may occur anywhere on the skin surface. Often, the napkin area is relatively spared. When the child begins to crawl, the exposed surfaces, especially the extensor aspect of the knees and elbows are most involved. The lesions consist of erythema and discrete or confluent oedematous papules. The papules are intensely itchy and may become exudative and crusted as a result of rubbing. Secondary infection and lymphadenopathy are common.

From 18 to 24 months onwards (childhood phase), the sites most characteristically involved are the elbow and knee flexures, a mixture of erythema, crusting, excoriation, hyper and hypopigmentation, and warty lichenification may be seen depending on the skin type on the sides of the neck, wrists, and ankles. The sides of the neck may show reticulate pigmentation, sometimes referred to as an atopic dirty neck. The erythematous and oedematous papules tend to be replaced by lichenification.

The picture in adults is essentially similar to that in later childhood, with lichenification, especially of the flexures and hands.
questions.learning: Atopic dermatitis — The presence of diffuse, erythematous, itchy plaques on the flexural aspects of the elbow of a child is suggestive of atopic dermatitis.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Spontaneous respiratory effort

The curare notch in the plateau phase of the capnograph indicates that the patient is trying to breathe spontaneously. The patient's inspiratory effort causes some fresh gas to be sucked in the capnometer, resulting in a lower carbon dioxide concentration and a notch.

Image below shows a capnograph with clefts during phase III which indicates spontaneous breathing efforts by the patient during controlled mechanical ventilation. It is also known as a curare notch or cleft.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: All of the following may be used to find the normalcy of data except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mantel-Haenszel test

Mantel-Haenszel method is used to calculate adjusted odds ratio during stratified analysis. It is not a test to detect normalcy of data.

A plot histogram and a box whisker plot are visual methods to assess if a given set of data is distributed normally. A normal distribution curve is an example of a plot histogram.

Sometimes just the visual representation of the data might not be enough to tell whether the data is normally distributed. This is where Shapiro-Wilk test comes in. It examines how closely a given set of data fits a normal distribution. The sample data is first ordered and standardized. An assessment is then made how the sample quantiles fit the standard normal quantiles. Shapiro-Wilk test is commonly used on small samples.

Stratified analysis of the data is done to reduce confounding. In such a scenario, multiple odds ratios are obtained — one for each stratum of the data. These have to be combined to give an adjusted odds ratio. This represents the effect of the exposure adjusted for the confounding factor. Mantel-Haenszel method is used for this purpose.
questions.learning: Mantel-Haenszel test Mantel-Haenszel method is used to calculate adjusted odds ratio during stratified analysis. It is not a test to detect normalcy of data.

questions.text: Deficiency of which of the following mineral(s) can lead to hypocalcemia by impairing the ability of the parathyroid gland to secrete parathyroid hormone? 1. Phosphate 2. Magnesium 3. Sodium 4. Potassium Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2 only

To recognize severe magnesium deficiency as an important cause of hypocalcemia due to impaired PTH secretion and peripheral PTH resistance.

1. Phosphate: Incorrect

• Phosphate excess can cause hypocalcemia by binding calcium, but phosphate deficiency does not impair PTH secretion.

2. Magnesium: Correct

• Severe hypomagnesemia impairs PTH secretion and causes resistance to PTH, resulting in hypocalcemia.

3. Sodium: Incorrect

• Sodium deficiency does not directly impair PTH secretion.

• Potassium deficiency does not cause hypocalcemia by impairing PTH secretion.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What type of ulcer is most likely in a 42-year-old barber with a history of a healed ulcer on the lower medial aspect of the right leg and visible varicose veins in both legs?
questions.explanation: The patient’s occupation (prolonged standing) and the presence of visible varicose veins are major risk factors for chronic venous insufficiency. Venous ulcers (Option C) classically occur in the "gaiter area," specifically on the lower medial aspect of the leg just above the medial malleolus. These ulcers are often preceded by skin changes like lipodermatosclerosis or stasis dermatitis and tend to be shallow and irregularly shaped. Neuropathic ulcers (Option A) occur on pressure points like the sole of the foot, often in diabetic patients. Arterial ulcers (Option B) are located distally on the toes or lateral malleolus and are extremely painful with a "punched-out" appearance. Tubercular ulcers (Option D) are rare on the legs and usually present as undermined, chronic lesions related to underlying lymph node involvement. Given the specific location and the association with varicose veins, a venous etiology is the most probable diagnosis. Compression therapy is the mainstay of management

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: An 18-year-old came with complaints of pain in the abdomen and bleeding PV for the last 2 days. Her last menstrual period was 6 weeks back. On examination, she has hypotension, tachycardia and cervical motion tenderness. Ultrasound of the abdomen shows free fluid in the pouch of Douglas and paracolic gutters. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ruptured ectopic pregnancy

The given clinical scenario with a triad of abdominal pain, amenorrhea and vaginal bleeding, along with the ultrasound findings of free fluid, is suggestive of a ruptured ectopic pregnancy.

An ectopic pregnancy is one in which the fertilized ovum is implanted and develops outside the normal endometrial cavity, with the Fallopian tubes being the most common site. The outcomes of such a pregnancy are varied with tubal rupture and massive intraperitoneal hemorrhage being one of them.

Clinical features :

• The incidence is maximum between the age of 20 and 30 years, the maximum fertility period. The onset is acute. The classic triad of symptoms is - abdominal pain (100%), preceded by amenorrhea of 6-8 weeks(75%), and lastly, the appearance of vaginal bleeding (70%).
• Abdominal pain is the most constant feature. Pain is located in the lower abdomen. Shoulder tip pain (25%) (referred pain due to diaphragmatic irritation from hemoperitoneum) may be present.
• Vomiting, fainting attack. Syncopal attack (10%) is due to reflex vasomotor disturbances following peritoneal irritation from the hemoperitoneum.
• Pallor and features of shock - feeble pulse with tachycardia, hypotension, cold clammy extremities.
• Pelvic examination - Vaginal mucosa is blanched white; uterus seems normal in size or slightly bulky; extreme tenderness on fornix palpation(75%).

Investigations :

Estimation of ß-hCG - The findings suggestive of ectopic are a lower concentration of hCG compared to normal intrauterine pregnancy, and doubling in plasma failing to occur in 2 days.

Sonography: Transvaginal sonography (TVS) is more informative. The diagnostic features are

• Absence of intrauterine pregnancy with a positive pregnancy test.
• Fluid (echogenic) in the pouch of Douglas.
• Adnexal mass clearly separated from the ovary (Blob sign).

Color Doppler sonography can identify the placental shape (ring-of-fire pattern) and enhanced blood flow pattern outside the uterine cavity.

Management of ruptured ectopic :

The principle in the management is resuscitation and laparotomy, and not resuscitation followed by laparotomy. Salpingectomy is the definitive surgery.

Other options :

Option A - Placenta previa is a type of antepartum hemorrhage occurring after 28 weeks of pregnancy. It presents as sudden onset painless, recurrent vaginal bleeding. USG findings reveal placenta occupying the lower segment of uterus.

Option B - Abruptio placenta is another form of antepartum hemorrhage occurring due to premature separation of the normally situated placenta. The majority of cases occur in the third trimester. The clinical features vary depending on whether the hemorrhage is concealed or revealed and include abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding. Ultrasound reveals a collection of blood in the retroplacental, subchorionic or preplacental region.

Option D - Missed abortion refers to when the fetus is dead and retained inside the uterus. Clinical features include the persistence of brownish vaginal discharge and subsidence of pregnancy symptoms. Examination findings are uterus size smaller than the period of gestation and closed cervical os. USG reveals an empty sac or a fetus without cardiac activity.
questions.learning: Ruptured ectopic pregnancy — The given clinical scenario with a triad of abdominal pain, amenorrhea and vaginal bleeding, along with the ultrasound findings of free fluid, is suggestive of a ruptured ectopic pregnancy.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 25-year-old man presents with recurrent urinary tract infections and progressively worsening difficulty in urination. Ultrasonography indicates a urinary tract obstruction, and further evaluation is planned to precisely determine the site and severity of obstruction before surgery. In which of the following conditions is the Whitaker test most appropriately indicated?
questions.explanation: The Whitaker test is a specialized invasive urodynamic procedure used to differentiate between a mechanically obstructed and a dilated, non-obstructed urinary system (Option A). It is most appropriately applied in patients with persistent hydronephrosis or hydroureter where non-invasive tests, such as a diuretic renogram, are inconclusive. The test involves placing a percutaneous needle into the renal pelvis and measuring the pressure required to drive fluid through the ureter at a constant rate. If the pressure gradient between the renal pelvis and the bladder is high, mechanical obstruction is confirmed. Posterior urethral valves (Option B), urethral atresia (Option C), and urethral strictures (Option D) are obstructions of the lower urinary tract that are typically diagnosed through voiding cystourethrography (VCUG) or cystoscopy rather than upper tract pressure studies . Therefore, the Whitaker test is specifically reserved for assessing complex cases of upper-tract dilation
questions.learning: The Whitaker test is a specialized invasive urodynamic procedure used to differentiate between a mechanically obstructed and a dilated, non-obstructed urinary system (Option A).

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient is brought to the emergency department following a road traffic accident. He has sustained bilateral fractures of both the femur and tibia. On examination, he is hypotensive, and London sign is positive in the right flank. After hemodynamic stabilization, what is the next best step in management?
options: External fixation of the femur and nailing of the tibia
External fixation of the tibia and nailing of the femur
External fixation of both the femur and tibia
Definitive nailing or plating based on the surgeon’s preference
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. External fixation of both the femur and tibia

Damage Control Orthopedics (DCO) is the preferred strategy for polytrauma patients with physiological instability or major associated injuries. The initial goal is rapid temporary stabilization of fractures using external fixation, thereby minimizing the “second hit” inflammatory response until the patient is fit for definitive fixation.

• This patient has:

• Bilateral femoral and tibial fractures (multiple long-bone fractures)
• Hypotension (hemodynamic instability)
• Positive London sign (suggesting significant retroperitoneal/associated trauma)

• Such patients are managed with Damage Control Orthopedics, where external fixation of both the femur and tibia is performed as temporary stabilization.

Why not the other options?

• A. External fixation of the femur and nailing of the tibia: Definitive fixation of one bone is avoided in unstable polytrauma patients.
• B. External fixation of the tibia and nailing of the femur: Intramedullary nailing can exacerbate the inflammatory response (“second hit”) in unstable patients.
• D. Definitive nailing or plating: Reserved for hemodynamically stable patients after adequate resuscitation (Early Total Care).
questions.learning: External fixation of both the femur and tibia Damage Control Orthopedics (DCO) is the preferred strategy for polytrauma patients with physiological instability or major associated injuries.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The RNA molecule contains the coding sequence 5' AACACCACAC 3'. What will be the corresponding DNA sequence in the template strand from which it was transcribed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 4

The RNA molecule contains the coding sequence 5' AACACCACAC 3', which corresponds to the DNA sequence 3' TTGTGGTGTG 5' in the template strand from which it was transcribed.

According to Chargaff's rule in cellular DNA regardless of species:

* Adenine= Thymine, Guanine = Cytosine

* Sum of purine = Sum of pyrimidines i.e A+G=C+T.

When DNA is transcribed into RNA, the process involves complementary base pairing. Adenine (A) in DNA pairs with thymine (T), but in RNA, thymine is replaced by uracil (U). Similarly, cytosine (C) in DNA pairs with guanine (G) in both DNA and RNA. During transcription, RNA polymerase reads the DNA template and adds complementary RNA nucleotides accordingly.

Note: Unless otherwise specified, all sequences are written in the 5′ to 3′ direction.

Pearl PF0706: Differences between DNA & RNA Synthesis

RNA synthesis

DNA synthesis

Ribonucleotides are used

Deoxyribonucleotides are used

Uracil is the complementary base for Adenine

Thymine is the complementary base for Adenine

Primer is not involved as RNA polymerases have the ability to initiate synthesis de novo

Primer is necessary because DNA polymerases can only attach new DNA nucleotides to an existing strand of nucleotides

Only portions of the genome are vigorously transcribed or copied into RNA

The entire genome must be copied, once and only once during DNA replication

No highly active, efficient proofreading function

Highly active, efficient proofreading function is performed by DNA polymerase
questions.learning: 4 The RNA molecule contains the coding sequence 5' AACACCACAC 3', which corresponds to the DNA sequence 3' TTGTGGTGTG 5' in the template strand from which it was transcribed.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What is the maneuver depicted in the image given below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Trotter’s method

The given image shows Trotter’s method in which the patient is made to sit, leaning a little forward over a basin to spit any blood and breathe quietly from the mouth. It is the first step to control epistaxis.

Other options:

Option A: Epley’s maneuver is used in the treatment of BPPV (Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo).

Option C: McGovern’s technique is used in choanal atresia. A feeding nipple with a large hole provides a good oral airway.

Option D: Valsalva maneuver is performed by forceful attempted exhalation against a closed nose and mouth. It is used as a test of cardiac function and autonomic nervous control of the heart, or to clear the ears and sinuses.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 13 year old male patient presents with unilateral nasal obstruction and recurrent episodes of epistaxis for past 6 months. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma

The most likely diagnosis is juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA), as there is unilateral nasal obstruction and recurrent epistaxis.

Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA) is a highly vascular and locally aggressive tumor seen almost exclusively in adolescent males, associated with significant morbidity and occasional mortality.

Patients usually present with:

• Epistaxis (most common presentation): Profuse, recurrent, and spontaneous
• Mass: A mass may be present in either the postnasal space, resulting in progressive nasal obstruction, or nasopharynx, where it may obstruct both choanae. The mass is firm in consistency, but digital palpation of the same should not be done. If the mass obstructs the eustachian tube, conductive hearing loss and otitis media with effusion may be observed.
• Proptosis, swelling of the cheeks, broadening of nasal bridge, and involvement of 2nd, 3rd, 4th and 6th cranial nerves may occur

JNA can be diagnosed using CT, MRI, and carotid angiography.

Anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus due to the presence of a mass in the pterygomaxillary space is a characteristic CT finding of JNA. This is known as the Holman-Miller sign or antral sign.

Recurrence has been reported up to 35%. Surgical excision is the treatment of choice. Recurrent angiofibroma is treated with revision surgery or radiotherapy when the tumor is inaccessible.
questions.learning: Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma — The most likely diagnosis is juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA), as there is unilateral nasal obstruction and recurrent epistaxis.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In a nerve, why is it impossible to generate a new action potential if a second stimulus is applied during the depolarization phase of the current action potential?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sodium channels are opened

During the absolute refractory period (which corresponds to the depolarization phase and early repolarization of the action potential), voltage-gated sodium (Na⁺) channels are already open or in the inactivated state and cannot be reopened by another stimulus. Therefore, no second action potential can be generated, regardless of the strength of the stimulus.

Why not the other options?

• A. Sodium channels are closed: Incorrect. During depolarization, sodium channels are open initially and then become inactivated, which is the actual reason for the refractory period.
• C. Potassium channels are closed: Incorrect. Voltage-gated potassium channels open during repolarization, not during the early depolarization phase.
• D. Neurons are hyperpolarized: Incorrect. Hyperpolarization occurs during the relative refractory period, when a stronger-than-normal stimulus can generate another action potential.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 16-year-old boy presents with recurrent episodes of abdominal pain and a history of blood in the stools. Physical examination reveals darkly pigmented macules on the lips and oral mucosa, and endoscopy shows multiple hamartomatous polyps in the small intestine. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The classic triad of hamartomatous GI polyps, mucocutaneous pigmentation (dark spots on lips and oral mucosa), and symptoms of intestinal obstruction or bleeding is diagnostic of Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome (PJS). PJS is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the STK11/LKB1 gene. Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (Option A) involves hundreds of adenomatous polyps in the colon but lacks the characteristic oral pigmentation. Juvenile Polyposis Syndrome (Option C) presents with hamartomas in younger children but also lacks perioral spotting. Cronkhite-Canada Syndrome (Option D) is a non-hereditary condition appearing in older adults, presenting with polyps alongside alopecia and nail atrophy, which are not present here. In adolescents with PJS, intussusception caused by large polyps is a frequent cause of the reported abdominal pain. Therefore, the specific pigmentation and polyp type confirm Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome
questions.learning: The classic triad of hamartomatous GI polyps, mucocutaneous pigmentation (dark spots on lips and oral mucosa), and symptoms of intestinal obstruction or bleeding is diagnostic of Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome (PJS).

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: All the following can be treated with supportive psychotherapy except
options: Person with cognitive decline and physical symptoms
Person who has good motivation and control over frustration
Patient with acute psychiatric illness along with crisis
Patient with severe chronic disease and ego dysfunctioning
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Person who has good motivation and control over frustration

Supportive psychotherapy is not indicated in a person who has good motivation and control over frustration. Such individuals are better treated by expressive psychotherapy.

Supportive psychotherapy places major etiological emphasis on external rather than intrapsychic events, particularly on stressful environmental and interpersonal influences on a severely damaged self. The general aim of supportive treatment is the amelioration or relief of symptoms through behavioral or environmental restructuring within the existing psychic framework. This often means helping the patient to adapt better to problems and to live more comfortably with his or her psychopathology.

Supportive therapy uses several methods, either singly or in combination, including warm, friendly, strong leadership; help in developing pleasurable activities (e.g., hobbies); removal of excessive strain, when possible; medication to alleviate symptoms; and guidance and advice in dealing with current issues. This therapy uses techniques to help patients feel secure, accepted, encouraged, and not anxious.

Supportive psychotherapy is generally indicated for those patients for whom classic psychoanalysis or insight-oriented psychoanalytic psychotherapy is typically contraindicated- those who have poor ego strength and whose potential for decompensation is high.

Amenable patients fall into the following major areas:

• Individuals in acute crisis or a temporary state of disorganization and inability to cope, whose intolerable life circumstances have produced extreme anxiety or sudden turmoil (e.g., individuals going through grief reactions, illness, divorce, job loss, or who were victims of crime, abuse, natural disaster, or accident);
• Patients with chronic severe pathology with fragile or deficient ego functioning (e.g., those with latent psychosis, impulse disorder, or severe character disturbance);
• Patients whose cognitive deficits and physical symptoms make them particularly vulnerable and, thus, unsuitable for an insight-oriented approach (e.g., certain psychosomatic or medically ill persons);
• Individuals who are psychologically unmotivated (e.g., patients who come to treatment in response to family or agency pressure and are interested only in immediate relief or those who need assistance in very specific problem areas of social adjustment as a possible prelude to more exploratory work).

Because support forms a tacit part of every therapeutic modality, it is rarely contraindicated as such. The typical attitude regards better-functioning patients as unsuitable not because they will be harmed by a supportive approach, but because they will not be sufficiently benefited by it.
questions.learning: Person who has good motivation and control over frustration Supportive psychotherapy is not indicated in a person who has good motivation and control over frustration.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Third part of vertebral artery is related to which of the following ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2

The third part of the vertebral artery (V3) is related to the area marked 2, which is the posterior arch of the first cervical vertebra or the atlas.

The given image shows the first cervical vertebra - atlas.

• The area marked 1 is the posterior tubercle.
• The area marked 2 is the posterior arch. The superior surface bears a groove for the of vertebral artery and venous plexus immediately behind.
• The area marked 3 is the superior articular facet.
• The area marked 4 is the posterior surface of the anterior arch. It gives attachment to the apex of dens from the second cervical vertebra.

The vertebral artery arises from the first part of the subclavian artery. It passes through the foramina of transverse processes of C6 to C1 cervical vertebrae and enters the cranium through the foramen magnum. The vertebral arteries of both sides join to form the basilar artery. In its course, it is divided into four parts:

The first part, V1, begins at its origin from the subclavian artery and ends at its entry into the transverse process of the C6 cervical vertebra. This part is crossed by the inferior thyroid artery on both sides, and thoracic duct on the left side, and the right lymphatic duct on the right side.

The second part, V2 is that part of the artery ascending through the foramina in the transverse process of the cervical vertebrae.

The third part, V3 is curved backward behind the atlas. In this position, it lies in a groove on the posterior arch of the atlas. This part of the artery lies in the suboccipital triangle.

The fourth part, V4 pierces the dura and arachnoid mater and unites with the contralateral vertebral artery to form the midline basilar artery at the lower border of pons.
questions.learning: 2 The third part of the vertebral artery (V3) is related to the area marked 2, which is the posterior arch of the first cervical vertebra or the atlas.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following is not seen in an inner segment of the photoreceptor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Disc

Disc membranes are specifically located in the outer segment of the photoreceptor, not the inner segment.

The inner segment contains most cellular organelles, including:

• Mitochondria
• Endoplasmic reticulum (ER)
• Golgi apparatus
• Nucleus

The outer segment is characterized by the presence of disc membranes, which are crucial for phototransduction.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A 25-year-old male patient presents to the emergency department after a car crash. On examination, his BP was 80/40mmHg and pulses were feeble, neck veins distended, and heart sounds were muffled. Which of the following changes will you expect in the jvp of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Absent Y descent

The given clinical scenario with hypotension, muffled heart sounds, and distended neck vein suggests a diagnosis of cardiac tamponade. The JVP finding most likely to be seen is absent y descent.

Cardiac tamponade is the accumulation of fluid in the pericardial space. It results in the obstruction of the blood flow into the ventricles.

This manifests as Beck's triad which consists of the following:

* Distended neck veins (due to decreased venous return)

* Muffled heart sounds (fluid accumulation in the pericardial space)

* Hypotension

The physical examination findings in a patient with cardiac tamponade are:

* Tachycardia

* Hypotension

* Elevated JVP

* Pulsus paradoxus

Jugular venous pulse (JVP) findings include:

* Prominent 'x' descent (early systolic) but

* Lacks 'y' descent (early diastolic) due to reduced or absent early diastolic ventricular filling.

An eFAST is reliable and will show fluid in the pericardial space. A chest X-ray will show an enlarged heart shadow.

Cardiac tamponade can also be treated with open surgery procedures like sternotomy or left thoracotomy. This also allows for the heart to be repaired during the procedure.

Pearl PF0262: JVP waveform and the abnormalities

1) The a-wave corresponds to atrial contraction.

Abnormality
Conditions

Prominent a-waves
Pulmonary hypertension, right atrial thrombus/ mass, and tricuspid stenosis

Cannon a-waves

Complete AV block, ventricular tachycardia, and premature atrial/ junctional/ ventricular beats

Absent a-waves
Atrial fibrillation

2) The c-wave corresponds to the bulging of tricuspid valve into right atrium during ventricular contraction.

3) The x-descent corresponds to atrial relaxation during atrial diastole.

Abnormality
Conditions

Absent x-descent
Severe tricuspid regurgitation

Rapid x-descent
Cardiac tamponade

4) The v-wave corresponds to the venous filling of right atrium.

Abnormality
Conditions

Dominant v-waves
Tricuspid regurgitation

5) The y-descent corresponds to the passive emptying of the right atrium into right ventricle.

Abnormality
Conditions

Prolonged y-descent
Tricuspid stenosis

Rapid y-descent

Constrictive pericarditis and isolated severe tricuspid regurgitation

Absent y-descent
Cardiac tamponade

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old apparently healthy man, who was found to be carrying laxatives and an enema apparatus, develops abdominal pain at the airport. An abdominal X-ray is performed and shows the given findings. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Body packer syndrome, or "surgical mules syndrome," involves the intentional swallowing or internal planting of drug-filled packets (usually wrapped in condoms or plastic) for smuggling. The patient's history of carrying laxatives and enemas is a major clue, as smugglers use these to facilitate the expulsion of the packets. The abdominal X-ray demonstrates characteristic cylindrical, radio-opaque objects within the GI tract. Bezoar syndrome (Option A) involves an indigestible mass, such as hair, but would not appear as multiple discrete cylindrical containers. Pica (Option B) involves eating non-food items like soil but doesn't present with this specific packaging or medical kit. Fecalith (Option D) is a hard mass of stool that can cause obstruction but typically shows generalized bloating on X-ray rather than distinct containers. Thus, the X-ray findings and airport context confirm body packing
questions.learning: Body packer syndrome, or "surgical mules syndrome," involves the intentional swallowing or internal planting of drug-filled packets (usually wrapped in condoms or plastic) for smuggling.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient complained of pain in one side of the neck. She is afraid of eating food as it worsens the pain. Ultrasound imaging of the salivary glands is done and shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sialolithiasis

The given clinical scenario of pain on one side of the neck that worsens with food and the ultrasound image showing a stone within Wharton's duct is suggestive of sialolithiasis (salivary gland stone).

The submandibular gland has highly viscous secretions and hence forms the most common site for salivary gland stone formation. The two most common sites of stone impaction are near the punctum and the hilum of the gland where the duct bends over the mylohyoid muscle.

The patient usually presents with acute painful swelling in the submandibular region, which is aggravated with food intake. Symptoms resolve 1-2 hours after the meal is completed. On examination, a tender and enlarged submandibular gland can be noted on bimanual examination. Pus may be seen draining from the sublingual papilla or can be expressed on bimanual palpation of the gland.

Most submandibular stones are radio-opaque and visible in radiographs. Stones of size <4 mm are removed via a dormia basket using endoscopic or ultrasound-guided methods under local anesthesia. Stones of size >4 mm are broken first using intracorporeal or extracorporeal lithotripsy and then removed using a dormia basket.

Submandibular gland excision is done only when minimally invasive techniques have failed or there is evidence of a salivary gland tumor.

Nerves at risk during the removal of the submandibular gland:

• the marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve
• the lingual nerve
• the hypoglossal nerve
questions.learning: Sialolithiasis — The given clinical scenario of pain on one side of the neck that worsens with food and the ultrasound image showing a stone within Wharton's duct is suggestive of sialolithiasis (salivary gland stone).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 60-year-old man presents with abdominal pain and vomiting, along with a 2-day history of constipation and abdominal distension. On examination, the abdomen is distended with exaggerated, high-pitched bowel sounds, and an abdominal X-ray shows dilated loops of the small intestine. Based on these findings, what is the most likely cause of his condition?
questions.explanation: The patient's presentation of abdominal pain, vomiting, distension, and absolute constipation (obstipation) forms the classic quartet of symptoms for intestinal obstruction. The examination finding of high-pitched, tinkling bowel sounds further supports a mechanical blockage. The definitive diagnostic clue is the X-ray showing dilated loops of small bowel, which typically appear centrally located with valvulae conniventes that cross the entire width of the lumen. Colonic malignancy (Option A) would more likely cause large bowel obstruction, where the X-ray would show peripheral dilation and haustral markings. Acute pancreatitis (Option C) usually presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and elevated lipase, without specific dilated bowel loops unless a localized ileus (sentinel loop) is present. Gastric ulcers (Option D) typically cause dyspepsia or localized pain, not generalized distension and mechanical obstruction symptoms. Small bowel obstruction is a surgical emergency often caused by adhesions, hernias, or neoplasms, requiring prompt decompression and evaluation for strangulation
questions.learning: The patient's presentation of abdominal pain, vomiting, distension, and absolute constipation (obstipation) forms the classic quartet of symptoms for intestinal obstruction.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: True about the definition of Postural Hypotension:
options: Decrease in Systolic blood pressure 20 mmHg after 6 mins of standing
Decrease in Systolic blood pressure 20 mmHg after 3 min of standing
Decrease in Diastolic blood pressure 20 mmHg after 6 mins of standing
Decrease in diastolic blood pressure 20 mmHg after 3 mins of standing
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Decrease in Systolic blood pressure 20 mmHg after 3 min of standing

Orthostatic hypotension or postural hypotension is defined as a sustained drop in systolic BP of ≥20 mmHg or diastolic BP of ≥10 mmHg after 3 min of standing.

It can manifest as lightheadedness/dizziness, weakness or tiredness, difficulty thinking/concentrating, blurred vision, and anxiety.

In non-neurogenic causes of orthostatic hypotension such as hypovolemia, the drop in the blood pressure is accompanied by a compensatory increase in heart rate of >15 beats/min. In neurogenic causes, there is aggravation or precipitation of orthostatic hypotension by autonomic stressors like a meal, hot bath, or exercise.

Non-neurogenic causes of orthostatic hypotension include

• Cardiac pump failure - myocardial infarction, myocarditis, aortic stenosis
• Hypovolemia - dehydration, diarrhea, hemorrhage
• Metabolic - adrenocortical insufficiency, pheochromocytoma
• Venous pooling - sepsis, prolonged standing, or recumbency
• Medications - alpha-blockers, diuretics, phenothiazines, tricyclic antidepressants

Treatment includes removing reversible causes like drugs causing hypotension. Non-pharmacological interventions include patient education regarding staged moves from supine to upright, raising the head of the bed, and increasing dietary fluid and salt. If these fail, drugs like fludrocortisone and midodrine can be given.
questions.learning: Decrease in Systolic blood pressure 20 mmHg after 3 min of standing Orthostatic hypotension or postural hypotension is defined as a sustained drop in systolic BP of ≥20 mmHg or diastolic BP of ≥10 mmHg after 3 min of standing.
