questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Which provision of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) deals with offenses related to medical negligence?
questions.explanation: Section 304 A of the IPC specifically deals with causing death by negligence. It states that "whoever causes the death of any person by doing any rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide" shall be punished with imprisonment or a fine. In the medical field, this section is applied to cases of criminal medical negligence where a doctor's gross lack of care or rash action results in the patient's death. Section 302 (Option D) is for punishment for murder. Section 304 B (Option B) specifically pertains to "dowry death." Section 301 (Option A) deals with culpable homicide by causing death of a person other than the person whose death was intended. For a doctor to be convicted under 304 A, the prosecution must prove a "gross" degree of negligence that goes beyond mere error of judgment. This section is the primary legal framework for holding medical professionals accountable for fatal negligence
questions.learning: Section 304 — A of the IPC specifically deals with causing death by negligence. It states that "whoever causes the death of any person by doing any rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide" shall be punished with imprisonment or a fine.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which infection is typically associated with a creamy, fishy odor? (NEET PG 2015)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Gardnerella

Bacterial Vaginosis (BV) caused by Gardnerella vaginalis produces a characteristic fishy odor vaginal discharge. This distinctive odor is one of the key diagnostic criteria for BV. The discharge is typically thin, homogeneous, gray-white that coats the vaginal walls. The fishy smell becomes more pronounced during the "Whiff test" when 10% potassium hydroxide (KOH) is added to the discharge, releasing volatile amines.

Other Options:

Option A. Trichomonas: Trichomonas infection causes a greenish-yellowish discharge that is often frothy. It's associated with dysuria, dyspareunia, and the characteristic "strawberry cervix" appearance, but lacks the fishy odor.

Option C. Candida: Candida infection presents with thick curdy white discharge resembling cottage cheese or flakes adherent to the vaginal wall. It causes intense pruritus but has no fishy odor. The vaginal pH remains acidic (<4.5).

Option D. Chlamydia: Chlamydia typically causes mucopurulent cervical discharge but is not associated with fishy odor. It's often asymptomatic and is a common cause of cervicitis and PID when it ascends to the upper genital tract.
questions.learning: Gardnerella Bacterial Vaginosis (BV) caused by Gardnerella vaginalis produces a characteristic fishy odor vaginal discharge. This distinctive odor is one of the key diagnostic criteria for BV.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Morbidity of a disease is on the rise. Which of the following statements is correct with respect to this?
options: Incidence will increase and prevalence will decrease
Incidence and prevalence are not related to it
Incidence will decrease and prevalence will increase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Incidence and prevalence will increase

The incidence and prevalence will increase when the morbidity increases.

Morbidity refers to any deviation, whether subjective or objective, from a state of physical well-being. It encompasses conditions such as sickness, illness, and disability. Morbidity is typically measured by morbidity rates or ratios, which include frequency, duration, and severity. Disease frequency is indicated by incidence and prevalence rates.

Incidence refers to the number of new cases of a disease that occur in a population during a specific time period, while prevalence represents the total number of cases, both new and existing, in a population at a given time. Additionally, the average duration of illness, represented by the disability rate, and the severity of illnesses, indicated by the case fatality rate, are also used as measures.

As morbidity increases in a population, both incidence and prevalence rates tend to rise. This is because a higher morbidity indicates a greater number of people experiencing illness (increased incidence) and a larger number of existing cases (increased prevalence). The increased duration of illness (disability days) and the severity of conditions also contribute to the overall morbidity burden.

Pearl PF0231: Mortality and morbidity indicators in epidemiology

Crude death rate = ( Number of deaths during the year/Mid year population ) x 1000

Age specific death rate = ( Number of deaths in specific age groups/Mid year population of that age group ) x 1000

Sex specific death rate = ( Number of deaths per year of that sex/Mid year population of that sex ) x 1000

Case fatality rate = ( Total number of deaths due to a particular disease/Total number of cases due to same disease ) x 100

Proportional mortality from a particular disease = ( Number of deaths from a specific disease in a year/ Total deaths from all causes in a year ) x 100

Under 5 mortality rate = ( Number of deaths under 5 yrs of age in a year/Total live birth in that year ) x 1000

Survival rate = ( Total number of patients alive after 5 yrs /Total number of patients diagnosed or treated ) x 100

Mortality Indicators

Morbidity Indicators

1. Crude Death Rate
2. Life Expectancy
3. Age-specific Death Rates
4. Infant Mortality Rate
5. Child Death Rate
6. Under 5 Proportionate Mortality Rate
7. Adult Mortality Rate
8. Maternal Mortality Rate
9. Disease-Specific Mortality Rate
10. Proportional Mortality Rate
11. Case fatality rate
12. Years of Potential Life Lost

1. Incidence and Prevalence
2. Notification Rates
3. Attendance Rates at OPD
4. Admission, Discharge & Readmission Rates
5. Duration of Stay in Hospital
6. Spells of Sickness or absence from work or school

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following is a childhood onset epilepsy syndrome characterized by multiple seizure types, developmental delay and slow (<3 Hz) spike-and-wave discharges on an electroencephalogram?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lennox–Gastaut Syndrome

Lennox–Gastaut syndrome (LGS) is a severe childhood-onset epileptic encephalopathy characterized by:

• Multiple seizure types — especially tonic seizures and atonic (“drop”) attacks
• Developmental/cognitive impairment
• Characteristic EEG showing slow (<3 Hz) generalized spike-and-wave discharges, typically around 1.5–2.5 Hz
• Abnormal background activity

Why not the others?

• A. Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy: Adolescent onset; myoclonic jerks, generalized tonic-clonic seizures and absence seizures; EEG shows 3–6 Hz generalized spike/polyspike-and-wave.
• C. Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy: Focal seizures with temporal lobe features; EEG may show temporal sharp waves, not generalized slow spike-and-wave.
• D. Rasmussen syndrome: Childhood-onset progressive unilateral cerebral hemispheric inflammation, causing focal seizures, hemiparesis, and cognitive decline.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A middle-aged man presents to the outpatient department with ear pain and hearing loss following trauma to the right ear. Otoscopic examination shows blood clots in the external auditory canal along with irregular perforations of the tympanic membrane. What should be the next step in management?
options: Aspirate the clot and perform audiometric tests
Maintain dry ear with systemic analegesics
questions.explanation: Following acute traumatic perforation of the tympanic membrane, the best management is conservative. The primary goal is to maintain a dry ear to prevent secondary infection, which allows the vast majority of these perforations to heal spontaneously within 6–12 weeks. Systemic analgesics can be used to manage pain. Aspirating clots or performing extensive tests (Option A) should be avoided in the acute stage to minimize irritation. Syringing (Option B) is absolutely contraindicated in the presence of a perforation as it can introduce bacteria and water into the middle ear, causing otitis media. Routine antibiotic ear drops (Option D) are generally avoided unless active infection is present, as some drops (like Gentamycin) can be ototoxic if they reach the inner ear through the perforation. Patients should be counseled to avoid blowing their nose forcefully and to keep water out of the ear during bathing. If the perforation fails to heal after 3 months, surgical repair (myringoplasty) may then be considered

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Under the Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK), how frequently are health check-ups conducted for children in the 9–18 years age group?
questions.explanation: The Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK) is an Indian initiative aimed at the early identification and management of the "4 Ds": Defects at birth, Diseases, Deficiencies, and Developmental delays including disability. For older children and adolescents aged 9 to 18 years who are enrolled in schools, health screenings are scheduled once a year. These check-ups are typically conducted by mobile health teams consisting of medical officers and paramedics who visit the schools. Options B, C, and D are incorrect frequencies for this specific age group under the national guidelines. For younger children (0 to 6 years), the screening frequency is higher, occurring bi-annually at Anganwadi centers. Annual screening for school children is designed to detect conditions like vision impairment, hearing loss, or learning disabilities that might interfere with their education and long-term development. Early detection allows for timely referral to District Early Intervention Centers (DEICs) for comprehensive management and rehabilitation
questions.learning: The Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK) is an Indian initiative aimed at the early identification and management of the "4 Ds": Defects at birth, Diseases, Deficiencies, and Developmental delays including disability.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Procidentia as a degree of uterovaginal prolapse is characterised by descent of:
options: Uterine cervix outside vagina but uterine body inside vagina
Uterine body with fundus outside vagina with eversion of entire vagina
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Uterine body with fundus outside vagina with eversion of entire vagina

Procidentia is complete (third-degree) uterovaginal prolapse, in which the entire uterus, including the fundus, protrudes outside the vaginal introitus, accompanied by complete eversion of the vagina.

Why not the other options?

• A. Uterus into vagina: Describes first-degree prolapse.
• B. Uterine cervix outside vagina but uterine body inside vagina: Describes second-degree prolapse.
• C. Uterine cervix below ischial spine: Not the definition of procidentia.
questions.learning: Uterine body with fundus outside vagina with eversion of entire vagina Procidentia is complete (third-degree) uterovaginal prolapse, in which the entire uterus, including the fundus, protrudes outside the vaginal introitus, accompanied by complete eversion…

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A town has 100 live births, 200 deaths, and a mid-year population of 20,000. What is the crude birth rate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 5

Crude Birth Rate (CBR) = (Number of live births / Mid-year population) × 1000

= (100 / 20,000) × 1000

= 5 per 1,000 population
questions.learning: 5 Crude Birth Rate (CBR) = (Number of live births / Mid-year population) × 1000 = (100 / 20,000) × 1000 = 5 per 1,000 population

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 4-year-old unvaccinated child presents with fever, rash, and Bitot spots. What is the most appropriate line of management in this case?
questions.explanation: The presence of a maculopapular rash and fever in an unvaccinated child suggests an active measles infection, while Bitot spots (keratinized patches on the conjunctiva) indicate severe concurrent Vitamin A deficiency. In cases of measles, Vitamin A supplementation is the critical intervention required to reduce morbidity and prevent blindness. The Measles vaccine (Option A and B) is not useful once the child is already symptomatic, as the infection itself will provide lifelong natural immunity. While general supportive care (Option D) is necessary for managing symptoms like fever, it does not address the specific and urgent need for Vitamin A in a child with ocular signs of deficiency. Therefore, the priority management focuses exclusively on high-dose Vitamin A to stabilize the corneal surface and support recovery from the viral insult
questions.learning: The presence of a maculopapular rash and fever in an unvaccinated child suggests an active measles infection, while Bitot spots (keratinized patches on the conjunctiva) indicate severe concurrent Vitamin A deficiency.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: MOA of botulinum toxin is:
questions.explanation: The mechanism of action of botulinum toxin is the inhibition of acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction. The toxin is endocytosed into the nerve terminal, where its light chain cleaves specific SNARE proteins, preventing the fusion of synaptic vesicles with the membrane. Without acetylcholine release, the muscle fiber cannot contract, leading to flaccid paralysis. Inhibiting Elongation Factor 2 (Option A) is the mechanism for Diphtheria and Pseudomonas toxins, which stop protein synthesis. Inhibiting GABA release (Option B) is the mechanism for Tetanus toxin, which acts on inhibitory neurons in the spinal cord to cause spastic paralysis. Increasing cAMP (Option D) is characteristic of toxins like Cholera and Pertussis, which affect fluid secretion and immune signaling. Botulinum toxin’s specific targeting of cholinergic nerves makes it both a dangerous poison and a valuable therapeutic tool
questions.learning: The mechanism of action of botulinum toxin is the inhibition of acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction. The toxin is endocytosed into the nerve terminal, where its light chain cleaves specific SNARE proteins, preventing the fusion of synaptic…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the most frequent association of lung malignancy?
questions.explanation: Occupational lung diseases are significantly associated with various respiratory complications. Among the choices, Asbestosis (Option A) has the strongest and most frequent association with lung malignancy, including both bronchogenic carcinoma and mesothelioma . In fact, individuals with asbestosis who also smoke have a synergistically increased risk (roughly 50–90 fold) of developing lung cancer. Silicosis (Option B) is associated with an increased risk of lung cancer and tuberculosis but is less frequently cited as the primary driver compared to asbestos. Bagassosis (Option C, from moldy sugarcane) and Byssinosis (Option D, from cotton dust) are hypersensitivity and reactive airway diseases that do not typically carry a direct, high-frequency link to lung cancer. Therefore, because of its powerful carcinogenic potential and widespread historical industrial use, asbestosis is the definitive choice for the strongest association with lung malignancy. Prevention involves strict workplace safety standards and total avoidance of fibers
questions.learning: Occupational lung diseases are significantly associated with various respiratory complications. Among the choices, Asbestosis (Option A) has the strongest and most frequent association with lung malignancy, including both bronchogenic carcinoma and…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy with a known history of asthma presents with sudden breathlessness and wheezing. In the emergency department, his pulse is 140/min, respiratory rate is 28/min, and FEV₁ is 40% of predicted. What is the most appropriate next step in managing this acute asthma exacerbation?
options: A high concentration of oxygen should be given by a face mask + Salbutamol nebulization
High doses of SABA to be given by a nebulizer only
Sedatives should be added to alleviate anxiety
Nebulized anticholinergics to be added immediately as the mainstay of treatment
questions.explanation: The child is experiencing an acute, severe asthma exacerbation, as indicated by tachycardia (140 bpm) and a significantly low FEV1 (40%). The absolute priority in initial management is to ensure adequate oxygenation and provide rapid bronchodilation. Therefore, the combined administration of oxygen via a face mask and nebulized Salbutamol (SABA) is the definitive next step (Option A). SABA alone (Option B) is insufficient if the patient is hypoxic. Sedatives (Option C) are strictly contraindicated in acute asthma because they can suppress the respiratory drive, leading to fatal respiratory failure. While nebulized anticholinergics (Option D) are useful adjuncts in severe cases, they are not the "mainstay" compared to beta-agonists. Therefore, the standard emergency protocol focuses on reversing bronchospasm and preventing hypoxia simultaneously. Rapid intervention is critical to prevent the child from progressing to respiratory exhaustion. Consequently, Option A represents the most comprehensive and life-saving management
questions.learning: The child is experiencing an acute, severe asthma exacerbation, as indicated by tachycardia (140 bpm) and a significantly low FEV1 (40%). The absolute priority in initial management is to ensure adequate oxygenation and provide rapid bronchodilation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 21-year-old woman, gravida 1 para 0, at 36 weeks’ gestation presents to the hospital after being found to have a blood pressure of 190/110 mm Hg in the office. Initial laboratory studies show elevated serum creatinine and transaminases. She is treated with nifedipine and magnesium sulfate, and labor is induced with oxytocin. Six hours later, her blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg. She now complaints of nausea, headache, generalized muscle weakness, and respiratory distress. On examination, deep tendon reflexes are absent. What is the most likely cause of the findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Renal insufficiency

This patient with severe preeclampsia was treated with magnesium sulfate, which is used to prevent eclamptic seizures.

Magnesium sulfate is excreted by the kidneys, so renal impairment can lead to magnesium accumulation and toxicity.

Features of magnesium toxicity:

• Loss of deep tendon reflexes (early sign)
• Muscle weakness
• Nausea and headache
• Respiratory depression/distress
• Severe cases → cardiac arrest

In this patient, elevated serum creatinine indicates renal insufficiency, which reduces magnesium excretion, leading to magnesium toxicity.

Management of magnesium toxicity:

• Stop magnesium sulfate
• Administer IV calcium gluconate as an antidote
• Provide respiratory support if needed
questions.learning: Renal insufficiency — This patient with severe preeclampsia was treated with magnesium sulfate, which is used to prevent eclamptic seizures. Magnesium sulfate is excreted by the kidneys, so renal impairment can lead to magnesium accumulation and toxicity.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient undergoes an emergency tracheostomy for acute airway obstruction. In the postoperative period, subcutaneous crepitus is noted over the neck and upper chest, consistent with surgical emphysema. Based on this finding, what is the most likely cause of this complication?
questions.explanation: After an emergency tracheostomy, the presence of subcutaneous emphysema (crepitus over neck and chest) indicates leakage of air into surrounding tissues. One of the most common causes in this setting is a high tracheostomy, where the incision is made too close to the larynx (above the 2nd–3rd tracheal rings). A high tracheostomy can lead to improper placement of the tube and inadequate sealing of the airway, allowing air to escape into the subcutaneous tissue planes during respiration. This results in surgical emphysema, especially in emergency procedures where anatomical landmarks may be difficult to identify. Why other options are less appropriate: (B) Tear in posterior tracheal wall → Can cause emphysema but is less common (C) Block in tracheostomy → Leads to respiratory distress, not air leakage (D) Tight suture → Causes local issues, not widespread emphysema
questions.learning: After an emergency tracheostomy, the presence of subcutaneous emphysema (crepitus over neck and chest) indicates leakage of air into surrounding tissues.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 64-year-old man from a village in Assam presents with genu valgum and requires a stick for walking. He reports that many other elderly individuals in his village have similar complaints. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the investigation?
options: Collect and analyze water sample for fluoride content
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Collect and analyze water sample for fluoride content

The clinical scenario of an elderly man presenting with genu valgum, along with reports of similar complaints among other elderly individuals in his village, strongly suggests an endemic cause such as skeletal fluorosis. Hence the next step in investigation is the collection and analysis of the water sample in his village for the fluoride content.

Fluorosis occurs when drinking water contains excess amounts of fluorine, in the range of 3-5mg/L. It is endemic in parts of India.

Symptoms correspond to levels of fluoride intake:

* Dental fluorosis: (1.5mg/L) Occurs if excess fluoride is ingested during the period of tooth calcification, i.e. in the first 7 years of life. Best seen on the upper incisors and almost exclusively affects only permanent teeth. It causes mottling on dental enamel, the appearance of chalky-white patches on the teeth, and loss of shine in the early stages. The white spots progressively turn yellow and can even become brown-black. The loss of enamel gives a corroded appearance.

* Skeletal fluorosis: (3-6mg/L) Occurs due to the heavy deposition of fluoride in the skeleton. Fluorosis stimulates osteoblastic activity, fluorapatite crystals are laid down in bone and these are usually resistant to secondary osteoclastic resorption. This leads to calcium retention, osteosclerosis, and osteophytosis. Ossification of ligaments and fascial attachments is characteristic.

* Crippling fluorosis: (>10mg/L) Can lead to permanent disability.

Genu valgum and osteoporosis of the lower limb are seen in a newer form of fluorosis in Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh. It is seen in people consuming jawar (sorghum), as it promotes greater retention of ingested fluoride.

Interventions for Fluorosis:

* Change the drinking water source with a lower fluoride content (0.5 to 0.8 mg/L). Running surface water contains lower quantities of fluorides than groundwater sources.

* The National Environmental Engineering Research Institute, Nagpur developed a technique for removing fluoride by a chemical treatment called the Nalgonda technique.

* Fluoride supplements should not be prescribed for children who drink fluoridated water.

* The use of fluoride toothpaste in areas of endemic fluorosis is not recommended for children up to 6 years of age

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the most likely cause of irregular menstrual cycles in a 20-year-old woman, based on the ultrasound findings shown in the image?
questions.explanation: The ultrasound image displays an ovary with the characteristic "string of pearls" appearance—defined as 12 or more small follicles (2–9 mm in diameter) arranged peripherally around a dense echogenic stroma. This is the pathognomonic radiological finding for Polycystic Ovarian Disease (PCOD) or PCOS. Clinically, PCOD is the most common cause of irregular periods (oligomenorrhea) in young women. Obesity (Option B) and Hirsutism (Option C) are common features or comorbid conditions associated with PCOD, but they are not the primary underlying "cause" or the diagnosis itself based on the scan . Turner's syndrome (Option D) would show "streak ovaries" on ultrasound, indicating a total lack of follicles. The diagnosis of PCOS typically follows the Rotterdam criteria, requiring two of three features: polycystic ovaries on scan, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and ovulatory dysfunction. Thus, the visual of follicular carpeting confirms PCOD
questions.learning: The ultrasound image displays an ovary with the characteristic "string of pearls" appearance—defined as 12 or more small follicles (2–9 mm in diameter) arranged peripherally around a dense echogenic stroma.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is NOT considered a component of the urban health care delivery system?
questions.explanation: The Subcenter is the peripheral-most unit of the rural health care delivery system in India, serving a population of 3,000 to 5,000. It is not a standard structural component of the Urban health care delivery system. Under the National Urban Health Mission (NUHM), the primary tier in cities is the Urban Primary Health Centre (U-PHC) (Option A), which serves approximately 50,000 people. Secondary care is provided by Urban Community Health Centres (U-CHC) (Option B) or small hospitals. District Hospitals (Option C) serve as the tertiary referral centers for both urban and rural populations within the district. Urban health systems also rely on community-level workers like ASHAs and Mahila Arogya Samitis, but they lack the physical "Subcenter" building found in the rural three-tier model. Recognizing these structural differences is essential for public health administration and ensuring that healthcare services are tailored to the specific demographic needs of urban dwellers
questions.learning: The Subcenter is the peripheral-most unit of the rural health care delivery system in India, serving a population of 3,000 to 5,000. It is not a standard structural component of the Urban health care delivery system.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: 18-year-old female presented with high fever and pain in knee and ankle joints. On examination, the patient had a pan-systolic murmur at the apex. Rheumatoid factor is negative. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acute Rheumatic Fever

Acute rheumatic fever presents with migratory polyarthritis of large joints and carditis following streptococcal infection.

A pan-systolic murmur at the apex indicates mitral regurgitation due to rheumatic carditis.

Diagnosis of ARF is based on Modified Jones Criteria.

Major Criteria

| Major feature

| -------------

| Carditis

| Migratory polyarthritis

| Chorea

| Erythema marginatum

| Subcutaneous nodules

Minor Criteria

| Minor feature

| -------------

| Fever

| Arthralgia

| Elevated ESR / CRP

| Prolonged PR interval

Evidence of recent streptococcal infection is also required.

Rheumatoid factor is negative, supporting a non-RA etiology.

Septic arthritis is usually monoarticular, and ankylosing spondylitis involves axial joints.
questions.learning: Acute Rheumatic Fever Acute rheumatic fever presents with migratory polyarthritis of large joints and carditis following streptococcal infection. A pan-systolic murmur at the apex indicates mitral regurgitation due to rheumatic carditis.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A person was stabbed in the anterior thigh and later died. The body is brought for postmortem examination. What type of injury is this classified as?
questions.explanation: A penetrating wound occurs when a sharp object, such as a knife, pierces the skin and enters deeper tissues or a body cavity. In this case, the stab to the anterior thigh involves depth that is greater than the surface length of the wound, which characterizes it as a stab or penetrating injury. Regarding the distractors, an incised wound (Option A) is a clean cut that is typically longer on the skin surface than it is deep. A puncture wound (Option (C) is generally used to describe stabs involving only soft tissues without entering a body cavity or viscus, though "penetrating" is a more comprehensive medical term for this fatal injury. Blunt force injury (Option D) involves trauma from non-sharp objects like clubs or hammers and does not involve the sharp penetration seen in stabbing. Since the injury was deep enough to cause death, it is classified as a penetrating stab wound

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Inhibitory control by the hypothalamus is exerted on:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Prolactin and growth hormone

Inhibitory control by the hypothalamus is exerted mainly on prolactin and growth hormone.

The major hypothalamic releasing hormones are:

• Thyrotropin releasing hormone (TRH)
• Corticotropin releasing hormone (CRH)
• Growth hormone releasing hormone (GHRH)
• Gonadotropin releasing hormone (GnRH)

The major hypothalamic inhibitory hormones are:

• Prolactin inhibitory hormone or dopamine
• Growth hormone inhibitory hormone (GHIH), also called Somatostatin.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Whole-body CT scan protocol for a trauma patient includes all, except ______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. CT Limbs

The whole-body CT of a trauma patient does not include CT limbs.

Whole-body CT or trauma CT or pans can is increasingly being used in the context of trauma patients with a dangerous mechanism of injury:

* Non-contrast CT of head

* Non-contrast CT of neck

* Contrast-enhanced CT of chest (arterial phase)

* Contrast-enhanced CT of abdomen (portal venous phase)

The purpose of the scan is to rapidly evaluate life-threatening injuries and accurately diagnose known and unknown injuries.

While limb injuries can certainly occur in trauma cases, they are usually assessed through physical examination, X-rays, or targeted CT scans if there is suspicion of a specific injury. Including limb imaging as part of the standard whole-body CT scan protocol would increase the scan time and radiation exposure for the patient without significantly impacting the detection of life-threatening injuries.

Therefore, CT limbs is the exception and is not typically included in the whole-body CT scan protocol for trauma patients.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 12-year-old girl has begun developing breast tissue and pubic hair. Her mother asks which pubertal change is most likely to occur next.
questions.explanation: The physical milestones of female puberty follow a predictable sequence known as Tanner stages. The typical order is thelarche (breast budding), then pubarche (pubic hair), followed by peak height velocity (growth spurt), and finally menarche (onset of menstruation). Since the patient already has breast and pubic hair, the next expected milestone in this sequence is the attainment of peak height. Menarche (Option C) typically occurs about 2–2.5 years after thelarche, after the peak height velocity has been reached. Axillary hair (Option D) usually appears after pubic hair is well-established. Vaginal discharge (Option A) often immediately precedes menarche. Thus, peak growth is the immediate next step

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Complex IV is inhibited by?
questions.explanation: The electron transport chain (ETC) in mitochondria consists of several complexes responsible for ATP production. Complex IV, also known as cytochrome c oxidase, is the final enzyme in the chain that transfers electrons to oxygen. It is specifically inhibited by cyanide, which binds tightly to the ferric iron (Fe3+) in cytochrome a3, preventing the reduction of oxygen to water. Carbon monoxide and hydrogen sulfide are also known inhibitors of this complex. Rotenone (Option A) is a classic inhibitor of Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase). Carboxin (Option C) inhibits Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase). Antimycin A (Option D) acts on Complex III (cytochrome bc1 complex). Because cyanide blocking prevents the entire ETC from functioning, it leads to rapid cellular asphyxiation and death. Consequently, cyanide is the definitive answer for the inhibition of Complex IV
questions.learning: The electron transport chain (ETC) in mitochondria consists of several complexes responsible for ATP production. Complex IV, also known as cytochrome c oxidase, is the final enzyme in the chain that transfers electrons to oxygen.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Kidney responds to shock by _______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Increasing afferent arteriole resistance

Kidney responds to shock by increasing afferent arteriolar resistance.

During shock, both afferent and efferent arterioles in kidney are constricted, however, the efferent vessels are constricted much more.
The glomerular filtration rate and the plasma renal flow is decreased during shock. As plasma renal flow is decreased to a greater extent, the filtration fraction increases. (Option 1 & 3)
questions.learning: Increasing afferent arteriole resistance Kidney responds to shock by increasing afferent arteriolar resistance. During shock, both afferent and efferent arterioles in kidney are constricted, however, the efferent vessels are constricted much more.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A polysaccharide vaccine against Streptococcus pneumoniae has 23 serotypes. In which of the following patients is this vaccine most beneficial?
options: A patient with sickle cell disease
A patient with recurrent otitis media
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A patient with sickle cell disease

The polysaccharide vaccine against Streptococcus pneumoniae (PPSV-23) is most beneficial for patients with sickle cell disease.

S. pneumoniae is an encapsulated organism that is detected by the spleen and is removed. However, in sickle cell disease, the sickled cells block the vessels in the spleen which results in splenic infarction. This hyposplenism results in an increased risk of pneumococcal infection. Hence, pneumococcal vaccine (PPSV-23) is given to these patients as a prophylactic measure to reduce this risk.
questions.learning: A patient with sickle cell disease — The polysaccharide vaccine against Streptococcus pneumoniae (PPSV-23) is most beneficial for patients with sickle cell disease.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In a 30-year-old man presenting with bleeding gums and iron deficiency anemia, deficiency of which vitamin is most likely to be present?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a sexually active young female with lower abdominal pain, high-grade fever (103°F), tachycardia (109/min), vomiting, and foul-smelling vaginal discharge strongly suggests an acute ascending genital tract infection. The most significant diagnostic finding in this case is cervical motion tenderness, also known as the Chandelier sign, which is a hallmark clinical feature of Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID). PID results from the ascending spread of microorganisms from the lower genital tract to the uterus, fallopian tubes, and adjacent pelvic structures. It is commonly polymicrobial, with Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae being frequent causative agents. The presence of systemic signs such as fever and tachycardia indicates active infection and inflammation. Endometriosis (Option B) and adenomyosis (Option C) typically present with chronic pelvic pain and dysmenorrhea, not acute fever or purulent discharge. Appendicitis (Option D) may cause fever and abdominal tenderness but does not produce cervical motion tenderness or vaginal discharge. Prompt diagnosis and early antibiotic therapy are crucial in PID to prevent long-term complications such as infertility, chronic pelvic pain, and ectopic pregnancy
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of a sexually active young female with lower abdominal pain, high-grade fever (103°F), tachycardia (109/min), vomiting, and foul-smelling vaginal discharge strongly suggests an acute ascending genital tract infection.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The following maneuver is performed during delivery—what is its purpose?
options: To expedite the second stage of labor
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. To prevent perineal trauma

The image above shows Ritgen’s manoeuvre, a technique performed during the second stage of labor to aid in the controlled delivery of the fetal head and reduce the risk of perineal tears and trauma.

Steps in Ritgen’s Maneuver:

* The right hand is draped with a sterile towel.

* The fingers of the right hand pressing posterior to the rectum exerts upward pressure to the chin and extends the head. The extension of the head prevents the head from slipping back in between the contractions.

* The left hand placed over the occiput exerts a downward counterpressure to prevent the rapid extension of the head

* The ritgen’s manoeuvre thus helps in the controlled delivery of the head of the fetus.

Steps to prevent perineal trauma:

* Controlled delivery of fetal head.

* Avoid delivery by early extension.

* Delivery of head in between contractions.

* Perform timely episiotomy (only when indicated)

Other options:

Option A: There are many methods for reducing the risk and control of PPH prophylactically, they include:

* intranatal:

* Active management of the third stage, for all women in labor.

* Examination of the placenta and membranes should be a routine to detect at the earliest any missing part.

* Exploration of the uterovaginal canal for evidence of trauma following difficult labor or instrumental delivery. etc

* Antenatal: This involves regular screening of high-risk cases, making blood arrangments, localization of placenta etc

Option C: Methods done for fetal rotation includes External cephalic version. A procedure to manually turn a breech baby to a head-down position before labor.

Option D: Methods like the augmentation of labour with oxytocin and instrumental delivery are methods to expedite to the second stage of labor.
questions.learning: To prevent perineal trauma — The image above shows Ritgen’s manoeuvre, a technique performed during the second stage of labor to aid in the controlled delivery of the fetal head and reduce the risk of perineal tears and trauma.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: An industrial worker was admitted to the hospital with complaints of visual disturbances. On examination, there is iron deposits in his eye. What is the most likely diagnosis behind this occular finding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Siderosis bulbi

The presence of iron deposits in the eye especially in industrial workers is called siderosis bulbi.

Siderosis bulbi refers to the ocular degenerative changes produced by an iron foreign body. It usually occurs 2 months to 2 years after the injury. This condition is due to the electrolytic dissociation of the metal by an intrinsic resting current in the eye which disseminates the metal, combining it with cellular proteins and causing atrophy.

Clinical features:

* Iris: First stained greenish and later turned reddish-brown, causing heterochromia iridis.

* Pupil: iron deposition in the sphincter leads to mydriasis.

* Lens: iron deposition in a radial fashion on the anterior capsule of the lens, leading to anterior capsular cataract.

* Retina: pigmentary retinopathy; followed by atrophy of the retina and retinal pigmentary epithelium.

* Secondary open-angle Glaucoma: due to damage to the trabecular meshwork.

Option B: Chalcosis refers to the electrolytic dissociation of copper particles and its deposition in the eye forming a brown coloured ring similar to the KF ring in Wilson's disease.

Option C: Kayser-Fleischer ring refers to the golden brown arc along the limbus seen at the level of descemets membrane in copper metabolism disorder Wilson

Option D: Retinitis pigmentosa refers to the degenrative disease of the retinal pigmental epithelium. It presents with scotomas and otherwise normal on general and slit lamb examination
questions.learning: Siderosis bulbi — The presence of iron deposits in the eye especially in industrial workers is called siderosis bulbi. Siderosis bulbi refers to the ocular degenerative changes produced by an iron foreign body.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In the jugular venous pressure waveform, what does the "a" wave correspond to?
options: Ttricuspid valve bulging into right atria
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Atrial contraction

The ‘a’ wave of the JVP corresponds to atrial contraction.

Pearl PF0262: JVP waveform and the abnormalities

1) The a-wave corresponds to atrial contraction.

Abnormality
Conditions

Prominent a-waves
Pulmonary hypertension, right atrial thrombus/ mass, and tricuspid stenosis

Cannon a-waves

Complete AV block, ventricular tachycardia, and premature atrial/ junctional/ ventricular beats

Absent a-waves
Atrial fibrillation

2) The c-wave corresponds to the bulging of tricuspid valve into right atrium during ventricular contraction.

3) The x-descent corresponds to atrial relaxation during atrial diastole.

Abnormality
Conditions

Absent x-descent
Severe tricuspid regurgitation

Rapid x-descent
Cardiac tamponade

4) The v-wave corresponds to the venous filling of right atrium.

Abnormality
Conditions

Dominant v-waves
Tricuspid regurgitation

5) The y-descent corresponds to the passive emptying of the right atrium into right ventricle.

Abnormality
Conditions

Prolonged y-descent
Tricuspid stenosis

Rapid y-descent

Constrictive pericarditis and isolated severe tricuspid regurgitation

Absent y-descent
Cardiac tamponade

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with several weeks of eye dryness and discomfort, along with complaints of night blindness. The history reveals a poor diet deficient in fruits and vegetables. Which vitamin deficiency is most likely responsible for these symptoms?
questions.explanation: Vitamin A (retinol) is essential for maintaining the health of the ocular surface and the function of the retina. Night blindness (nyctalopia) is often the earliest clinical symptom of Vitamin A deficiency because the vitamin is a precursor to rhodopsin, the pigment in the retina's rod cells responsible for low-light vision. Prolonged deficiency leads to xerophthalmia, a spectrum of eye disease starting with conjunctival dryness (xerosis) and discomfort, potentially progressing to Bitot's spots (foamy keratin plaques), corneal xerosis, and eventually keratomalacia (corneal melting and blindness). The patient's history of a poor diet lacking fruits and vegetables (sources of beta-carotene) is a significant risk factor. Vitamin B (Option B) deficiencies cause conditions like beriberi or pellagra. Vitamin C deficiency (Option C) causes scurvy, and Vitamin D deficiency (Option D) leads to rickets or osteomalacia; neither primarily presents with night blindness and xerosis. Therefore, based on the specific combination of night blindness and ocular dryness, Vitamin A deficiency is the definitive diagnosis

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the most common cause of puberty menorrhagia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anovulation

The most common cause of puberty menorrhagia is anovulatory cycles.
Anovulatory cycles → unopposed estrogen → endometrial hyperplasia → prolonged and heavy periods.

Other causes

Endocrine dysfunction:

• Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS
• Hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism.

Hematological:

• Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura
• Von-Willebrand’s disease  leukaemia.

Pelvic tumors:

• Fibroid uterus
• Sarcoma botryroides
• Estrogen producing ovarian tumor

Pregnancy complications (abortion)

Treatment:

Reassurance and psychological support. Rest and correction of anemia is done.In refractory cases, progestogens, such as medroxyprogesterone acetate or norethisterone 5 mg thrice daily is given till bleed- ing stops. Usually, the bleeding is controlled within 3–7 days. Medication is continued for 21 days. The condition usually becomes normal following 2–3 courses and then normal cycles resume. In emergency, conjugated equine estrogen 20–40 mg IV is given every 6–8 hours. Once the bleeding is controlled, combined oral pills are started.

Regular menstrual cycle will be established once the hypothalamo-pituitary-ovarian axis is matured.
questions.learning: Anovulation — The most common cause of puberty menorrhagia is anovulatory cycles. Anovulatory cycles → unopposed estrogen → endometrial hyperplasia → prolonged and heavy periods.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the primary location of the Thermogenin protein?
questions.explanation: Thermogenin, also known as Uncoupling Protein 1 (UCP1), is a specialized protein found in the inner mitochondrial membrane of brown adipose tissue. Its primary function is non-shivering thermogenesis, a process vital for maintaining body temperature in neonates and hibernating animals. Thermogenin works by allowing protons to leak across the inner mitochondrial membrane, bypassing ATP synthase. This collapses the proton gradient, and instead of producing ATP, the energy is released directly as heat. The Golgi complex (Option A), Endoplasmic reticulum (Option B), and Nucleus (Option D) do not contain thermogenin or participate in this specific uncoupling of the electron transport chain. Because thermogenin’s physiological role is strictly tied to the uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation, which occurs only in the mitochondria, its localization is definitively mitochondrial

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with a known penicillin allergy presents with fever and burning micturition, along with hearing impairment and dizziness. Which drug would be the most appropriate choice for management in this case?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with symptoms of a urinary tract infection (UTI) and pre-existing hearing/balance issues. Given the penicillin allergy, beta-lactams like Ampicillin-Clavulanic acid (Option D) are contraindicated. Ciprofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone, is highly effective against common Gram-negative uropathogens and is safe for penicillin-allergic patients. Regarding the other choices, Amikacin (Option B) is an aminoglycoside that provides excellent UTI coverage but is notoriously ototoxic and nephrotoxic; using it in a patient who already has hearing problems and dizziness would be dangerous. Azithromycin (Option A) is a macrolide that has poor urinary tract penetration and is not a first-line agent for UTI. Ciprofloxacin offers the best balance of efficacy for burning micturition while avoiding exacerbation of the patient’s otologic symptoms. Therefore, Ciprofloxacin is the most appropriate and safest management choice in this specific clinical scenario
questions.learning: The patient presents with symptoms of a urinary tract infection (UTI) and pre-existing hearing/balance issues. Given the penicillin allergy, beta-lactams like Ampicillin-Clavulanic acid (Option D) are contraindicated.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 54-year-old man presents with nasal obstruction and difficulty breathing through his nose. Examination reveals an irregular mass extending from the posterior nasal apertures (choanae). Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: An antro-choanal polyp (ACP) is a benign growth that originates from the maxillary sinus and exits through the natural ostium to extend into the nasopharynx via the posterior choana. Clinically, it presents with progressive unilateral nasal obstruction that is characteristically worse on expiration (the "ball-valve" effect). On examination, it appears as a smooth, greyish-white mass seen behind the soft palate. Thornwaldt cyst (Option A) is a benign midline bursa in the nasopharynx, not a polypoid mass. Hypertrophic rhinitis (Option C) involves generalized swelling of the turbinates, not a discrete choanal mass. Adenoid hypertrophy (Option D) is a common cause of posterior nasal obstruction in children, but is rare in a 54-year-old man. Diagnosis of ACP is confirmed by CT scan showing the polyp originating in the maxillary sinus. Management is surgical, requiring complete removal of the polyp and its stalk, typically through Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery (FESS) to prevent recurrence
questions.learning: An antro-choanal polyp (ACP) is a benign growth that originates from the maxillary sinus and exits through the natural ostium to extend into the nasopharynx via the posterior choana.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In which of the following cases does paradoxical splitting occur? 1. Severe aortic stenosis 2. Right bundle branch block 3. Right ventricular pacing 4. Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 3 and 4

Paradoxical (reversed) splitting of the second heart sound (S2) occurs due to delayed closure of the aortic valve (A2). As a result, P2 occurs before A2, the split is heard during expiration, and narrows or disappears during inspiration.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Severe aortic stenosis ✔️ – Delays left ventricular ejection → delayed A2.
• 2. Right bundle branch block ❌ – Delays P2, causing wide physiological splitting, not paradoxical splitting.
• 3. Right ventricular pacing ✔️ – Produces an LBBB-like activation pattern, delaying LV contraction and A2.
• 4. Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy ✔️ – Prolonged LV ejection delays A2.
questions.learning: 1, 3 and 4 Paradoxical (reversed) splitting of the second heart sound (S2) occurs due to delayed closure of the aortic valve (A2). As a result, P2 occurs before A2, the split is heard during expiration, and narrows or disappears during inspiration.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In a study investigating insulin regulation, which of the following factors was found to inhibit insulin secretion?
questions.explanation: Insulin secretion from the pancreatic beta cells is tightly regulated by various neurological and hormonal signals. Epinephrine (and sympathetic stimulation) has a potent inhibitory effect on insulin secretion by binding to -adrenergic receptors on the beta cells. This mechanism is critical during stress or exercise (the "fight or flight" response) to prevent hypoglycemia and ensure that glucose is available for use by the brain and muscles. In contrast, Gastric Inhibitory Polypeptide (Option B), now better known as Glucose-dependent Insulinotropic Polypeptide (GIP), is an incretin hormone that stimulates insulin release in response to food. Acetylcholine (Option C), representing parasympathetic (vagal) stimulation, also stimulates insulin secretion, particularly during the cephalic phase of digestion. None of the above (Option D) is incorrect as epinephrine is a well-established inhibitor. Understanding these regulatory pathways is fundamental for comprehending metabolic homeostasis and the pharmacological management of glucose disorders. The -mediated inhibition by epinephrine is a classic example of autonomic control over endocrine function

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Which of the following statements is/are true about skeletal muscle?

1. Extracellular calcium is not important for contraction.
2. Calcium is mainly released from mitochondria.
3. Calcium is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
4. Voltage-gated calcium channel on sarcolemma has no role in excitation-contraction coupling.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Only 3

The true statement about skeletal muscle is that the calcium is released from sarcoplasmic reticulum.

Excitation-contraction coupling refers to the process by which the membrane depolarization of the muscle fiber (excitation) leads to the contraction of the muscle.

For the maximum contraction of the skeletal muscle, the current has to penetrate deeply into the muscle fiber to the vicinity of the separate myofibrils. This penetration of current is achieved by transmission of action potentials along transverse tubules (T tubules). The T tubules penetrate through the muscle fiber, from one side of the fiber to the other.

Sarcoplasmic reticulum contains calcium ions in high concentration within its vesicular tubules. These ions are released from each vesicle when an action potential occurs in the adjacent T tubule. (Statement 3)

This action potential when it reaches the T tubule, it is sensed by the dihydropyridine receptors linked to calcium release channels. Actvation of this receptor leads to the opening of calcium release channels that releases the calcium ions into the sarcoplasm surrounding the myofibrils and causing contraction. (Statement 4)

In skeletal muscles, extracellular calcium supply partially contributes for the maintenance of skeletal muscle contraction.(Statement 1)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 20-year-old female patient consumed a cleaning product containing 90% sodium hydroxide. She is having complete dysphagia. What is the best step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Feeding jejunostomy

This patient with a corrosive esophageal injury with complete dysphagia requires a feeding jejunostomy for enteral feeding.

The injury caused by alkali ingestion is deeper due to the process of saponification of fats and dehydration. The injury caused by acids is more superficial because they cause coagulative necrosis with eschar formation, which prevents the deeper penetration of the acid.

Severe corrosive injury may lead to esophageal perforation, bleeding, stricture, and death. Patients can develop dysphagia or odynophagia, which implies esophagal damage.

Minor injuries cause mucosal edema that resolves rapidly with no late sequelae and these patients can be safely fed. In case of severe injuries, a feeding jejunostomy may be appropriate until the patient can swallow saliva satisfactorily.

Management of corrosive esophagitis:

• Hemodynamic stabilization and management of patient's airway
• Endoscopic evaluation of injuries
• Surgical management includes laparotomy for bleeding or perforation. Esophageal replacement is done for very long or multiple strictures.

Stenting is used in patients who do not respond to repeated dilatations for esophageal strictures. They are not used as a treatment in acute settings.
questions.learning: Feeding jejunostomy — This patient with a corrosive esophageal injury with complete dysphagia requires a feeding jejunostomy for enteral feeding. The injury caused by alkali ingestion is deeper due to the process of saponification of fats and dehydration.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: According to the MTP Act, termination of pregnancy due to contraceptive failure can be done up to what period of gestation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 20 weeks

According to the MTP Act, termination of pregnancy due to contraception failure can be done up to 20 weeks of gestation.

Upper limit of MTP:

* Up to 24 weeks of gestation in victims of rape and incest, fetal anomalies, or congenital malformations

* Up to 20 weeks in case of contraception failure (any female with her partner)

* At any gestational age for substantial fetal anomalies decided by the medical board

Opinion of doctors:

* Till 20 weeks - 1 doctor's opinion

* 20 to 24 weeks - 2 doctors' opinion

* For substantial fetal anomalies - approval from the medical board consisting of an obstetrician, paediatrician, radiologist and a person appointed by the state.

Consent:

Only the patient's consent is required for MTP; her partner's consent is not required. Consent of parent/guardian is needed if the age of the patient is <18 years or if the patient is mentally ill.

If the woman is not willing, abortion cannot be performed at the request of the husband alone. The woman need not produce proof of her age. It is enough for the woman to say that she was raped, and it is not necessary that a complaint be lodged with the police.

Pearl PF1638: Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act - MTP Act 1971

MTP Act with 2021 amendments

Indications:

* Therapeutic - to save the life of the mother

* Eugenic - to prevent the risk of the child being born with serious mental or physical abnormality i.e. first-trimester viral infections, teratogenic drug intake, radiation exposure

* Humanitarian - pregnancy resulted from rape or incest

* Social - pregnancy resulted from failure of contraceptives

Rules:

* Only a registered medical practitioner who is qualified (one who has assisted in the performance of 25 cases of MTP in a recognized hospital) can terminate a pregnancy.

* MTP should be carried out in a government or government-recognized hospital. Private hospitals may take up MTP if they obtain a license from the chief medical officer of the district.

* The termination of pregnancy by a person, who is not a registered medical practitioner (the person concerned), or in an unrecognised hospital (administrative head) shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term not less than 2 years, but which may extend to 7 years.

Consent:

The consent of the woman is required for conducting an abortion. The written consent of the guardian is required if the woman is minor or mentally ill. Consent of the husband or partner is not necessary.

If the woman is not willing, abortion cannot be performed at the request of the husband alone. The woman need not produce proof of her age. It is enough for the woman to say that she was raped, and it is not necessary that a complaint was lodged with the police.

Opinion of doctors:

* Till 20 weeks - 1 doctor's opinion

* 20 to 24 weeks - 2 doctors' opinion

* For substantial fetal anomalies - approval from the medical board consisting of obstetrician, paediatrician, radiologist and a person appointed by the state

Upper limit of MTP:

* Up to 24 weeks of gestation in victims of rape and incest, fetal anomalies, or congenital malformations

* Up to 20 weeks in case of contraception failure (any female with her partner)

* At any gestational age for substantial fetal anomalies decided by the medical board

Confidentiality:

A register for recording the details of MTP must be kept for at least 5 years. The patient's name must not be entered, only the reference number is used. Unlawful disclosure of patient's details is punishable with 1-year imprisonment ± fine.
questions.learning: 20 weeks According to the MTP Act, termination of pregnancy due to contraception failure can be done up to 20 weeks of gestation. Upper limit of MTP: * Up to 24 weeks of gestation in victims of rape and incest, fetal anomalies, or congenital malformations…

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following antidepressant drugs act by inhibiting the reuptake of both serotonin and noradrenaline?
questions.explanation: Venlafaxine belongs to the class of Serotonin-Noradrenaline Reuptake Inhibitors (SNRIs). As its name suggests, it works by inhibiting the reuptake transporters for both serotonin and norepinephrine in the synaptic cleft, thereby increasing the concentrations of these neurotransmitters to alleviate depressive symptoms. Fluoxetine (Option A) and Paroxetine (Option C) are Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs), which primarily target only the serotonin transporter. Dapoxetine (Option D) is a short-acting SSRI specifically used for the treatment of premature ejaculation rather than major depression. SNRIs like Venlafaxine or Duloxetine are often chosen for patients who have not responded to SSRIs or for those who also have chronic pain conditions, as noradrenaline modulation can help in pain processing. Common side effects of SNRIs include hypertension due to the increased noradrenergic tone. Understanding these pharmacological categories is essential for managing psychiatric disorders and predicting drug-specific adverse effects

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with a pituitary tumor that overproduced growth hormone underwent surgical removal of the tumor. The resection was found to be incomplete. What is the first-line treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Octreotide

The above scenario with a pituitary tumor producing growth hormone is likely to cause acromegaly in the patient. Octreotide is the first-line treatment for this condition.

Octreotide is a synthetic analog of somatostatin.

Octreotide can be used in the following conditions:

• Acromegaly
• Secretory diarrheas associated with carcinoid, AIDS, cancer chemotherapy, or diabetes- by suppression of hormones that enhance intestinal mucosal secretion.
• Bleeding esophageal varices- reduces hepatic blood flow and helps stop bleeding.
• Dumping syndrome in post gastric surgery patients

Adverse effects of octreotide are:

• Abdominal pain
• Nausea
• Steatorrhea
• Gall stones (due to biliary stasis)
• Hyperglycemia

Other options:

Option A: Leuprolide is a long-acting GnRH agonist. It is used for palliation of carcinoma prostate, uterine fibroids, endometriosis, and precocious puberty. Side effects include hot flashes, decreased bone mineral density, vaginal dryness, and erectile dysfunction.

Option B: Goserelin is also a GnRH agonist used for the treatment of endometriosis, dysfunctional uterine bleeding, and for prostate and breast cancer.

Option C: Nafarelin is a long-acting GnRH agonist. It is used for the treatment of endometriosis, uterine fibroids, and central precocious puberty.
questions.learning: Octreotide — The above scenario with a pituitary tumor producing growth hormone is likely to cause acromegaly in the patient. Octreotide is the first-line treatment for this condition.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 35-year-old patient with a history of bronchial asthma is planned for a minor surgical procedure. Which combination of induction agent and muscle relaxant would be the safest choice for anesthesia in this patient?
questions.explanation: For an asthmatic patient, the safest anaesthesia combination involves agents that do not trigger bronchospasm. Ketamine is the preferred induction agent because it is a potent bronchodilator. Vecuronium is the safest muscle relaxant as it does not cause significant histamine release, which is a major trigger for bronchial hyperreactivity. Regarding the distractors, Succinylcholine (Option A) and d-tubocurarine (Option B) can stimulate histamine release and are risky in asthma. Thiopental (Option D) may lead to respiratory depression and is generally avoided in unstable asthmatics. While Propofol is also a bronchodilator, the specific combination of Ketamine and Vecuronium is highlighted as ideal for its stability and lack of histaminergic effects. Therefore, this pairing minimizes the risk of intraoperative bronchospasm, ensuring airway safety for the asthmatic patient
questions.learning: For an asthmatic patient, the safest anaesthesia combination involves agents that do not trigger bronchospasm. Ketamine is the preferred induction agent because it is a potent bronchodilator.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old female patient presents with dyspnea and palpitations. ECG is given below. Which of the following is false about her condition?
options: Is a rare finding in a morphologically normal heart
Treated with intravenous digoxin to control ventricular rate
Should be treated with cardioversion in all cases
Difference in PR and HR can be used to diagnose
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Should be treated with cardioversion in all cases

In this patient presenting with palpitations, and irregular RR intervals with absent P waves on ECG, the most likely diagnosis is atrial fibrillation. The false statement is that atrial fibrillation should be treated with cardioversion in all cases.

Cardioversion, whether electrical or pharmacological, is not always appropriate for every patient with AF. The decision to perform cardioversion depends on several factors, including the duration of the AF episode, the presence of underlying heart disease, the patient's symptoms, and the risk of thromboembolism. In some cases, rate control and anticoagulation may be the preferred treatment approach rather than attempting to restore sinus rhythm immediately. Therefore, while cardioversion is a treatment option for some patients with AF, it is not universally indicated for all cases.

Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a supraventricular tachycardia caused by ectopic foci or small reentry circuits within the atria. It has an atrial rate of 400-600/min and a ventricular rate of 100-160/min.

Risk factors for developing AF include:

• Age- usually above 60 years of age
• Underlying heart disease
• Hypertension
• Diabetes mellitus
• Obesity
• Sleep apnea
• Post-cardiac surgery
• Inflammatory pericarditis
• Acute alcohol consumption

Features include heart rate typically ranges from 110-160 beats/minute. It is irregular and rapid. Presyncope and syncope can be seen. Thrombus formation can occur and thromboembolic events can take place.

Typically, ECG shows an absent P wave and irregular RR intervals.

Management is mainly by control of rate and rhythm, avoiding the thromboembolism risk and modifiable risk factors.

Other options:

Option A: Atrial fibrillation is usually seen in a patient with underlying heart disease and is a rare occurrence in morphologically normal hearts.

Option B: Intravenous digoxin can be used to control the ventricular rate in atrial fibrillation, especially in patients with heart failure or those who are not suitable for beta-blockers or calcium channel blockers. However, digoxin is not always the first-line treatment for rate control.

Option D: The difference between the pulse rate (PR) and the heart rate (HR) can indeed be used to diagnose atrial fibrillation. This discrepancy, known as a pulse deficit, occurs because not all heartbeats result in a palpable pulse due to the irregular and often rapid ventricular response.
questions.learning: Should be treated with cardioversion in all cases — In this patient presenting with palpitations, and irregular RR intervals with absent P waves on ECG, the most likely diagnosis is atrial fibrillation.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not a part of the global hunger index?
questions.explanation: The Global Hunger Index (GHI) is a multidimensional tool used to measure and track hunger at national and regional levels. It is calculated using four key indicators: 1. Undernourishment: Representing the share of the population with inadequate food supply (Option C). 2. Child Wasting: Reflecting acute malnutrition (Option B). 3. Child Stunting: Reflecting chronic malnutrition. 4. Child Mortality: Specifically the Under-Five Mortality Rate (U5MR) (Option A). The Infant Mortality Rate (death before 1 year of age) (Option D) is not a specific component of the GHI, as the index focuses on the broader under-five category to capture the long-term effects of hunger and poor nutrition. GHI scores are used to raise awareness about hunger levels and to advocate for policies that improve food security. While infant mortality is an important health indicator, it is not one of the direct variables used to calculate this specific index

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: When does the secondary oocyte complete the second meiotic division?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Just after fertilization

The secondary oocyte is arrested in metaphase II at the time of ovulation.

It completes the second meiotic division only after fertilization, when sperm entry triggers completion of meiosis II and formation of the:

• Mature ovum
• Second polar body

Therefore, the correct answer is D. Just after fertilization.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What level of prevention is involved when a government intends to establish tobacco control regulations?
questions.explanation: Primordial prevention is the level of prevention that targets the social, economic, and environmental factors that contribute to the emergence of risk factors. By establishing tobacco control regulations (such as bans on advertising or public smoking), the government is working to prevent the emergence of the habit in the population, effectively stopping the development of a major cardiovascular and oncological risk factor before it even starts. Primary prevention (Option B) focuses on individuals who already have the risk factor (e.g., advising a current smoker to quit) to prevent the disease. Secondary prevention (Option C) involves early diagnosis (e.g., screening for lung cancer). Tertiary prevention (Option D) focuses on rehabilitation after a disease has occurred. Primordial prevention is considered the most cost-effective and population-wide strategy for managing non-communicable diseases. It targets the "causes of the causes," aiming to change the underlying societal norms and environments to promote a tobacco-free lifestyle for future generations
questions.learning: Primordial prevention is the level of prevention that targets the social, economic, and environmental factors that contribute to the emergence of risk factors.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following gene mutations are involved in carcinoma of the colon?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. APC, k-ras, p53

APC, k-ras, and p53 gene mutations are implicated in carcinoma of the colon.

In the adenoma to carcinoma sequence, the loss of one normal copy of the tumor suppressor gene APC is the first hit, followed by the loss of the intact second copy of the APC gene (second hit). Other changes in the sequence include the mutation of k-ras and the inactivation of the tumor suppressor gene p53, leading to the emergence of carcinoma. The accumulation of these mutations is more important than their occurrence in a specific order. This is known as the Fearon-Vogelstein adenoma-carcinoma multistep model of colorectal neoplasia.

A number of other genes on chromosome 18q are implicated in colorectal cancer, including SMAD2, SMAD4, and DCC.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient following a crush injury is passing red color urine due to myoglobinuria. Which of the following will most likely be seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hyperkalemia

In this clinical scenario, a patient with a crush injury develops red-colored urine due to myoglobinuria from rhabdomyolysis. This process results in the release of intracellular potassium, leading to hyperkalemia, and also contributes indirectly to the development of acute kidney injury (AKI).

Rhabdomyolysis is defined as a pathological condition of skeletal muscle cell damage leading to the release of toxic intracellular material into the blood circulation. The causes of rhabdomyolysis include:

* Crush injury

* Hypothyroidism (precipitated by exertion, alcohol, infection)

* Electric shock

* Prolonged seizures

* Malignant hyperthermia

* Exertion

* Drugs like fibrates, statins

* Polymyositis / Dermatomyositis

* McArdle's disease (GSD-5) causes recurrent rhabdomyolysis.

Rhabdomyolysis is a cause of AKI due to myoglobin release from injured muscle due to excessive strenuous exercise, heat stroke, or traumatic crush injuries. Pathogenic factors for AKI due to endogenous toxins include intrarenal vasoconstriction, direct proximal tubular toxicity, and mechanical obstruction of the distal nephron lumen. Patients often present with muscle pain and high-colored urine(myoglobinuria). The following features are also seen:

* High serum creatinine kinase (> 5 times normal)

* High serum myoglobin

* High serum LDH

* Hyperkalemia

* Hypermagnesemia

* Hyperphosphatemia

* Hypocalcemia

* Hyperuricemia

* Once AKI develops, high serum creatinine and urea

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following drugs are not used in the management of a thyrotoxic crisis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Aspirin

Aspirin has no role in the management of a thyrotoxic crisis. All of the other options listed are used in managing the symptoms. Aspirin and other NSAIDs are to be avoided as they can interfere with protein binding and further exacerbate the condition.

Thyroid storm/ Thyrotoxic crisis:

It is a rare but severe life-threatening complication of hyperthyroidism induced by the release of excessive thyroid hormones.

Causes:

• Abrupt cessation of antithyroid medications
• Infection
• When a thyrotoxic patient has been inadequately prepared for thyroidectomy.
• Thyroid or non-thyroid surgery
• Trauma in patients with untreated thyrotoxicosis
• Amiodarone administration
• Exposure to iodinated contrast agents
• Following RAI (radioactive iodine) therapy

Features:

• They present 12–24 hours after surgery with hyperpyrexia and severe dehydration
• Cardiovascular: Circulatory collapse, hypotension, palpitations, tachycardia, cardiac arrhythmias, cardiac failure
• GI symptoms: vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice.
• Neurological symptoms: restlessness, irritability, delirium, tremor, convulsions, and coma

Treatment:

• Supportive measures – rehydration by proper fluid therapy, tepid sponging, cooling blankets
• Acetaminophen for fever.
• Thionamides like Propylthiouracil (PTU) or methimazole or carbimazole are used. They inhibit thyroid hormone synthesis. Propylthiouracil also inhibits the peripheral conversion of T4 to T3. Hence, PTU is the preferred drug in thyroid storm. However, the risk for severe liver injury and acute liver failure associated with PTU therapy makes either carbimazole or methimazole first-choice in patients with deranged liver function tests.
• Lugol’s iodide is given one hour after intake of thionamides. They inhibit thyroid hormone synthesis by Wolff- Chaikoff effect. Large doses of iodide inhibit organic binding of the iodide and hence decrease thyroid hormone synthesis.
• Propranolol is used to reduce tachycardia and other adrenergic manifestations. It also reduces the peripheral conversion of T4 to T3.
• Glucocorticoids – reduce the peripheral conversion of T4 to T3 and controls the shock.
• Digitoxin, cardiac monitoring is crucial.
questions.learning: Aspirin Aspirin has no role in the management of a thyrotoxic crisis. All of the other options listed are used in managing the symptoms.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The primary oocyte is arrested in which of the following stages?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Prophase

Primary oocytes arrest in prophase I (diplotene stage) from fetal life until puberty. Secondary oocyte arrests later in metaphase II until fertilization.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 28 year old software engineer visits a psychiatry clinic as he is suffering from sleep disturbances, low mood, stress in his current job from the past 3 months. He cannot work properly and has difficulty balancing family and work. He has no prior psychiatry history. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Adjustment disorder

The given scenario where a software engineer is stressed in his job from the last 3 months suggests it is an adjustment disorder.

Adjustment disorder is a common psychiatric condition, especially seen in adolescents and women, where an individual develops a maladaptive response to a stressful life event. According to ICD-10, it begins within 1 month of a significant stressor and is typically seen in those with poor coping skills or vulnerable personality traits. The disorder usually lasts less than 6 months, except in cases of prolonged depressive reaction. Subtypes include brief or prolonged depressive reaction, mixed anxiety and depression, or predominant disturbance of emotions or conduct. Supportive psychotherapy is the treatment of choice, and most patients recover within about 3 months.

Diagnosing criteria for adjustment disorder include:

* Development of emotional or behavioural response within 3 months of the onset of the stressor.

* The symptoms or behaviour are clinically significant, where, any one of the following are met:

* The response is out of proportion to the severity or intensity of stressor.

* Significant impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of functioning.

* Stress-related disturbance does not meet criteria for another mental disorder or exacerbation of pre-existing mental disorder.

* The symptoms do not represent normal bereavement.

* Once the stressor is terminated, the symptoms do not persist for more than an additional 6 months.

Other options:

Option B: It is not Generalized anxiety disorder as it requires ≥6 months of symptoms. Here the duration is only 3 months. Generalized anxiety disorder is defined as excessive worry and anxiety about several activities and events for most days during a 6 month period which interferes with various aspects of life.

Option C: Acute stress disorder is characterised by intrusive symptoms like distressing memories, dreams and flashbacks of the event occurring after death, serious injury, or sexual violation lasting less than one month.

Option D: PTSD requires a traumatic event + symptoms persisting >1 month (re-experiencing, avoidance, hyperarousal). The treatment modalities for PTSD and acute stress disorder include trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy, eye movement desensitization and reprocessing therapy (EMDR), and SSRIs.

Here, there is no trauma and only job stress, so it's not PTSD.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The disruption of which of the following is responsible for watery diarrhea in cholera caused by Vibrio?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Zonula occludens

The disruption of zonula occludens is responsible for watery diarrhea in cholera caused by Vibrio cholerae.

Zonula occludens toxin (Zot) is an enterotoxin elaborated by Vibrio cholerae that increases intestinal permeability by interacting with a mammalian cell receptor with subsequent activation of intracellular signaling leading to the disassembly of the intercellular tight junctions.

Mechanism of action of cholera toxin:

• The cholera toxin molecule consists of 1 A and 5 B subunits. The B (binding) units attach to the GM1 ganglioside receptors on the surface of jejunal epithelial cells. The A (active) subunit, on being transported into the enterocyte, dissociates into A1 and A2. A2 fragment only links biologically active A1 to the B subunit.
• A1 causes prolonged activation of cellular adenylate cyclase and accumulation of cAMP, leading to outpouring into the small intestinal lumen, of large quantities of water and electrolytes. This leads to watery diarrhea which is isotonic with plasma but contains much more potassium and bicarbonate.
• The toxin also inhibits the intestinal absorption of sodium and chloride.
• All clinical manifestations and complications in cholera result from the massive water and electrolyte depletion thus caused.
