questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The data which best explains the difference between the highest and the lowest values is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Range

Range gives the difference between the highest and lowest values in a given set of data.

In a dataset of marks of students in a subject, if the highest score is 100 and the lowest is 51, the range would be 49.

Option A: Variance (var or SD²) is the mean of the squares of all the deviation scores of the distribution. It is used to measure how far data is spread out.

Option B: Coefficient of variation (CV) is used to compare the variability. For example, whether the pulse varies more in old or young and growth varies more in boys or girls. It is calculated by expressing SD as a percentage of the mean, i.e., CV = SD/mean x 100. Since it is expressed as a percentage it doesn't have any units.

Option D: Quartiles divide the distribution into 4 equal groups. The difference between mid values of each quartile gives the interquartile range.
questions.learning: Range Range gives the difference between the highest and lowest values in a given set of data. In a dataset of marks of students in a subject, if the highest score is 100 and the lowest is 51, the range would be 49.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In the given image, the physician is trying to palpate which of the following arteries?
questions.explanation: The image illustrates the clinical assessment of the posterior tibial artery pulse. This artery is routinely palpated posterior to the medial malleolus and anterior to the Achilles tendon. Assessment of this pulse is essential for evaluating peripheral arterial disease (PAD) in the lower extremities. The anterior tibial artery (Option A) is located deep in the leg and is not easily palpable. The dorsalis pedis artery (Option C) is palpated on the dorsum of the foot, lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon. The lateral plantar artery (Option D) is a terminal branch of the posterior tibial artery and is also too deep for routine clinical palpation. Clinicians must be familiar with these anatomical landmarks to accurately perform a vascular examination, especially in diabetic patients where peripheral circulation must be monitored closely to prevent ulcers and gangrene
questions.learning: The image illustrates the clinical assessment of the posterior tibial artery pulse. This artery is routinely palpated posterior to the medial malleolus and anterior to the Achilles tendon.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The infant is suffering from which of the following abnormalities?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation in the infant, characterized by a specific lenticular opacity, is an "oil drop" cataract. This finding is pathognomonic for galactosemia, a metabolic disorder caused by a deficiency in the enzyme galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase. The accumulation of galactitol within the lens leads to osmotic swelling and the characteristic "oil drop" appearance on retroillumination. In contrast, "snowflake" cataracts are typically associated with uncontrolled diabetes mellitus (Option A). Options C and D refer to glycogen storage diseases: Hers disease involves liver phosphorylase deficiency, and Von Gierke's involves glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency; neither is primarily associated with this specific ocular finding. Early diagnosis of galactosemia is critical, as switching to a lactose-free diet can often lead to the regression of these early-stage cataracts and prevent systemic complications like liver failure and intellectual disability

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Stages of the demographic cycle with the same birth rate but variable death rate are?
questions.explanation: The demographic cycle describes the stages of population growth based on birth and death rates. Stage 1 (High Stationary) is characterized by high birth and high death rates. Stage 2 (Early Expanding) features a continued high birth rate, but the death rate begins to decline rapidly due to improvements in sanitation and healthcare. Consequently, Stages 1 and 2 share a similar, high birth rate while the death rate varies significantly between them. Option B is incorrect because the birth rate begins to fall in Stage 3 (Late Expanding). Option C is incorrect as Stage 5 often sees birth rates fall below death rates (Declining phase). Option D is incorrect as Stage 4 (Low Stationary) has stabilized low birth and death rates. Identifying these stages is vital for predicting population trends; the gap between the high birth rate and falling death rate in Stage 2 is what causes the "population explosion" typical of developing nations
questions.learning: The demographic cycle describes the stages of population growth based on birth and death rates. Stage 1 (High Stationary) is characterized by high birth and high death rates.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A girl with a history of contact lens use presents with eye pain and decreased vision. She does not follow proper lens hygiene. Which of the following organisms is the most likely causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acanthamoeba

Acanthamoeba keratitis is a severe corneal infection classically associated with contact lens use and poor hygiene.

• Severe pain disproportionate to findings
• Redness, photophobia, decreased vision
• Ring-shaped corneal infiltrate (late finding)

Risk factors:

• Improper lens cleaning
• Exposure to contaminated water (tap water, swimming)

Clinical importance: Often misdiagnosed early → can lead to vision loss

Why not others:

B. Herpes simplex → dendritic ulcer, ↓ corneal sensation

C. Fungal → vegetative trauma, feathery margins

D. Pneumococcus → bacterial ulcer, not linked to lenses

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.topic: General Pharmacology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 38-year-old man with multiple sclerosis presents with painful muscle spasms in the lower limbs. He is started on a drug that reduces spasticity by stimulating presynaptic α2-adrenergic receptors in the spinal cord, thereby inhibiting excitatory neurotransmitter release. Which of the following drugs was most likely prescribed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tizanidine

Tizanidine is a centrally acting muscle relaxant that reduces spasticity by stimulating presynaptic α2-adrenergic receptors in the spinal cord, thereby inhibiting release of excitatory neurotransmitters.

• Mechanism: α2 agonist → ↓ glutamate/aspartate release
• Site: spinal cord (central action)
• Indication: spasticity in multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury
• Adverse effects: sedation, hypotension, dry mouth

Differentiation:

• A. Baclofen: GABA-B agonist
• B. Dantrolene: acts peripherally on skeletal muscle (↓ Ca²⁺ release)
• D. Cyclobenzaprine: acts at brainstem, used for acute muscle spasm

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Identify the odor produced by the change seen in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Odorless

The image shows a mummified body and it is odorless.

Mummification is a modification of putrefaction. Dehydration or drying and shrivelling of the cadaver occurs from water's evaporation, but the body's natural appearance and general facial features are preserved.. The mummified body is odourless. It is a late sign of death.

It begins in the exposed parts of the body like the face, hands, and feet. Then it extends to the entire body including the internal organs which may later disappear due to putrefaction and maggot activity. During the process of mummification, the whole body loses weight up to 60 to 70% and all the internal organs become a single mass.

Factors necessary for the production of mummification are the absence of moisture in the air and the continuous action of dry or warm air. It occurs in bodies buried in shallow graves in dry sandy soils, where evaporation of body fluids is very rapid due to the hot dry winds in summer. Chronic arsenic or antimony poisoning favours the process. Differential decomposition is a condition in which some parts of the body show mummification and other parts show adipocere formation.
questions.learning: Odorless — The image shows a mummified body and it is odorless. Mummification is a modification of putrefaction.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which nerve is responsible for causing ear pain following a tonsillectomy procedure?
questions.explanation: Post-tonsillectomy ear pain is a common phenomenon known as "referred otalgia". This occurs because the tonsillar fossa is primarily supplied by the tonsillar branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX). This same nerve also provides sensory innervation to the middle ear via Jacobson’s nerve (the tympanic branch). When the nerve endings are irritated in the throat following surgery, the brain misinterprets the signals as originating from the ear. Option B (Facial nerve) and Option C (Trigeminal nerve) provide some sensory supply to the external ear, but they are not the primary mediators of post-tonsillectomy pain. Option D (Vagus nerve) can cause referred pain from the larynx or esophagus via Arnold's nerve, but not typically from the tonsils. Management of referred otalgia involves adequate systemic analgesia and counseling the patient that the ear itself is healthy. Persistent unilateral referred otalgia in an adult smoker can also be a red flag for an occult oropharyngeal malignancy
questions.learning: Post-tonsillectomy ear pain is a common phenomenon known as "referred otalgia". This occurs because the tonsillar fossa is primarily supplied by the tonsillar branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An elderly man, a follow-up patient of GERD with recurrent reflux symptoms, is found to have a nodule in the second part of the duodenum on endoscopy. Which hormone is most likely to be raised?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Gastrin

The given clinical scenario of a nodule in the second part of the duodenum in a patient with recurrent reflux (GERD) and symptoms suggestive of persistent acid-related disease is suggestive of a gastrinoma, a neuroendocrine tumor that secretes gastrin. Gastrinoma if associated with marked gastric acid production and recurrent peptic ulcer, is called Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.

Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome (ZES)/Gastrinoma is a neuroendocrinal tumour characterized by hypersecretion of gastrin resulting in gastrointestinal tract ulcers. It occurs more commonly in a sporadic pattern but can be associated with MEN-1 (multiple endocrine neoplasia-1) syndromes in the familial pattern. Gastrinoma is most commonly located in the gastrinoma triangle (Passaro's triangle) bounded by the lines connecting the:

* Cystic duct

* Junction between the second and third parts of the duodenum

* Junction between the neck and body of the pancreas

The most common presentations of gastrinoma are epigastric pain, diarrhoea, and peptic ulcers. The ulcers occur at typical locations (proximal duodenum) and atypical locations (distal duodenum, jejunum). Duodenal ulcers are the most common.

Treatment of ZES :

High-dose Proton Pump Inhibitor followed by surgery.

Surgeries that can be done are:

* Distal Pancreatectomy– if lesion in body or tail of the pancreas

* Enucleation– if the lesion is in the head of the pancreas

* Full-thickness excision– if the lesion is in duodenum

* MEN associated– surgery done only if size>2.5cm

Other options:

Option A: VIPoma is characterized by watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, and achlorhydria (WDHA syndrome). It is caused by the release of vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) from the tumor.

Option C: Glucagonomas, α-cell tumors are associated with increased serum levels of glucagon. The patient presents with mild diabetes mellitus, a characteristic skin rash (necrolytic migratory erythema), and anemia. They occur most frequently in perimenopausal and postmenopausal women and are characterized by extremely high plasma glucagon levels.

Option D: Insulinomas, β-cell tumors are the most common pancreatic endocrine neoplasms. These are usually benign and often cause symptomatic hypoglycemia. Hypoglycemic symptoms appear when blood glucose levels fall below 50 mg/dL. The symptoms usually develop after fasting or exertion and improve after glucose intake.

Pearl PF2047: Clinical features of gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome)

Most common symptom: Abdominal pain.

Gastrin hypersecretion stimulates gastric acid secretion, leading to peptic ulcers that occur at atypical sites like the duodenum and jejunum and are refractory and multiple.

Diarrhea is due to

* Acid-induced injury to the small intestine mucosa

* Inability of the intestinal tract to absorb large volumes of fluids secreted by the stomach

* Inactivation of pancreatic lipase by low pH

* Precipitation of bile salts.

The unique characteristic of acid-induced diarrhea is that it is controlled by nasogastric aspiration of gastric secretions.

Pearl PF1838: Diagnostic tests in Zollinger Ellison Syndrome

To confirm the diagnosis of ZES,

* Gastric pH <2.5 and

* Serum gastrin >1000pg/ml (normal <100pg/ml)

Provocative tests can be done like the secretin stimulation test when the diagnosis is in doubt. An increase in serum gastrin >200pg/ml following an IV bolus of secretin (2U/kg) is diagnostic.

Other tests:

* BAO >15mEq/h (or >5mEq/h if they have had a procedure for peptic ulcer)

* BAO: MAO ratio is increased (>0.6)

(BAO=Basal acid output; MAO=Maximal acid output)

For localization

* Initial investigation - CT or MRI

* Best investigation - Endoscopic ultrasound

* If the tumor is not localized - Somatostatin receptor scintigraphy.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Muscle inserted on lesser trochanter?
questions.explanation: The lesser trochanter is a posteromedial projection at the junction of the neck and shaft of the femur. It serves as the primary insertion point for the Iliopsoas complex, which includes the Psoas major and the Iliacus muscles. This muscle group is the most powerful flexor of the hip joint. Psoas minor (Option B) is absent in about 40% of the population and, when present, inserts onto the pectineal line and iliopubic eminence of the pelvis, not the femur. Obturator internus (Option C) and Piriformis (Option D) are lateral rotators of the hip that insert onto the greater trochanter (specifically the medial surface and apex, respectively). Knowledge of these insertions is clinically important in orthopedics, particularly regarding avulsion fractures of the lesser trochanter in adolescents or pathological fractures in adults, which often indicate significant mechanical stress or metastatic disease affecting the primary hip flexor's attachment point
questions.learning: The lesser trochanter is a posteromedial projection at the junction of the neck and shaft of the femur. It serves as the primary insertion point for the Iliopsoas complex, which includes the Psoas major and the Iliacus muscles.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Except for which of the following, all are cofactors for Dehydrogenase?
questions.explanation: Dehydrogenases are a class of oxidoreductase enzymes that catalyze the removal of hydrogen atoms from a substrate. These enzymes require specific electron-carrying cofactors to function, most notably NAD (Option C), NADP (Option A), and FAD (Option B) . These cofactors accept the hydrogen atoms and are reduced to NADH, NADPH, or FADH2, respectively. SAM (S-Adenosyl Methionine), however, is NOT a cofactor for dehydrogenase enzymes. Instead, SAM is the universal methyl group donor utilized by methyltransferase enzymes in biological systems. While NAD, NADP, and FAD are central to redox reactions and the electron transport chain, SAM is strictly involved in methylation reactions. Therefore, SAM is the correct "except" choice as it functions in a completely different class of biochemical reactions than the dehydrogenases. Understanding these cofactor specificities is fundamental to mastering metabolic pathway regulation
questions.learning: Dehydrogenases are a class of oxidoreductase enzymes that catalyze the removal of hydrogen atoms from a substrate. These enzymes require specific electron-carrying cofactors to function, most notably NAD (Option C), NADP (Option A), and FAD (Option B) .

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In which of the following situations is ventouse delivery contraindicated?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Preterm

Ventouse delivery is contraindicated in preterm babies as it increases the risk of scalp avulsion or sub-aponeurotic haemorrhage.

Contraindications of vacuum delivery:

* Any presentation other than vertex (such as face/breech)

* Preterm fetus (less than 34 weeks)

* Suspected fetal coagulation disorder

* Fetal macrosomia (more than 4 kg estimated weight)

A vacuum extractor is an instrument used in operative vaginal delivery by creating a vacuum between it and the fetal scalp.

The instrument consists of

* Suction cup

* Vacuum generator

* Traction tubing device.

The suction cup is placed on the fetal head at a point near the occiput called the flexion point, which is an imaginary point on the sagittal suture, located about 6 cm from the centre of the anterior fontanel or about 3 cm in front of the posterior fontanel. The flexion point is closer to the posterior fontanel as shown in the image below.

Pearl PF1954: Vacuum delivery- indications and contraindications

Indications of ventouse:

Therapeutic-

* Fetal distress in second stage

* Maternal distress in second stage

* Prolonged second stage

* Deep transverse arrest and persistent occipitoposterior

* High vacuum for second twin

Prophylactic-

* Preeclampsia

* VBAC

* Cardiac defects

* Anemia

* Preterm head

* Face presentation

* Fetal coagulopathy

* Fetal blood sampling

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which of the following is not a defense mechanism?
questions.explanation: Defense mechanisms are unconscious psychological strategies used by the mind to cope with anxiety and protect the self. Replacement is not a recognized psychological defense mechanism in standard psychoanalytic theory. Sublimation (Option A) is a mature defense mechanism where socially unacceptable impulses are transformed into socially acceptable actions. Displacement (Option B) involves redirecting an emotional impulse from its original target to a less threatening one. Altruism (Option D) is a mature defense where one deals with conflict by meeting the needs of others. Other common mechanisms include denial, projection, and reaction formation. Recognizing these mechanisms is essential in psychiatry and clinical practice to understand how patients cope with trauma and emotional stress. While "replacement" might describe a simple substitution in behavior, it does not fulfill the theoretical definition of an unconscious ego defense. **************
questions.learning: Defense mechanisms are unconscious psychological strategies used by the mind to cope with anxiety and protect the self. Replacement is not a recognized psychological defense mechanism in standard psychoanalytic theory.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient presents with meralgia paresthetica. Involvement of which nerve roots is responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. L2, L3

Meralgia paresthetica is due to compression of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (L2–L3), causing burning and numbness over the lateral thigh. It is commonly compressed under the inguinal ligament from tight clothing, obesity, pregnancy, or hip flexion.

The nerve lies in the triangle of pain, making it vulnerable during laparoscopic hernia repair, and can also be stretched in the McRoberts position during obstetric maneuvers.

Compression point:

• Under inguinal ligament near ASIS

Common causes:

• Tight belts / Obesity /Pregnancy / Diabetes

Clinical Features

• Numbness over anterolateral thigh

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 55-year-old female patient presented with a 4x3 cm lump in the right upper outer quadrant, with no axillary lymph node involvement. Mammography revealed BIRADS 4b staging. She underwent breast conservation surgery, and the final HPE report showed high nuclear grade DCIS with necrosis and 10 mm margin clearance. What is the further management?
options: Follow up 6 monthly for 2 years and then yearly follow up
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Adjuvant radiotherapy

The next step in the management in this patient with ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) would be adjuvant radiotherapy, according to the University of Southern California/Van Nuys Prognostic Index (USC/VNPI).

The USC/VNPI  is a scoring system that evaluates the following four factors to predict recurrence in patients with DCIS who are undergoing conservative treatment:

• Tumor size
• Margin width
• Pathological classification (based on nuclear grade, and presence or absence of comedonecrosis)
• Age

This index also provides recommendations for managing patients based on the calculated score.

The current recommendations for the management of DCIS according to this index are:

• Excision alone for scores 4,5, and 6

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which plasmodium species affects the brain?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Falciparum

The Plasmodium species that primarily affects the brain is Plasmodium falciparum. It causes severe forms of malaria, including cerebral malaria, which can lead to several neurological complications.

Cerebral malaria is diagnosed in the case of P. falciparum parasitemia with altered consciousness. Common features include seizures and hypoglycemia. Retinal haemorrhages, neurological findings like hemiplegia, absent or exaggerated deep tendon reflexes, and a positive Babinski sign can also be seen.

All patients with severe malaria should be treated with intravenous or intramuscular artesunate for at least 24 hours.
questions.learning: Falciparum — The Plasmodium species that primarily affects the brain is Plasmodium falciparum. It causes severe forms of malaria, including cerebral malaria, which can lead to several neurological complications.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A post-COVID patient, who is a known diabetic, develops unilateral facial pain and loosening of teeth. Which investigation would you do to confirm the diagnosis on this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Biopsy with histopathologic examination

The given scenario of a post-COVID diabetic patient with facial pain and loosening of teeth is suggestive of rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis. Among the given options, Biopsy with histopathologic examination would be the investigation for definitive diagnosis on this patient.

Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is the most common form of mucormycosis. It commonly occurs in patients with diabetes mellitus.

The presenting features are facial pain, numbness, loosening of teeth, conjunctival swelling, congestion, and blurry vision. When the disease spreads to the orbit, proptosis can be present. It can later spread to the frontal lobe of the brain and cavernous sinus.

A definitive diagnosis is done with a biopsy and histopathologic examination. It is the most sensitive and specific method. It reveals aseptate fungi with thick-walled, ribbon-like, hyphae branching at right angles.

Among the imaging techniques used for diagnosis, MRI is more sensitive to detecting orbital and nervous involvement than CT. Contrast-enhanced MRI is the imaging technique of choice. 1,3 beta D- glucan assay, which is helpful for the identification of most fungi, cannot be used for the diagnosis of mucormycosis.

Management is by amphotericin B and surgical debridement of the affected tissues. The underlying cause and risk factors should also be addressed.
questions.learning: Biopsy with histopathologic examination — The given scenario of a post-COVID diabetic patient with facial pain and loosening of teeth is suggestive of rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis.

The first symptom of xerophthalmia is nyctalopia.

The pathognomonic feature of xerophthalmia is the appearance of Bitot's spots.

Note:

Up to the level of Stage 2, the manifestations are reversible if treated with vitamin A supplements.

However, active conjunctival xerosis and Bitot’s spots begin to resolve within 2—5 days after supplementation. Most will disappear within 2 weeks, although a significant proportion of temporal lesions may persist in shrunken form and may therefore not be completely reversible.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What mechanism occurs within the zona pellucida of an oocyte to prevent the entry of multiple sperm cells after the initial fertilization?
options: Increased membrane potential of the oocyte
Decreased membrane potential of the oocyte
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cortical reaction

After the first sperm fertilizes the oocyte, mechanisms are activated to prevent polyspermy (entry of multiple sperm).

The cortical reaction is the main mechanism in humans:

• Fertilization triggers Ca²⁺ release inside the oocyte.
• Cortical granules beneath the oocyte membrane release enzymes into the zona pellucida.
• These enzymes modify the zona pellucida (zona reaction) and inactivate sperm-binding receptors (ZP3).
• This prevents additional sperm from binding or penetrating the oocyte.

Other options:

A. Acrosomal reaction: occurs in the sperm before fertilization to penetrate the zona pellucida.

B. and D. Membrane potential changes: important in some species but not the primary block in humans.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: CD-59 is involved in ____________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria

CD-59 is involved in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH).

Factors regulating complementary pathways:

• DAF or CD-55 inhibits C3 activation
• MIRL or CD-59 inhibits the membrane-activating complex

In PNH, DAF and MIRL are absent. Hence, there will be unregulated complement activation.

Clinical features of PNH include:

• Intravascular hemoglobinuria - cola-colored urine
• Pancytopenia + hypercellular bone marrow
• Thrombosis (if hepatic vein involved → Budd–Chiari syndrome)

Diagnosis of PNH is by the following methods:

• HAM’S test - acidified serum lysis
• Sucrose lysis test
• Flow cytometry - absence of CD 55 and CD 59 on RBC

Eculizumab is used to alleviate the hemolysis associated with PNH and its sequelae. Eculizumab does not alter the underlying defect of the disease.

Note: FDA has recently approved Pegcetacoplan for adults with PNH which acts by binding to complement protein C3 and increasing hemoglobin concentration.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient with a history of kidney stone removal two years ago presents with fever and flank pain. Imaging reveals findings suggestive of residual stones or a retained foreign body. What is the most appropriate management approach for this patient?
options: Perform a Laparotomy to remove the stones
Undertake Cystoscopic retrieval of the foreign body
Opt to leave the foreign body inside
Utilize Lithotripsy to remove recurrent stones
questions.explanation: In a patient with a history of urological surgery who presents with fever and flank pain (potential signs of infection or obstruction), imaging showing a "retained foreign body" often refers to a forgotten or migrated double-J stent. Stents left in place for too long become encrusted with minerals, mimicking new kidney stones. The most suitable management approach is the Cystoscopic retrieval of the foreign body. This minimally invasive procedure allows for the visualization and removal of the stent or foreign object via the urethra. Laparotomy (Option A) is excessively invasive for standard retrieval. Leaving the body inside (Option C) would lead to worsening infection (pyelonephritis), stone formation, and eventual renal failure. Lithotripsy (Option D) is used to break up large stones but would not be the primary choice for removing a mechanical foreign object like a stent. Clinicians must meticulously track all stents placed and ensure they are removed within the recommended timeframe (usually 6-12 weeks) to avoid these common urological complications
questions.learning: In a patient with a history of urological surgery who presents with fever and flank pain (potential signs of infection or obstruction), imaging showing a "retained foreign body" often refers to a forgotten or migrated double-J stent.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 12-year-old boy presented to the OPD with a scald injury of his arm. The lesion was pink, oozing, and painful to moving air and touch. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Collagen dressing

Scald injury (damage from contact with hot liquids) that appears pink in colour, has oozing, and pain is suggestive of a 2nd-degree burn (i.e. partial-thickness burn). Collagen dressing is the most appropriate management for this injury.

The best dressing for burn wounds is skin; collagen is a good substitute for skin, especially in partial-thickness burns. For full-thickness burns, sequential excision and grafting should be considered.

Initial treatment for burns includes cleaning burnt areas and removing loose dead skin. Blisters are de-roofed and an appropriate dressing is applied.

Biological dressing (collagen dressings, amniotic membrane, etc.) is the preferred dressing material, especially in partial thickness burns.

If this is not available then a non-adhesive dressing like paraffin gauze impregnated with silver sulfadiazine (SSD) cream, colloidal silver, ionic silver cream, or silver nitrate cream can be applied. Since increased resistance to SSD has recently emerged, it should be judiciously used and reserved for deep dermal, full thickness, infected, and old neglected burns.
questions.learning: Collagen dressing Scald injury (damage from contact with hot liquids) that appears pink in colour, has oozing, and pain is suggestive of a 2nd-degree burn (i.e. partial-thickness burn).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman with irregular bleeding is found to have an endometrial thickness of 15 mm. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Endometrial biopsy

In a 45-year-old with abnormal uterine bleeding and ET = 15 mm, the priority is to rule out endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma.

Even without ultrasound findings, guidelines recommend biopsy in all women ≥45 with AUB.

Normal endometrial thickness varies with menstrual cycle, but in AUB evaluation:

| Patient group | Suspicious ET

| ------------- | -------------

| Premenopausal with AUB
Perimenopausal | >12 mm

| Postmenopausal bleeding | >4 mm

This patient has 15 mm, which is abnormally thick.

Procedure : A catheter is inserted into the uterus to obtain endometrial tissue.

Advantages

• Outpatient procedure
• Quick and minimally invasive
• High sensitivity for endometrial carcinoma

Detects

• Endometrial hyperplasia
• Endometrial carcinoma
• Hormonal endometrial changes

B. Hysterectomy  is not the first step.

It is done only after:

• Confirmed malignancy
• Failed medical treatment

C. MRI Pelvis  is used for:

• Staging endometrial cancer
• Assessing myometrial invasion

D. Hysteroscopy and Fractional Curettage

This procedure is more invasive and usually performed when:

• Biopsy is inconclusive
• Focal lesion suspected
• Persistent bleeding despite normal biopsy

PALM-COEIN

| Structural causes (PALM) | Non-structural causes (COEIN)

| ------------------------ | -----------------------------

| Polyp | Coagulopathy

| Adenomyosis | Ovulatory dysfunction

| Leiomyoma | Endometrial

| Malignancy / hyperplasia | Iatrogenic / Not classified
questions.learning: Endometrial biopsy — In a 45-year-old with abnormal uterine bleeding and ET = 15 mm, the priority is to rule out endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma. Even without ultrasound findings, guidelines recommend biopsy in all women ≥45 with AUB.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 5-year-old child was brought to OPD with a history of URTI. He also has features of mouth breathing, sleep apnoea and nasal obstruction. The mother has noticed that the child increases the volume while watching TV. What is the appropriate management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Adenoidectomy with grommet insertion

The given clinical scenario of a child with mouth breathing, sleep apnoea, nasal obstruction, and decreased hearing points towards the diagnosis of serous otitis media secondary to adenoid hypertrophy. Adenoidectomy with grommet insertion would be the most appropriate management.

Adenoid hypertrophy causes typical facies characterized by an elongated face with a dull expression, an open mouth, a hitched-up upper lip, prominent upper teeth causing crowding (malocclusion of teeth), a high arched hard palate (due to loss of tongue's molding action on the palate), and a pinched-in nose due to disuse atrophy of the alae nasi.

Enlarged adenoids in children can present as nasal obstruction, recurrent acute otitis media, and serous otitis media. Chronic nasal obstruction resulting in mouth breathing leads to this characteristic facial appearance in children. Patients can also present with a speech disorder, most probably, rhinolalia clausa (hypo-nasality) due to adenoid hypertrophy.

Serous otitis media also known as secretory otitis media, mucoid otitis media, or glue ear is characterized by the accumulation of nonpurulent, serous effusion in the middle ear cleft. Glue ear can occur either due to eustachian tube dysfunction (adenoid hyperplasia, chronic sinusitis or tonsillitis or rhinitis, cleft palate, tumours of nasopharynx) or due to increased secretory activity of the middle ear mucosa (allergy, unresolved otitis media, viral infections). Glue ear is commonly seen in children aged 5-8 years and is associated with insidious onset of hearing loss (not exceeding 40 dB), mild ear aches, and a history of upper respiratory tract infections. Delayed or defective speech may also result from hearing loss.

Otoscopy shows:

* Dull and opaque tympanic membrane with loss of light reflex

* Thin leash of vessels along the handle of the malleus

* Fluid levels and air bubbles can be seen when the tympanic membrane is transparent.

The otoscopy image of serous otitis media is shown below:

Enlarged adenoids in children can present as nasal obstruction, rhinolalia clausa, recurrent acute otitis media, and serous otitis media. Adenoid facies, characterized by an elongated face, open mouth, teeth crowding, high arched hard palate, and pinched-in nose, may also be present.

The tuning fork test reveals a conductive type of hearing loss and audiometry reveals hearing loss in the range of 20–40 dB. The fluid accumulation in glue ear causes decreased mobility (compliance) of the tympanic membrane leading to a flat or dome-shaped curve or type B curve on a tympanogram.

Treatment is mainly aimed at the removal of fluid and preventing recurrence.

* Medical management includes decongestants, antihistamines, and antibiotics.

* Surgical management is done if the condition cannot be controlled with medications. It includes myringotomy and aspiration of fluid with grommet insertion. Adenoidectomy and tonsillectomy may be required and are usually done at the time of myringotomy.

Other options:

Option A: Grommet insertion alone will help resolve otitis media but the primary pathology of adenoid hypertrophy will not be addressed.

Option C: Myringotomy with grommet insertion- Myringotomy will relieve the glue ear but will not address adenoids and lead to the recurrence of symptoms.

Option D: Myringotomy involves creating a small incision in the eardrum that will relieve the otitis media but symptoms will recur due to persistent adenoid hypertrophy.
questions.learning: Adenoidectomy with grommet insertion — The given clinical scenario of a child with mouth breathing, sleep apnoea, nasal obstruction, and decreased hearing points towards the diagnosis of serous otitis media secondary to adenoid hypertrophy.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Seminal vesicles and vas deferens would be bilaterally absent congenitally in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cystic fibrosis

Seminal vesicles and vas deferens would be bilaterally absent, congenitally in cystic fibrosis. This is known as the congenital bilateral absence of vas deference (CBAVD).

Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive disorder that affects fluid secretion in the exocrine glands and in the epithelial lining. It is caused primarily due to a mutation in the CFTR gene, which codes for an anion channel in the apical membranes of epithelial cells. This leads to abnormally viscous secretions that obstruct organ passages, resulting in recurrent infections, pancreatic insufficiency, steatorrhea, malnutrition, hepatic cirrhosis, intestinal obstruction, and male infertility.

Infertility is due to azoospermia and CBAVD. In some patients, the bilateral absence of the vas deferens may be the only feature suggesting an underlying CFTR mutation.

On examination, a normal reproductive tract (including testis, and epididymis) is seen, with bilateral absence of vas deferens and atrophic or absent seminal vesicles. Semen analysis shows a low-volume (0.5 mL), acidic ejaculate that is devoid of fructose and seminal vesicle fluid. There may be associated renal agenesis in some patients.

Other options:

Option B: Klinefelter syndrome is a genetic disorder that results from a 47, XXY karyotype in phenotypically male patients. They present with gynecomastia, azoospermia, and infertility due to hyalinization of the seminiferous tubules and a small testis.

Option C: Kallmann syndrome is associated with a low or absent GnRH that is characterized by anosmia, hypogonadism, infertility, cryptorchidism, delayed pubertal maturation, and neurological abnormalities.

Option D: Kartagener syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder affecting ciliary motility; it is characterized by situs inversus, chronic sinusitis, and bronchiectasis. Male infertility may be present and is due to asthenospermia (immotile spermatozoa due to impaired sperm flagella function).
questions.learning: Cystic fibrosis Seminal vesicles and vas deferens would be bilaterally absent, congenitally in cystic fibrosis. This is known as the congenital bilateral absence of vas deference (CBAVD).

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: What is the clinical sign shown in the below picture?
questions.explanation: The image shows psoriatic plaques appearing linearly along a site of skin trauma/injury — classic demonstration of Koebner's phenomenon (isomorphic response), where skin lesions develop at sites of physical trauma in predisposed individuals. Key Clinical Features visible: 1. Linear arrangement of erythematous plaques following trauma line 2. Silvery scaly plaques characteristic of psoriasis 3. Lesions distributed along a mechanical injury site 4. Clearly demarcated erythematous patches Why other options are wrong: (A) Dermographism is incorrect because dermographism is urticarial whealing that appears after stroking the skin — it presents as linear raised wheal without scaly plaques and resolves within minutes. (B) Nikolsky sign is incorrect because Nikolsky sign refers to lateral sliding/separation of epidermis on gentle pressure seen in pemphigus and toxic epidermal necrolysis — it is not a visible skin lesion pattern. (D) Auspitz sign is incorrect because Auspitz sign refers to pinpoint bleeding seen when psoriatic scales are removed — it is a clinical test finding, not a pattern of lesion distribution as shown here
questions.learning: The image shows psoriatic plaques appearing linearly along a site of skin trauma/injury — classic demonstration of Koebner's phenomenon (isomorphic response), where skin lesions develop at sites of physical trauma in predisposed individuals.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 30-year-old presented with flaccid bullae on her skin which are easy to rupture. The biopsy revealed a suprabasal split. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pemphigus vulgaris

The given clinical vignette of a bullous disorder with the histologic picture pointing towards a suprabasal blister suggests the diagnosis of pemphigus vulgaris.

It is caused due to the production of antibodies mainly against desmoglein 3. Rarely antibodies against desmoglein 1 can also be found. The antibodies are commonly IgG antibodies. Desmoglein 3 is mainly present in the basal and suprabasal layers of the skin and mucosa.

The patients, therefore, present with flaccid bullae over the skin and mucosal ulcerations. Oral mucosa is commonly affected. Other areas where ulceration can be seen are conjunctiva, nasopharynx, larynx, etc. Cutaneous lesions are more common over the scalp, face, neck, upper chest, and back.

Direct immunofluorescence will show the deposition of antibodies around the keratinocytes in the epidermis. It presents with a characteristic fish-net appearance in the immunofluorescence assay It is treated with steroids, azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, rituximab, etc.

The images attached below depict the lesions, the suprabasal split, and the fish-net pattern respectively seen in a case of pemphigus vulgaris.

Option B: Pemphigus foliaceus is a benign form of pemphigus, an inflammatory blistering disorder. This is a form of a subcorneal blister, where the stratum corneum forms the roof of the bulla. It is caused by autoantibodies that result in the dissolution of intercellular attachments within the epidermis. Antibodies against desmoglein 1 are mainly seen in pemphigus foliaceous. There is no involvement of the mucosal epithelium in pemphigus foliaceus.

Lesions are most common on the scalp, face, chest, and back. Bullae are superficial and mainly present as areas of erythema and crusting. These represent superficial erosions at sites of blister rupture.

Option C: Pemphigus vegetans is a rare form of the bullous disorder that presents with large, moist, verrucous, vegetating plaques studded with pustules on the groin, axillae, and flexural surfaces. It is associated with eosinophilic microabscess. It has two types, a severe Neumann type, and a milder Hallopeau type.

Option D: Erythema multiforme is a self‐limiting cytotoxic dermatitis resulting from cell‐mediated hypersensitivity most commonly to infection or drugs. The common triggers are

• Herpes simplex infection
• Mycoplasma infection
• Bacterial infections
• Fungal infections
• Vaccinations
• Malignancy: carcinoma, lymphoma, leukemia
• Drug reactions: sulfonamides, cotrimoxazole, penicillins
• Miscellaneous: Lupus erythematosus (Rowell Syndrome), Sarcoidosis, Polyarteritis Nodosa

It presents clinically with macular, papular, or urticarial lesions, along with the classic acral iris or target lesions. The lesions are distributed on the distal extremities, palms or trunk, and oral and genital mucous membranes.

Target lesions are less than 3 cm in diameter, rounded, and have three zones:

• The central area of dusky erythema or purpura
• Middle paler zone of edema
• The outer ring of erythema with a well‐defined edge

Atypical lesions will have only 2 zones. They fade in 1-2 weeks leaving dusky discoloration.
questions.learning: Pemphigus vulgaris — The given clinical vignette of a bullous disorder with the histologic picture pointing towards a suprabasal blister suggests the diagnosis of pemphigus vulgaris.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: All are ocular manifestations of dengue except ________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cataract

Cataract is not an ocular manifestation of dengue.

Dengue has varied manifestations, in different organ systems, mainly of inflammation and bleeding. The mechanisms for ocular manifestations in dengue include a direct viral effect on the eye, an immune-mediated vasculitis, and a variety of secondary effects related to dengue-induced vascular leakage and hemostatic abnormalities.

Ocular manifestations of dengue are:

• visual impairment which can be either painless or painful
• Retro orbital pain
• Conjunctival injection and subconjunctival hemorrhage(option B)
• Uveitis(option C)
• Complications such as retinal hemorrhage(option D), retinal edema, macular ischemia, macular edema, vitreous hemorrhage, vitritis, and optic neuritis or papillitis.

Depending on the severity of the disease, gradual improvement in vision occurs, although in rare cases permanent visual impairment may be seen.
questions.learning: Cataract Cataract is not an ocular manifestation of dengue. Dengue has varied manifestations, in different organ systems, mainly of inflammation and bleeding.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department unconscious after a road traffic accident, with nausea and vomiting. Based on the non-contrast CT (NCCT) brain findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient's history of trauma (RTA) followed by a loss of consciousness and vomiting is a classic neurosurgical presentation. The NCCT brain image provides the definitive diagnosis, showing a hyperdense, biconvex (lens-shaped) collection of blood between the skull and the dura mater. This is pathognomonic for an Extradural Hemorrhage (EDH), which is typically caused by a rupture of the middle meningeal artery associated with a skull fracture. A Subdural Hemorrhage (Option B) would instead appear as a crescent-shaped (concavo-convex) collection that spreads across suture lines. Intraparenchymal hemorrhage (Option C) would show blood within the brain tissue itself. Subarachnoid hemorrhage (Option D) presents with blood filling the sulci and cisterns (see Q.288). EDH is a life-threatening emergency because the biconvex shape indicates blood under high pressure, leading to rapid herniation if not surgically evacuated. Therefore, based on the characteristic CT morphology, EDH is the diagnosis

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: If 100 couples have used a method for a period of 2 years and have resulted in 10 pregnancies, what will be the effectiveness of the method used?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. High

100 couples used the contraceptive method for 2 years:

• Total exposure = 100 × 2 = 200 couple-years
• Pregnancies = 10

Pregnancy rate:

= (10 / 200) × 100

= 5 pregnancies per 100 couple-years

Therefore, the method has an effectiveness of approximately: 100 − 5 = 95%

So, the method is considered highly effective.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Given below is the demonstration of tetanization in the gastrocnemius muscle of a frog. Identify the tetanising frequency.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 30-35 Hz

Tetanizing frequency demonstrated by the muscle is 33Hz. In the above graph, we know,

• The speed of the paper is 1000mm/sec.
• The y-axis represents millivolts, the x-axis represents time.
• The scale on the x-axis is 10mm.
• The area under the graph represents the muscle contraction.

Contraction period (latent period to maximum force of contraction) includes 3 scales = 30 mm.

As paper speed is 1000mm/sec,

Contraction period = 30mm = (30/1000) = 30 msec.

Tetanizing frequency = 1/contraction period = 1000/30 = 33Hz.

Tetanization

The features of muscle contraction can be demonstrated by eliciting single muscle twitches. The adding together of individual twitch contractions to increase the intensity of overall muscle contraction is Summation. Summation occurs in two ways:

• by increasing the number of motor units contracting simultaneously, which is multiple ﬁber summations.
• by increasing the frequency of contraction, which is called frequency summation and can lead to tetanization.

When the frequency of a contraction reaches a critical level, the successive contractions eventually fuse together, and the whole muscle contraction appears to be completely smooth and continuous, this is called tetanization.

Tetanization occurs in two ways:

• Complete tetanus occurs when no relaxation occurs between stimuli.
• Incomplete tetanus when periods of incomplete relaxation take place between the summated stimuli.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A male patient with infertility presents with a combination of situs inversus, chronic sinusitis, and bronchiectasis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Kartagener’s syndrome is a specific variant of Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia (PCD) characterized by the classic triad of situs inversus, chronic sinusitis, and bronchiectasis. It results from a genetic defect in the axonemal dynein arms of motile cilia, leading to immotile or dyskinetic cilia. Because ciliary motion is essential for mucociliary clearance, affected individuals develop recurrent respiratory tract infections, chronic sinusitis, and progressive bronchiectasis. The same dynein arm defect also affects flagellar movement of sperm, resulting in male infertility due to immotile sperm. Cystic fibrosis (Option B)—also known as mucoviscidosis (Option C)—can cause bronchiectasis and infertility, but it does not cause situs inversus, which is the key distinguishing feature here. Klinefelter syndrome (Option D) leads to primary testicular failure and infertility but is not associated with respiratory disease or situs inversus. Thus, the presence of situs inversus (e.g., dextrocardia on imaging) is the crucial diagnostic clue confirming Kartagener’s syndrome
questions.learning: Kartagener’s syndrome is a specific variant of Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia (PCD) characterized by the classic triad of situs inversus, chronic sinusitis, and bronchiectasis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which nerve supplies the hybrid muscle partially spared in a patient who presented with sciatica and tender hamstrings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Obturator nerve

The hybrid muscle referred to is the adductor magnus, which has a dual nerve supply—the hamstring (ischiocondylar) part by tibial nerve and the adductor part by obturator nerve.

In sciatica, tibial nerve fibers are affected, but the obturator nerve supply partially spares the muscle.

Thus, residual function of adductor magnus points to obturator nerve involvement.
questions.learning: Obturator nerve — The hybrid muscle referred to is the adductor magnus, which has a dual nerve supply—the hamstring (ischiocondylar) part by tibial nerve and the adductor part by obturator nerve.

questions.text: According to the Factories Act 1948, what is the maximum work hours per week including overtime work hours?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 60 hours

Maximum work hours per week including overtime work hours is 60 hours.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following types of cataract would be present in a patient after a blunt trauma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Rosette cataract

A rosette cataract typically follows closed globe injuries (blunt trauma).

In blunt trauma, there may be minute ruptures in the lens capsule resulting in an influx of aqueous humor, leading to hydration and subsequent opacification of the lens. Commonly there is posterior subcapsular opacification in a flower shape along the posterior sutures. Hence it is called rosette cataract.

Iridodialysis occurs due to dehiscence of the iris from the ciliary body at its root. The pupil becomes D-shaped.

The following image shows a rosette cataract.

Apart from this, blunt trauma can cause a ring-shaped anterior subcapsular opacity underneath the Vossius ring.

Other options:

(a) Sunflower cataract: Sunflower cataract is associated with Wilson's disease, a genetic disorder that leads to copper accumulation in the body. It is not related to blunt trauma.

(c) Christmas tree cataract: Christmas tree cataract is often seen in cases of myotonic dystrophy, a genetic neuromuscular disorder. It is not related to blunt trauma.

(d) Sparkle cataract: It does not correspond to a well-defined category of cataract associated with blunt trauma or any other specific condition.

Pearl PF1394: Diseases and Associated Cataracts - Images

Wilson's Disease/Chalcosis: Sunflower Cataract

Diabetes mellitus:  Snowflake cataract

Blunt trauma: May present as rosette-shaped cataract

Myotonic dystrophy - Christmas tree cataract

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 30-year-old female patient with hearing loss underwent an audiogram, which is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Otosclerosis

The above Pure tone audiogram is characteristic of Otosclerosis.

In the above audiogram,

* An air-bone gap is present.

* BC > AC

This is suggestive of Conductive Hearing loss. In the above options, only Otosclerosis causes conductive hearing loss. Carhart’s notch is the characteristic dip in the BC curve at 2000 Hz seen in otosclerosis. It disappears after successful stapes surgery.

PTA in Sensorineural hearing loss :

* Shows no Air Bone gap.

* Both BC and AC are in hearing loss range (>25 DB)

Other options:

* Meniere’s disease shows a low-frequency loss in the SNHL curve.

* Noise-induced hearing loss is SNHL and PTA shows characteristic Acoustic dip at 4000 Hz.

* Ototoxicity causes SNHL and shows high-frequency hearing loss in the SNHL curve.
questions.learning: Otosclerosis — The above Pure tone audiogram is characteristic of Otosclerosis. In the above audiogram, * An air-bone gap is present. * BC > AC This is suggestive of Conductive Hearing loss.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is a nuclear neuroendocrine immunohistochemical marker?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. INSM1

INSM1 is a nuclear marker for neuroendocrine tumours.

Insulinoma-associated protein 1 is a nuclear protein that serves as a transcription factor and has gained prominence as a neuroendocrine marker in pathology. Originally identified in insulinomas, INSM1 has been to be a reliable marker for various neuroendocrine tumors (NETs).

Other options:

Option A: Synaptophysin is a glycoprotein located in the membrane of presynaptic vesicles. It is a marker for neuroendocrine cells and tumors, but it is found in the cytoplasm, not the nucleus.

Option B: NCAM 1 (Neural Cell Adhesion Molecule 1), also known as CD56, this marker is a cell surface glycoprotein involved in cell adhesion. It is often used in the diagnosis of neuroendocrine tumors, but it is not a nuclear marker.

Option D:  Chromogranin A is a protein found in the secretory vesicles of neuroendocrine cells. It is another commonly used marker for neuroendocrine tumors and is located in the cytoplasm.
questions.learning: INSM1 INSM1 is a nuclear marker for neuroendocrine tumours. Insulinoma-associated protein 1 is a nuclear protein that serves as a transcription factor and has gained prominence as a neuroendocrine marker in pathology.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 27-year-old woman presents with a one-week history of foul-smelling vaginal discharge. She has a positive Whiff test, and Gram stain shows clue cells. What is the recommended treatment for her condition?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a foul-smelling vaginal discharge with a positive Whiff’s test (fishy odor on adding KOH) and the pathognomonic finding of "clue cells" on a Gram stain is diagnostic of Bacterial Vaginosis (BV) . BV is caused by a shift in vaginal flora, specifically an overgrowth of anaerobes like Gardnerella vaginalis. The preferred first-line treatment for BV is Metronidazole (Option A), administered either orally or intravaginally. Nystatin (Option B) is used for vaginal candidiasis. Tetracycline (Option C) and Azithromycin (Option D) are used for STIs like Chlamydia but are not effective for the anaerobic shift of BV. Therefore, based on the classic Amsel criteria provided in the scenario, metronidazole is the definitive pharmacological choice. Treating the sexual partner is not routinely required for BV, unlike for trichomoniasis. Effective treatment rapidly resolves the odor and discharge symptoms
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of a foul-smelling vaginal discharge with a positive Whiff’s test (fishy odor on adding KOH) and the pathognomonic finding of "clue cells" on a Gram stain is diagnostic of Bacterial Vaginosis (BV) .

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A man falls into a deep sleep with one arm under his head. Upon waking, he is unable to move the arm, though he still feels tingling and pain. The reason for the loss of motor function while maintaining pain sensation is?
options: B fibers are more susceptible to pressure than A fibers
A fibers are more sensitive to pressure than C fibers
C fibers are more sensitive to pressure than A fibers
Motor nerves are more affected by sleep than sensory nerves
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A fibers are more sensitive to pressure than C fibers

In the above scenario, the patient has developed paresis (partial paralysis), but the pain sensation is intact (no numbness). This is because A fibers that carry motor, touch, and pressure sensations are more susceptible to pressure changes/compression than C fibers that carry pain sensations.

The compression of a large-diameter nerve fiber leads to a reversible physiologic conduction block, or neuropraxia. The susceptibility of the nerve fibers to pressure is A>B>C. This is responsible for Saturday night or Sunday morning paralysis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Thiamine deficiency results in decreased energy production, because TPP _______
options: Is coenzyme for pyruvate and alpha ketoglutarate dehydrogenase
Interferes with energy production from amino acids
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Is coenzyme for pyruvate and alpha ketoglutarate dehydrogenase

Thiamine deficiency results in decreased energy production because thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) is a coenzyme of pyruvate and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, which are required for the production of ATP using NADH.

Thiamine pyrophosphate is an important coenzyme in three multienzyme complexes that catalyze oxidative decarboxylation reactions:

• Pyruvate dehydrogenase in carbohydrate metabolism.
• α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase in the citric acid cycle.
• Branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase involved in the metabolism of leucine, isoleucine and valine.

NAD is a co-factor in pyruvate and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase. Hence in thiamine deficiency, there is decreased ATP production owing to reduced NADH entering into the electron transport chain.

Option A: Thiamine does not interfere in alcohol metabolism but alcohol interferes directly with the absorption of thiamine and with the synthesis of thiamine pyrophosphate.

Option B: Thiamine is also the coenzyme for transketolase in the pentose phosphate pathway (HMP shunt) but there is no ATP synthesized in this pathway.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which structure arises from the left 6th pharyngeal (aortic) arch artery?
questions.explanation: The embryological development of the arterial system involves several pharyngeal arch arteries. The left 6th pharyngeal arch artery gives rise to the proximal part of the left pulmonary artery and the ductus arteriosus. The ductus arteriosus is a critical fetal structure that shunts blood from the pulmonary artery to the aorta, bypassing the non-functional fetal lungs. After birth, it closes to become the ligamentum arteriosum. The arch of the aorta (Option A) develops from the left 4th arch artery. The common carotid arteries (Option C) develop from the 3rd arch arteries. The right subclavian artery (Option D) develops from the right 4th arch artery and the right seventh intersegmental artery. On the right side, the 6th arch artery distal part disappears, while the proximal part forms the right pulmonary artery. Understanding these developmental origins is vital for comprehending congenital vascular anomalies, such as Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA) or a right-sided aortic arch
questions.learning: The embryological development of the arterial system involves several pharyngeal arch arteries. The left 6th pharyngeal arch artery gives rise to the proximal part of the left pulmonary artery and the ductus arteriosus.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In the conduct of a randomized controlled trial (RCT), participants are enrolled and followed using a predefined methodological sequence. Which of the following represents the correct chronological order of key steps in an RCT?
options: Data analysis → Blinding → Application of inclusion and exclusion criteria → Random allocation
Blinding → Application of inclusion and exclusion criteria → Random allocation → Data analysis
Application of inclusion and exclusion criteria → Random allocation → Blinding → Data analysis
Application of inclusion and exclusion criteria → Blinding → Random allocation → Data analysis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Application of inclusion and exclusion criteria → Random allocation → Blinding → Data analysis

A Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT) begins with defining inclusion and exclusion criteria to select an appropriate study population.

Eligible participants are then randomized into intervention and control groups, followed by blinding to reduce bias.

Finally, outcomes are assessed and subjected to statistical analysis, completing the trial process.
questions.learning: Application of inclusion and exclusion criteria → Random allocation → Blinding → Data analysis A Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT) begins with defining inclusion and exclusion criteria to select an appropriate study population.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A mental health practitioner is evaluating aripiprazole for a patient with psychotic symptoms. Compared to other antipsychotics, how do its pharmacological properties and side effect profile differ?
options: No intrinsic activity, high affinity for D2 receptor, less extrapyramidal symptoms, and more weight gain
High intrinsic activity, no affinity for D2 receptor, more extrapyramidal symptoms, and less weight gain
Low intrinsic activity, high affinity for D2 re- ceptor, less extrapyramidal symptoms, and less weight gain
High intrinsic activity, high affinity for D2 re- ceptor, less extrapyramidal symptoms, and less weight gain
questions.explanation: Low intrinsic activity, high affinity for D2 receptor, less extrapyramidal symptoms, and less weight gain Aripiprazole is a unique "third-generation" atypical antipsychotic. Its pharmacological hallmark is being a D2 receptor partial agonist. This means it has a high affinity for the D2 receptor but only low intrinsic activity (Option C) . This allow it to act as an antagonist in areas of dopamine excess (improving positive symptoms) and as an agonist in areas of dopamine deficiency. Because of its partial agonist mechanism, it is associated with significantly less extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS) and minimal elevation of prolactin levels. Furthermore, compared to other atypicals like olanzapine, it has a very low risk of metabolic side effects, resulting in less weight gain. Options A, B, and D are incorrect descriptions of its receptor profile or clinical tolerability. Therefore, the combination of high affinity, low intrinsic activity, and a favorable metabolic profile makes Option C the definitive pharmacological description of aripiprazole.
questions.learning: Low intrinsic activity, high affinity for D2 receptor, less extrapyramidal symptoms, and less weight gain Aripiprazole is a unique "third-generation" atypical antipsychotic.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department due to progressive lethargy, fatigue, and nausea over the past month. She has also experienced constipation, muscle weakness, increased thirst, and frequent urination. She reports taking high doses of calcium and vitamin D supplements after reading they could improve bone health. On examination, she is stuporous and has dry mucous membranes. The metabolic abnormality most likely responsible for this patient’s clinical findings can also occur in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sarcoidosis

Excess intake of calcium and vitamin D can lead to hypercalcemia, which presents with:

• Lethargy, confusion, stupor
• Constipation
• Polyuria and polydipsia
• Muscle weakness
• Dehydration

This patient’s symptoms are classic for hypercalcemia. Hypercalcemia can also occur in sarcoidosis because activated macrophages in granulomas express 1-α hydroxylase, which converts vitamin D to its active form (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D).

This leads to increased intestinal calcium absorption → hypercalcemia and hypercalciuria.
questions.learning: Sarcoidosis Excess intake of calcium and vitamin D can lead to hypercalcemia, which presents with: • Lethargy, confusion, stupor • Constipation • Polyuria and polydipsia • Muscle weakness • Dehydration This patient’s symptoms are classic for hypercalcemia.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy had painful sores in the mouth with a rash over the hands along with fever. Which of these is the causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Coxsackievirus

The presence of fever, along with painful sores in the mouth and small, tense vescicles with surrounding erythema on the palms and soles in a child point towards the diagnosis of hand-foot-mouth disease. The most common cause of which worldwide is coxackievirus A16.

Spread is by droplets or faecal contamination and the incubation period is 7 days. The fever is generally mild, and is followed by the appearance of lesions. The characteristic lesions are slightly oval, with a grey blister roof and a narrow rim of erythema. The oral lesions are aphthoid and are less painful than aphthous ulcers.

Only symptomatic treatment is given. The lesions generally disappear in 7 - 10 days.
questions.learning: Coxsackievirus — The presence of fever, along with painful sores in the mouth and small, tense vescicles with surrounding erythema on the palms and soles in a child point towards the diagnosis of hand-foot-mouth disease.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is an oral factor Xa inhibitor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rivaroxaban

Rivaroxaban is an oral direct factor Xa inhibitor. They represent a new class of oral anticoagulant drugs that do not require monitoring.

This group of drugs inhibit factor Xa in the final common pathway of clotting [conversion of Prothrombin (Factor II) to thrombin (Factor IIa)]. They are given as fixed doses and have a rapid onset of action.

Oral direct factor Xa inhibitors are indicated in:

• Prevention of embolic stroke in patients with atrial fibrillation (without valvular heart disease)
• Venous thromboembolic disease (VTE)
• Postoperative thromboprophylaxis in patients undergoing hip and knee arthroplasty
questions.learning: Rivaroxaban Rivaroxaban is an oral direct factor Xa inhibitor. They represent a new class of oral anticoagulant drugs that do not require monitoring.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Choose the correct sequence with respect to the stages of changes that the breast undergoes in a female?
questions.explanation: The physiological development and functioning of the breast follow a strictly programmed sequence. 1. Mamogenesis: Growth and development of the mammary glands (primarily during puberty and pregnancy). 2. Lactogenesis: The initiation of milk secretion (typically occurring in the late stages of pregnancy and immediately postpartum). 3. Galactokinesis: The ejection of milk from the breast (the "let-down reflex," primarily mediated by oxytocin in response to suckling). 4. Galactopoiesis: The ongoing maintenance of established milk production (primarily mediated by prolactin and the regular removal of milk). Options A, B, and D provide incorrect chronological orders of these biological events. Understanding this sequence is vital for diagnosing and managing lactation-related disorders. For example, a failure in lactogenesis prevents the initial milk "coming in," while a failure in galactokinesis prevents the child from receiving the milk despite its production. Proper knowledge of these terms and their hormonal drivers (Estrogen/Progesterone for mamogenesis, Prolactin for lactogenesis/galactopoiesis, and Oxytocin for galactokinesis) is essential for obstetric and pediatric care
questions.learning: The physiological development and functioning of the breast follow a strictly programmed sequence. Mamogenesis: Growth and development of the mammary glands (primarily during puberty and pregnancy).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Identify the phenomenon shown below
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Complementation

The image shows a schematic of the blue-white assay used in the screening of recombinant vectors for inserted DNA fragments. It uses the phenomenon of complementation (α-complementation of the β-galactosidase gene).

Blue–white assay:

The DNA of interest is ligated into a vector. The vector is then inserted into a competent host cell viable for transformation, which is then grown in the presence of X-gal (X-gal detects active β-galactosidase). Cells transformed with vectors containing recombinant DNA will produce white colonies; cells transformed with non-recombinant plasmids (i.e., only the vector) grow into blue colonies.

The image below shows the result of a blue–white assay.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A female patient with hearing loss is examined and is found to be Rinne’s negative at 256 Hz and 512 Hz, while Rinne positive at 1024 Hz. What is the expected air conduction and bone conduction gap?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 30-45 dB

The Rinne test becomes negative only when the air–bone gap (ABG) exceeds a certain threshold, and this threshold varies with tuning fork frequency.

• Lower frequencies (256, 512 Hz): Rinne becomes negative earlier (smaller ABG needed)
• Higher frequency (1024 Hz): Requires a larger ABG to turn negative

Interpretation of the question:

• Rinne negative at 256 & 512 Hz → significant conductive hearing loss
• Rinne still positive at 1024 Hz → ABG not large enough to affect higher frequency

This pattern corresponds to an air–bone gap of \~30–45 dB

• ABG \~15–30 dB: Rinne may turn negative at 256 Hz only
• ABG \~30–45 dB: Negative at 256 & 512 Hz, positive at 1024 Hz
• ABG >45–60 dB: Negative at all frequencies

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The parents notice that their child is tired and that he has shortness of breath on climbing stairs and while lying down. What is the first investigation that you would do?
options: MRI to rule out enlarged heart
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chest x-ray

The first investigation to be done for a child who feels shortness of breath on climbing stairs and in the supine position is a chest x-ray.

The child having shortness of breath on climbing stairs is known as dyspnea on exertion. The most common cause is congestive heart failure. The child feeling shortness of breath in the supine position is orthopnea. It is relieved on sitting or standing.

Respiratory causes include asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disorder (COPD), pneumonia, and pulmonary embolism. Cardiovascular causes include congestive heart failure(CHF), pulmonary edema, valvular heart defect, and pulmonary hypertension.

Evaluation begins with assessing the airway, breathing, and circulation of the patient. Oxygen saturation can appear normal at rest, and hence oxygen saturation during physical activity should be obtained. A chest x-ray is the first diagnostic test which can show pulmonary pathology or pumonary edema and other signs of CHF that could help in identifying the cause and further evaluation.

Other options:

Option A: An echocardiogram can be done if the chest X-ray is abnormal. It is done to evaluate cardiac function, valvular function, and pericardial space.

Option C: Spirometry is done when the chest x-ray is normal. It is done to determine lung function. Abnormal spirometry can indicate either an obstructive pathology such as asthma, or COPD or a restrictive disease such as interstitial fibrosis.

Option D: Cardiac MRI (Magnetic resonance imaging) is an emerging modality done to look for cardiomegaly. It is for the accurate evaluation of left and right ventricular mass, size, and function. It is also used for localizing ischemic and non-ischemic causes such as myocarditis.
questions.learning: Chest x-ray — The first investigation to be done for a child who feels shortness of breath on climbing stairs and in the supine position is a chest x-ray.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most common type of gastric sarcoma?
questions.explanation: Gastric sarcomas represent a rare subset of stomach malignancies, accounting for less than 5% of all primary gastric tumors. Among the specific mesenchymal options listed, leiomyosarcoma is historically recognized as the most frequent primary sarcoma arising from the smooth muscle layers of the gastric wall. While many tumors previously labeled as leiomyosarcomas are currently classified as Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors (GIST), leiomyosarcoma remains the classical answer in standard surgical examinations. Lipomas (Option A) are benign fatty tumors that are rarely malignant. Glomus tumors (Option B) are typically benign perivascular lesions and are extremely uncommon in the stomach. Leioblastomas (Option D) are rare variants of smooth muscle tumors that are less common than standard leiomyosarcomas. Leiomyosarcomas often present with hematemesis or a large palpable mass. Because they originate in the muscularis propria, they tend to expand toward the serosa. Surgical resection remains the primary treatment modality for localized disease

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 52-year-old man with long-standing diabetes presents with fatigue and decreased urine output. Blood investigations are advised including serum urea estimation to assess renal function. Which of the following methods is most commonly used in clinical laboratories for estimation of serum urea?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Urease–GLDH method

• Serum urea estimation in clinical laboratories is most commonly performed using the Urease–GLDH (glutamate dehydrogenase) enzymatic method, which is highly specific, sensitive, and widely automated.
• Principle of Urease–GLDH method:

• Urease hydrolyzes urea → ammonia (NH₃) + CO₂
• Ammonia reacts with α-ketoglutarate in the presence of GLDH, converting NADH → NAD⁺
• The decrease in NADH absorbance (at 340 nm) is proportional to serum urea concentration

Why not other options:

A. Jaffe reaction:

• Used for serum creatinine, not urea
• Based on reaction with picric acid

C. Biuret method: Used for total protein estimation

D. Diazotization method: Used for bilirubin estimation
