questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Circuits between the basal ganglia and the motor cortex constitute the extrapyramidal system which controls muscle tone, body posture and the initiation of movement. Lesions of the extrapyramidal system present clinically with:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tremor and rigidity

The extrapyramidal system comprises the basal ganglia and their neural connections, which regulate muscle tone, posture, and the initiation and smooth coordination of voluntary movements. Unlike pyramidal tract lesions, extrapyramidal lesions do not cause muscle weakness; instead, they present with abnormal involuntary movements and altered muscle tone, classically tremor and rigidity.

• Clinical features of extrapyramidal lesions:

• Resting tremor
• Rigidity (lead-pipe/cogwheel)
• Bradykinesia
• Postural instability
• Chorea, athetosis, dystonia

• Common causes:

• Parkinson disease
• Huntington disease
• Wilson disease
• Drug-induced extrapyramidal syndrome (antipsychotics, metoclopramide)
questions.learning: Tremor and rigidity — The extrapyramidal system comprises the basal ganglia and their neural connections, which regulate muscle tone, posture, and the initiation and smooth coordination of voluntary movements.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the management of undulant fever?
questions.explanation: "Undulant fever" is the classic clinical description for Brucellosis, a zoonotic infection. The standard of care for uncomplicated brucellosis involves a combination antibiotic regimen to ensure eradication and prevent the high risk of relapse. The most widely recommended treatment is Doxycycline (100 mg twice daily) combined with Rifampicin (600–900 mg daily), both administered for 6 weeks. Monotherapy with doxycycline alone (Option A) is insufficient and associated with high failure rates. The combination with azithromycin (Option C) is not a standard or validated regimen. Ceftriaxone (Option D) is generally reserved for complicated cases, such as neurobrucellosis or endocarditis, and is not the first-line choice for uncomplicated undulant fever. Thus, the synergistic combination of doxycycline and rifampicin is the definitive management
questions.learning: "Undulant fever" is the classic clinical description for Brucellosis, a zoonotic infection. The standard of care for uncomplicated brucellosis involves a combination antibiotic regimen to ensure eradication and prevent the high risk of relapse.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 25-year-old man presents to the emergency department with features of gastric outlet obstruction, including persistent vomiting. As part of his initial management, which intravenous fluid would be the most appropriate choice?
questions.explanation: In cases of gastric outlet obstruction, persistent vomiting of gastric contents leads to a profound loss of hydrochloric acid and potassium. This results in the characteristic metabolic derangement: hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. The most appropriate and standard fluid for initial resuscitation in this scenario is Normal Saline (0.9% NaCl). Normal saline is chosen specifically because its high chloride content is essential to correct the underlying hypochloremia and halt the kidney's paradoxical acid excretion. Ringer's Lactate (Option B) is less ideal because the lactate is metabolized into bicarbonate, which can potentially worsen the existing metabolic alkalosis. Dextrose solutions (Options C and D) do not provide the necessary electrolytes (sodium and chloride) to fix the volume deficit and metabolic alkalosis. Therefore, intravenous normal saline constitutes the definitive pharmacological intervention for stabilizing the patient's chemistry before surgical correction
questions.learning: In cases of gastric outlet obstruction, persistent vomiting of gastric contents leads to a profound loss of hydrochloric acid and potassium. This results in the characteristic metabolic derangement: hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A 32-year-old traveler was lost in the desert. He was found after 2 days. He says that he has not consumed food or water for more than 24 hours. His vitals were normal. Which of the following part of the kidney must have been the site of maximum water reabsorption in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Proximal convoluted tubule

The proximal convoluted tubule is the site of maximum water reabsorption about 67% of the filtered water.

The driving force for water reabsorption is a transtubular osmotic gradient established by reabsorption of solutes.

Based on the ultrastructure proximal tubule is divided into three segments:

* S1 segment: 1st half of PCT

* S2 segment: 2nd half of PCT and 1st half of proximal straight tubule

* S3 segment: 2nd half of proximal straight tubule

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: General Pathology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman on chemotherapy for choriocarcinoma develops oral mucositis and GI ulceration. Which nucleotide synthesis step is most directly impaired by this drug?
options: Purine ring synthesis via glycinamide ribotide formation
Conversion of dUMP to dTMP via thymidylate synthase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Conversion of dUMP to dTMP via thymidylate synthase

Methotrexate, a key chemotherapeutic agent used in choriocarcinoma, inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), leading to depletion of tetrahydrofolate required for one-carbon transfer reactions. This impairs thymidylate synthase–mediated conversion of dUMP to dTMP, resulting in defective DNA synthesis and toxicity in rapidly dividing tissues such as the oral and gastrointestinal mucosa.

Why not the other options?

• A. Purine ring synthesis via Glycinamide ribotide formation – an early step in de novo purine synthesis; not the primary target tested here.
• C. Ribonucleotide reduction to deoxyribonucleotides – inhibited by hydroxyurea via ribonucleotide reductase inhibition.
• D. Orotic acid → UMP – Catalyzed by UMP synthase; defective in hereditary orotic aciduria.
questions.learning: Conversion of dUMP to dTMP via thymidylate synthase Methotrexate, a key chemotherapeutic agent used in choriocarcinoma, inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), leading to depletion of tetrahydrofolate required for one-carbon transfer reactions.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient's Hepatitis B virus serology panel shows HBsAg +ve, Anti-HBc IgM +ve, HBeAg –ve, Anti-HBs –ve. Choose the correct diagnosis.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acute hepatitis

• The single most decisive marker here is Anti-HBc IgM, which is the specific serological marker of recent/acute HBV infection (appears within weeks of HBsAg and persists \~6 months). Its presence, together with HBsAg positivity (active viral surface antigen) and absent anti-HBs (no recovery/immunity), confirms acute hepatitis B.
• The HBeAg-negative status does not exclude acute infection — it may reflect the late/resolving phase of acute illness (HBeAg is transient, appearing early and disappearing before HBsAg) or infection with a precore mutant strain, which cannot produce HBeAg despite active replication.

Other options:

• B. Chronic hepatitis → requires HBsAg persisting >6 months with Anti-HBc IgG (not IgM) positive.
• C. Window period → HBsAg negative and anti-HBs negative, with Anti-HBc IgM the ONLY positive marker — here HBsAg is positive, so it is excluded.
• D. Vaccination → isolated Anti-HBs positive; all core markers and HBsAg negative (vaccine contains only surface antigen).

Pearl:

• Anti-HBc IgM = acute infection / window period
• Anti-HBc IgG + Anti-HBs = past natural infection with recovery
• Anti-HBs alone = vaccination
• HBsAg > 6 months = chronic carrier
questions.learning: Acute hepatitis • — The single most decisive marker here is Anti-HBc IgM, which is the specific serological marker of recent/acute HBV infection (appears within weeks of HBsAg and persists \~6 months).

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: What is the needle shown in the picture ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tuohy needle

This is the image of a Tuohy needle that is used to provide epidural anesthesia. It can be recognized by its curved (Huber) tip and the markings made at 1 cm intervals along its length.

Other options:

Options A and B: The image below shows spinal needles are long thin needles that are classified based on their tip into:

* Cutting needles: Quincke-Babcock, Pitkin

* Pencil tip needles: Whitacre and Sprotte

Option D: The instrument below is the Quincke Needle used in spinal anesthesia.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with reduced visual acuity after cataract surgery and is found to have posterior capsular opacification on examination. Which type of laser is used for its treatment?
questions.explanation: Posterior capsular opacification (PCO), often referred to as "after-cataract," is the most common late complication following successful cataract surgery. It occurs when remaining lens epithelial cells migrate and proliferate across the posterior capsule, causing blurred vision and glare. The Neodymium-doped Yttrium Aluminum Garnet (Nd:YAG) laser is the gold standard for treating this condition through a procedure called a YAG laser capsulotomy. This laser uses photodisruption to create a small, clear opening in the center of the clouded capsule, instantly restoring visual clarity without the need for invasive surgery. Femto lasers (Option A) are used for precision incisions during the initial cataract surgery but not for PCO. Argon lasers (Option D) and Argon fluoride (Option C) produce thermal or photoablative effects used in retinal photocoagulation or refractive surgery (LASIK), respectively, but they lack the photodisruptive properties required to "punch" a hole in the posterior capsule. Consequently, the Nd:YAG laser remains the primary and most effective non-invasive treatment for secondary opacification
questions.learning: Posterior capsular opacification (PCO), often referred to as "after-cataract," is the most common late complication following successful cataract surgery.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Renal compensation in metabolic acidosis takes time because:
options: Initially the pH of tubular fluid increases
Low pH normally decreases bicarbonate excretion
It takes hours to days for kidney to synthesize enzymes that produce NH4+
Other ions in the tubule interfere with buffer action
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It takes hours to days for kidney to synthesize enzymes that produce NH4+

Compensation in metabolic acidosis happens late in the kidney because it takes hours to days for it to synthesize enzymes that produce NH4+(ammonium ions).

Acid-base balance equation: CO2 + H2O -----> H2CO3 -----> H+(acid) and HCO3-(base)

• First line of defence (in seconds): Buffers ( phosphate and ammonium )
• Second line of defence (in Minutes): Lungs
• Third line of defence (in hours - days): Kidney

The kidneys regulate the acid-base balance by two major mechanisms: the reabsorption of bicarbonate and the generation of new bicarbonate via ammonia production and distal nephron acid secretion. Urinary NH4+ is produced primarily in the proximal tubule cells by converting glutamine to glutamate.

Renal failure leads to a buildup of acids due to loss of excretory function of the kidney. The decreased glomerular filtration rate also leads to diminished excretion of the renal buffers phosphate and ammonium. Thus, bicarbonate reabsorption decreases, resulting in metabolic acidosis.
questions.learning: It takes hours to days for kidney to synthesize enzymes that produce NH4+ Compensation in metabolic acidosis happens late in the kidney because it takes hours to days for it to synthesize enzymes that produce NH4+(ammonium ions).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman experiences a difficult labor and, seven days after surgery, complains of continuous dribbling of urine. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical scenario of continuous, involuntary dribbling of urine following a difficult or obstructed labor is the classic presentation of a Vesicovaginal Fistula (VVF). VVF is an abnormal passage between the bladder and the vagina, usually caused by tissue necrosis from prolonged compression by the fetal head. In developing countries, obstructed labor is the most common cause. Ureterovaginal fistula (Option B) is more common following gynecological surgeries like hysterectomy rather than labor. Rectovaginal fistula (Option C) results in the passage of feces or gas through the vagina, not urine. Vesicouterine fistula (Option D) involves a connection to the uterus and often presents with menstrual blood in the urine (menouria). Diagnosis is usually confirmed via a dye test (methylene blue) or cystoscopy. Thus, the history of difficult labor combined with urinary incontinence makes VVF the most likely diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical scenario of continuous, involuntary dribbling of urine following a difficult or obstructed labor is the classic presentation of a Vesicovaginal Fistula (VVF).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child suffering from steroid-dependent nephrotic syndrome is brought to the OPD for vaccination. Which of the following is true about vaccination in this child?
options: All live vaccines under NIS can be given as per schedule
All killed vaccines under NIS can be given
Only pneumococcal vaccine should be given to the child in acute phase
Live vaccines are contraindicated in the child’s sibling
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. All killed vaccines under NIS can be given

In a child with steroid-dependent nephrotic syndrome, all killed vaccines can be given.

Option A: Live virus vaccines are administered with caution in children receiving corticosteroid therapy. They can be given to patients in whom the prednisone dose is below 1mg/kg daily or 2mg/kg on alternate days. If the patient is receiving corticosteroid-sparing agents (cyclophosphamide, cyclosporine), live virus vaccines are contraindicated.

Option C: Only live vaccines are contraindicated in this child. Full pneumococcal vaccination (with the 13-valent conjugate vaccine and 23-valent polysaccharide vaccine) and influenza vaccination can be given annually to the child and their household contacts.

Option D: Immunization of siblings/healthy household contacts with live vaccines is necessary to reduce the risk of infection transmission to the immunosuppressed child. Direct exposure to the gastrointestinal/respiratory secretions of the household contacts is avoided for about 3-6 weeks after vaccination.

Minimal change nephrotic syndrome is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome. It is characterized by heavy proteinuria, edema, hypoalbuminemia, and hyperlipidemia. The diagnosis is confirmed by performing a urinalysis and urine protein: creatinine ratio. Nephrotic range proteinuria is proteinuria greater than 3.5 g per 24 hours (3+ or 4+) or a urine protein : creatinine ratio exceeding 2.

The recommended initial treatment for nephrotic syndrome is a daily dose of 2mg/kg (max 60mg) of prednisolone for 6 weeks followed by an alternate dose of 1.5mg/kg (max 40mg) for the next 6-8 weeks.

Definitions regarding the course of nephrotic syndrome:

• Frequently relapsing nephrotic syndrome: ≥2 relapses in 6 months or 3 or more relapses in 12 months.
• Steroid-dependent nephrotic syndrome: Relapse during steroid tapering or within 2 weeks of discontinuation.
• Steroid resistance: Failure to achieve remission despite therapy with daily prednisolone for 6 weeks

Alternative drugs used in steroid-dependent patients, frequent relapsers, steroid-resistant patients, and those with severe corticosteroid toxicity are cyclophosphamide, calcineurin inhibitors: cyclosporine and Tacrolimus, mycophenolate, levamisole, and rituximab (a chimeric monoclonal antibody against CD20).
questions.learning: All killed vaccines under NIS can be given — In a child with steroid-dependent nephrotic syndrome, all killed vaccines can be given. Option A: Live virus vaccines are administered with caution in children receiving corticosteroid therapy.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A girl presented with multiple episodes of loss of consciousness. The episodes usually happen in the presence of the family members in the morning. She regains consciousness after 15 to 30 minutes and usually remembers the events during these episodes. There is no history of tongue bite or urinary incontinence. What should be done in this scenario?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Start behavioural therapy

In this scenario, the girl is experiencing episodes of loss of consciousness that may suggest conversion disorder. The most appropriate management is to start behavioural therapy to help address her symptoms and underlying stressors.

Conversion disorder, also referred to as functional neurological symptom disorder in the DSM-5, involves symptoms or deficits that affect voluntary motor or sensory functions, suggesting another medical condition. However, these symptoms are believed to arise from psychological factors, often triggered by conflicts or stressors. The symptoms are not intentionally produced, are not the result of substance use, and are not limited to pain or sexual issues. The primary gain associated with conversion disorder is psychological rather than social, monetary, or legal.

Common presenting symptoms include:

• Non-epileptic seizures
• Weakness and/or paralysis
• Movement disorders
• Speech or visual impairment
• Swallowing difficulty
• Sensory disturbances
• Cognitive symptoms

Resolution of conversion disorder symptoms often occurs spontaneously but can be enhanced through supportive or behavioural therapy. For patients who are resistant to psychotherapy, it can be beneficial to focus on stress and coping strategies rather than directly addressing their symptoms as imaginary, as this may exacerbate their condition.

Additional techniques, such as hypnosis, anxiolytics, and behavioural relaxation exercises, may also be effective in managing symptoms. In certain cases, medications like parenteral amobarbital or lorazepam can help gather further information, especially if the patient has experienced a recent traumatic event.

Psychodynamic approaches, including psychoanalysis and insight-oriented psychotherapy, allow patients to explore their internal conflicts and the symbolic meanings of their symptoms.
questions.learning: Start behavioural therapy — In this scenario, the girl is experiencing episodes of loss of consciousness that may suggest conversion disorder. The most appropriate management is to start behavioural therapy to help address her symptoms and underlying…

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Name the surgical procedure in which the instrument shown below is used?
questions.explanation: The instrument shown is a bone-biting punch (specifically a Citelli or Hajek punch), which is an essential tool in Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR). During a DCR, the surgeon must remove a portion of the lacrimal bone and the frontal process of the maxilla to create an ostium (opening) into the nasal cavity. This punch is designed specifically to clip away these small sections of bone safely. Evisceration (Option A) and Enucleation (Option B) are procedures to remove the internal contents or the entirety of the globe, respectively; these surgeries involve scalpels, scissors, and distractors, not specialized bone-biting punches. Cataract surgery (Option C) is a microscopic intraocular procedure utilizing fine forceps and phacoemulsification probes rather than heavy orthopedic-style tools. Therefore, because the creation of a bony window is the defining mechanical step of DCR, the bone-biting punch is definitively associated with that procedure. Recognizing specialized instrumentation is a core skill in surgical clinical examinations

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In which part of the fallopian tube does fertilization occur?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ampulla

Fertilization usually occurs in the ampulla of the fallopian tube.

During ovulation, the ovum is released and it enters the fallopian tube. It is propelled towards the uterine cavity by the peristaltic action of the fallopian tubes, prostaglandins in the male seminal fluid and oxytocin. It can only be fertilized within 24 hours of ovulation.  If coitus takes place during this period, the spermatozoa swimming up into the tubes meet the ovum in the ampulla.
questions.learning: Ampulla Fertilization usually occurs in the ampulla of the fallopian tube. During ovulation, the ovum is released and it enters the fallopian tube.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the condition characterized by painless vision loss among the options provided?
questions.explanation: The image shows a classic “blood and thunder” appearance of the retina, characterized by diffuse retinal hemorrhages, dilated and tortuous veins, and optic disc edema. This is typical of central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO). CRVO occurs due to thrombosis of the central retinal vein, leading to impaired venous drainage, retinal ischemia, and widespread hemorrhages. Clinically, CRVO presents with sudden, painless loss of vision, which is a key feature highlighted in the question. The involvement is diffuse, affecting the entire retina, which helps distinguish it from branch occlusions. Why other options are wrong: (B) Branch retinal vein occlusion (BRVO) → hemorrhages limited to one quadrant, not diffuse (C) Central retinal arterial occlusion (CRAO) → pale retina with cherry-red spot, not hemorrhagic (D) Branch retinal arterial occlusion (BRAO) → localized retinal whitening
questions.learning: The image shows a classic “blood and thunder” appearance of the retina, characterized by diffuse retinal hemorrhages, dilated and tortuous veins, and optic disc edema.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What is the earliest indicator of left atrial enlargement in cases of mitral stenosis? (NEET PG 2015)
options: Elevation of the right main bronchus
Enlargement of the left atrial appendage
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Enlargement of the left atrial appendage

In mitral stenosis, left atrial enlargement follows a predictable radiographic sequence. The left atrial appendage (left auricle) forms part of the normal left heart border between the pulmonary trunk and the left ventricle. It is the first structure to enlarge, producing straightening — or even bulging — of the left heart border, obliterating the normal concavity. This is the earliest and most sensitive plain film sign.

The sequence of progressive left atrial enlargement on CXR is:

| Stage | Radiographic Sign

| ----- | -----------------

| Earliest | Straightening of left heart border (LAA prominence)

| Intermediate | Splaying of carina (>70°), double density sign

| Late | Elevation of left main bronchus, posterior oesophageal displacement

Why the other options are wrong:

• Elevation of the right main bronchus (A) — not a feature of LA enlargement; it is the left main bronchus that is elevated and splayed as the LA expands superiorly
• Widening of the carina (C) — occurs after significant LA enlargement; an intermediate sign, not the earliest
• Oesophageal displacement (D) — seen on barium swallow or lateral CXR only after substantial posterior LA enlargement; a late sign

High-yield pearl: The four classic signs of LA enlargement in mitral stenosis on PA CXR in order — left heart border straightening → double density sign → left main bronchus elevation → splayed carina. Oesophageal displacement is best seen on lateral view with barium.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Ammonia in the brain is detoxified to form _________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glutamine

Ammonia in the brain is detoxified to form glutamine.

Glutamine synthetase combines ammonia with glutamate to form glutamine. It requires the hydrolysis of ATP.

Deficiency of glutamine synthetase in neonates results in severe brain damage, multiorgan failure, and death.

Note: Glutamine is the transport form of ammonia from the brain and intestine to the liver; while alanine is the transport form from the muscle.
questions.learning: Glutamine Ammonia in the brain is detoxified to form glutamine. Glutamine synthetase combines ammonia with glutamate to form glutamine.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A middle-aged woman develops hoarseness following a total thyroidectomy. On laryngoscopic examination, there is complete vocal cord palsy on left side. What is the best management in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Speech therapy, medialization of cord

Unilateral vocal cord paralysis following thyroidectomy is most commonly due to recurrent laryngeal nerve injury and leads to hoarseness due to a paramedian, immobile vocal cord.

Best management: Speech therapy + medialization of vocal cord

• Injection laryngoplasty or thyroplasty
• Improves glottic closure and voice quality
• Prevents aspiration

Why not others:

• Tracheostomy → only for bilateral paralysis with airway compromise
• Lateralization → done in bilateral paralysis to improve airway
• Gutzmann maneuver → used in functional voice disorders
questions.learning: Speech therapy, medialization of cord Unilateral vocal cord paralysis following thyroidectomy is most commonly due to recurrent laryngeal nerve injury and leads to hoarseness due to a paramedian, immobile vocal cord.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following is seen on the microscopy in patients with lichen planus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Colloid bodies

Colloid bodies can be seen on microscopy in patients with lichen planus.

Lichen planus (LP) is an idiopathic inflammatory disease affecting the skin and mucous membrane. Microscopy will show :

* Acanthosis of the epidermis.

* Irregular thickening of the granular layer.

* Hyperkeratosis.

* Colloid (civatte) bodies due to degenerating basal epidermal cells.

* Sawtooth appearance of rete ridges.

* Max Joseph spaces due to focal separation from the dermis.

* Band‐like infiltrate of lymphocytes and histiocytes near the dermo-epidermal junction.

Patients present with pruritic, purple, polygonal, papules. The lesions have thin white lines on their surface known as Wickham’s striae. They are commonly seen on the volar aspect of the wrists, the lumbar region, and around the ankles.

The mucosal involvement is also seen. The commonest mucosal sites are buccal mucosa and tongue, rarely it can also be found on the anus and genitalia.

Nail involvement can be seen as thinning of nail plate leading to an exaggeration of longitudinal lines, and linear depressions. The nails can also be destroyed leading to anonychia. Involvement of nail bed may give rise to longitudinal melanonychia, hyperpigmentation, subungual hyperkeratosis, or onycholysis.

Other options

Option A- Pautrier's microabscess is the intraepidermal lymphocytic microabscess in the absence of marked spongiosis. The cells within the epidermis may show nuclear hyperchromatism or atypia. It is seen in Mycosis fungoides.

The image below shows atypical lymphocytes showing epidermotropism and the formation of Pautrier's microabscesses in mycosis fungoides.

Option B- Munro microabscess is the accumulation of neutrophils in the stratum corneum. The lesions present as well-demarcated red scaly plaques. They might have a circle of clear zone around it which is known as the Woronoff ring. This finding is seen in psoriasis.

Option D- Michaelis–Gutmann bodies are large, foamy macrophages mixed with occasional multinucleate giant cells and lymphocytes. It occurs due to defective phagosomes presenting as basophilic concretions. These are pathognomonic of malakoplakia. Grossly, malakoplakia appears as soft, yellow, slightly raised mucosal plaques.
questions.learning: Colloid bodies Colloid bodies can be seen on microscopy in patients with lichen planus. Lichen planus (LP) is an idiopathic inflammatory disease affecting the skin and mucous membrane.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following muscle is responsible for ptosis in horner's syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Muller's muscle

Ptosis in Horner's syndrome is due to the paralysis of Muller's muscle. Muller's muscle(superior tarsal muscle) maintains the elevation of the upper eyelid. It is innervated by the sympathetic nervous system.

Fasanella-Servat operation is indicated in cases having mild ptosis(< 2 mm) and good levator function. In this surgery, the upper tarsal border along with its attached Muller’s muscle and conjunctiva are resected.
questions.learning: Muller's muscle Ptosis in Horner's syndrome is due to the paralysis of Muller's muscle. Muller's muscle(superior tarsal muscle) maintains the elevation of the upper eyelid.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which one of the following terms correctly denotes the mechanism and phenotypic changes that are not a result of variation in the underlying DNA sequence, but are caused by secondary modifications of DNA or histones in response to other heritable or environmental influences?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Epigenetics

Epigenetics refers to heritable changes in gene expression and phenotype that occur without alteration of the underlying DNA sequence. These changes can result from modifications such as:

• DNA methylation
• Histone modification
• Chromatin remodeling
• Regulatory non-coding RNAs

Why not other options?

• A. Pleiotropy: One gene produces multiple phenotypic effects.
• B. Epigenetics: Correct. Changes in gene expression without changing the DNA sequence.
• C. Co-dominance: Both alleles are expressed simultaneously in the heterozygous state.
• D. Epistasis: One gene masks or modifies the expression of another gene.
questions.learning: Epigenetics Epigenetics refers to heritable changes in gene expression and phenotype that occur without alteration of the underlying DNA sequence. These changes can result from modifications such as: • DNA methylation • Histone modification • Chromatin…

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 26-year-old woman underwent a workup for primary infertility. On hysterosalpingography, there was a bilateral cornual block. What is the next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hysteroscopy and laparoscopy-guided surgery

In the given clinical scenario, the next step in management will be hysteroscopy and laparoscopy-guided surgery.

Tubal contractions, particularly cornual spasms, can give an incorrect impression of proximal fallopian tube obstruction (a false-positive result) on hysterosalpingography. Laparoscopy with chromotubation is therefore considered to confirm the diagnosis of cornual spasm. Laparoscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic in this condition.

Hysteroscopy is an operative procedure that provides an endoscopic view of the endometrial cavity and tubal ostia via the cervix, performed in the preovulatory phase. It can be diagnostic or therapeutic. It is the gold standard investigation for visualizing the uterine cavity and tubal ostia.

Therapeutic indications of hysteroscopy
Diagnostic indications of hysteroscopy

• Uterine septum
• Asherman syndrome
• Retained IUCD
• Polypectomy
• Submucous fibroid
• Abnormal uterine bleeding
• Tubal sterilization using sclerosing agents

• To study the endocervical mucosal lining
• Congenital malformations of the uterus
• Endometrial tuberculosis
• Misplaced IUCD
• Endometrial lesions
• Endometrial polyp
• Asherman syndrome
• Cornual tubal blockage

Contraindications to hysteroscopy are as follows:

• Acute genital tract infection (Eg: genital herpes infection)
• Viable intrauterine pregnancy
• During menstruation, the view is obscured, and the infection rate is high.
• Scarred uterus and enlarged uterus of size ≥ 12 weeks are relative contraindications.
• Cervical stenosis can cause cervical tears and uterine perforation.
• Cardiopulmonary disorder due to increased risk of fluid overload and pulmonary edema.
• Known cases of cervical cancer

Laparoscopy is the gold standard for the evaluation of tubal factors in infertility, commonly done in the proliferative phase. It can be diagnostic or therapeutic.

Diagnostic
Therapeutic (Operative)

• Age >35 years
• History of pelvic pain, dyspareunia, pelvic surgery, adhesions
• Abnormal HSG
• Failure to conceive after a reasonable period (6 months) with normal HSG
• Women with comorbid pelvic pathology (PID, endometriosis)

• Unexplained infertility
• Reconstructive tubal surgery
• Adhesiolysis
• Fulguration of endometriotic implants
• Ovarian drilling in PCOS
• GIFT and ZIFT procedures

Benefits of laparoscopic evaluation:

• Tubes: For detection of tubal patency, block (site and side), motility, hydrosalpinx change, peritubal adhesions, fimbrial agglutination
• Ovaries: PCOS changes, endometriosis, PID, adhesions
• Uterus: Anomalies, fibroids
• Peritoneal factors: Adhesions, PID, endometriosis, tuberculosis
• Therapy at the same sitting (as appropriate)
questions.learning: Hysteroscopy and laparoscopy-guided surgery — In the given clinical scenario, the next step in management will be hysteroscopy and laparoscopy-guided surgery.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: According to the New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional classification, into which class does a person fall if they have mild limitation of physical activity, develop dyspnea with ordinary activities, but are comfortable at rest?
questions.explanation: The New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional classification provides a simple way of classifying the extent of heart failure. Class II (Option B) is defined as "slight limitation of physical activity" where patients are comfortable at rest, but ordinary physical activity (such as walking on level ground or climbing one flight of stairs) results in fatigue, palpitations, or dyspnea. Class I (Option A) involves no limitation of physical activity. Class III (Option C) involves a "marked limitation" where even less-than-ordinary activity causes symptoms. Class IV (Option D) is characterized by an inability to carry out any physical activity without discomfort and symptoms may be present even at rest. This classification is widely used to monitor the progression of heart failure and the response to medical therapy. Therefore, the description of mild restriction during ordinary activity corresponds precisely to NYHA Class II
questions.learning: The New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional classification provides a simple way of classifying the extent of heart failure. Class II (Option B) is defined as "slight limitation of physical activity" where patients are comfortable at rest, but…

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 9-month-old child is brought to the PHC with a fever and cough. She is feeding well and has normal urine output. On examination, a respiratory rate of 48 breaths/min is found and no chest indrawing is seen. What is the next step of management?
options: Explain danger signs and send home
No pneumonia - Give amoxyclav + paracetamol and send home
Refer as the child has severe pneumonia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Explain danger signs and send home

In the given clinical scenario, a 9-month-old child with normal breathing (> 50/min RR for infants 2 months to 12 months is considered as fast breathing) and no chest indrawing is seen. So, the next step in management would be to explain danger signs and send them home.

According to the IMNCI, three key clinical signs are used to assess a sick child with suspected pneumonia:

• Respiratory rate (RR): distinguishes children who have pneumonia from those who do not. Children are classified under pneumonia if:

• > 60 breaths per minute if age  is < 2 months
• > 50/min RR for infants 2 months to 12 months
• > 40/min RR for children 12 months to 5 years of age

• Lower chest wall indrawing refers to the indrawing of the lower chest wall with respect to the child's breathing and indicates pneumonia
• Stridor indicates those with severe pneumonia requiring hospital admission.

The revised classification of acute respiratory infections is simplified to include only two categories of pneumonia:

• Cough and cold, no pneumonia - requires home remedy
• Pneumonia - with fast breathing and/or chest indrawing, which requires home therapy with oral amoxicillin.
• Severe pneumonia - pneumonia with any general danger sign, which requires a referral and injectable therapy.

Danger signs of severe pneumonia are:

• Not able to drink
• Persistent vomiting
• Convulsions
• Lethargic or unconscious
• Stridor in a calm child
• Severe malnutrition
questions.learning: Explain danger signs and send home — In the given clinical scenario, a 9-month-old child with normal breathing (> 50/min RR for infants 2 months to 12 months is considered as fast breathing) and no chest indrawing is seen.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presented with multiple yellowish raised plaques on eyelids, xanthomas on the achilles tendon. What is the likely cause for the patient's presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Familial hypercholesterolemia

The clinical presentation with yellowish, raised plaques on eyelids, and tendon xanthomas points to a diagnosis of familial hypercholesterolemia (FH).

Familial hypercholesterolemia (type IIa hyperlipoproteinemia) is an inherited disorder due to defects in LDL receptors and Apo B100. This decreases the uptake of Low-density lipoprotein and cholesterol leading to their increased levels in the blood. The increased LDL accumulates in the blood vessels causing atherosclerosis (premature coronary artery disease)and in the Achilles tendon causing tendon xanthomas. Xanthomas are tumorous masses produced by foamy cell clusters (lipid-laden macrophages) found in the connective tissue of the skin and tendons. Patients can also have yellowish plaques around the eyes (Xanthelasma) and corneal arcus.

Treatment includes lifestyle changes, restriction of a fatty diet, and pharmacotherapy with statins in heterozygous FH patients.

The images below show Achilles tendon xanthoma and xanthelasma respectively:

Other options:

Option B: Tangier’s disease is a hypolipoproteinemia caused by a mutation of the ABCA1 gene. Enlarged orange tonsils are pathognomonic. Low HDL levels are seen. There is an increased risk for atherosclerosis.

The image below shows enlarged yellow-orange coloured tonsils in Tangier's disease.

Option C: Xanthomatosis is the deposition of lipids in various parts of the body like tendon xanthomas, xanthelasma, eruptive and tuberous xanthomas. This is a sign of underlying lipid metabolism disorders.

Option D: Fabry's disease is a lysosomal storage disorder with a defect in alpha-galactosidase. It causes angiokeratomas, hypohidrosis and characteristic Maltese cross deposits in urine.
questions.learning: Familial hypercholesterolemia — The clinical presentation with yellowish, raised plaques on eyelids, and tendon xanthomas points to a diagnosis of familial hypercholesterolemia (FH).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the cranial nerve that passes through the marked foramen marked in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Oculomotor nerve

The marked structure is the superior orbital fissure and the oculomotor nerve passes through this fissure.

Superior orbital fissure is divided into three compartments by the common tendinous ring. The oculomotor nerve passes through its intermediate compartment.
questions.learning: Oculomotor nerve — The marked structure is the superior orbital fissure and the oculomotor nerve passes through this fissure. Superior orbital fissure is divided into three compartments by the common tendinous ring.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presents to your outpatient department with the findings shown in the image below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Kwashiorkor

The image showing flaky paint dermatosis is seen characteristically in Kwashiorkor.

Kwashiorkor is a form of severe acute malnutrition (SAM) characterized by edema and apathy. It usually affects infants and children, most often around the age of weaning till the age of 5.

Children with kwashiorkor have moon-shaped faces. Edema is most likely to appear first in the feet and then in the lower legs soon developing into generalized edema. Abdominal distension occurs with or without dilated bowel loops and hepatomegaly and fatty infiltrate.

Skin changes occur over the swollen limbs and include dark, crackled peeling patches with pale skin underneath forming patches of hyper and hypopigmentation called flaky paint dermatosis or crazy paving. The skin gets easily infected.

The hair is dull, brittle, sparse, and can easily be pulled out. It may lose its curl. In dark-haired children, the hair may turn pale or reddish. Alternating bands of light and normal color hair may be seen, known as the flag sign. Children are miserable, apathetic, and often refuse to eat. There is marked muscle atrophy and growth retardation.

Clinical features seen in marasmus are:

* Simian facies

* Lethargic and irritable,apathetic

* Bradycardia

* Thin, dry skin

* Thin and brittle hair,easily pluckable.

* hypotension, and hypothermia

* The reduction of buccal fat pad gives rise to a wrinkled or aged look, while the term “baggy pants appearance” describes sagging skin of the buttocks that hangs downward.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A wildlife photographer returns from a trip to sub-Saharan Africa and presents with acute fever, jaundice, and hemorrhagic symptoms. Liver biopsy shows intranuclear Councilman/Torres bodies. Which vaccine could have prevented this infection?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 17D

Yellow fever, a viral hemorrhagic disease caused by a Flavivirus, presents with fever, jaundice, and hemorrhage, and is characterized histologically by Councilman bodies (apoptotic hepatocytes) in the liver.

·         Transmission: Aedes mosquito (endemic in sub-Saharan Africa, South America)

·   Clinical features:

o    Fever, myalgia

o    Jaundice + hemorrhage (“yellow” fever)

o    Severe cases → liver failure

·         Prevention: 17D vaccine = live attenuated vaccine → highly effective

Why not others:

·         Nakayama vaccine: Japanese encephalitis

·         Weigl’s vaccine: epidemic typhus

·         Jeryl Lynn strain: mumps vaccine

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child with recurrent episodes of cough and cold is diagnosed with an acyanotic congenital heart disease suggestive of a ventricular septal defect (VSD). Which type of murmur is most commonly heard?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pansystolic

Ventricular septal defect (VSD) is the most common congenital heart disease and classically produces a harsh pansystolic (holosystolic) murmur, best heard at the left lower sternal border due to left-to-right shunting across the ventricular septum.

Key clinical features:

• Small VSD: Loud, harsh pansystolic murmur with a palpable thrill.
• Large VSD: Softer murmur (due to equalization of ventricular pressures), recurrent respiratory infections, failure to thrive, and signs of congestive heart failure.

Exam Pearl:

• VSD → Pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border.
• Large left-to-right shunts may produce an apical mid-diastolic flow murmur due to increased mitral inflow, but the characteristic murmur of VSD remains the pansystolic murmur.
• Untreated large VSDs can progress to pulmonary hypertension and Eisenmenger syndrome, resulting in reversal of the shunt (right-to-left) and cyanosis.
questions.learning: Pansystolic Ventricular septal defect (VSD) is the most common congenital heart disease and classically produces a harsh pansystolic (holosystolic) murmur, best heard at the left lower sternal border due to left-to-right shunting across the ventricular septum.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A mother delivers a baby in a rural area with the assistance of a skilled birth attendant. The attendant cuts the umbilical cord cleanly, ties the ends with new threads, bathes the baby with warm water, wipes the baby’s eyes with a sterile wet cloth from the medial to lateral corner, and then hands the baby to the mother for skin-to-skin contact. Which of these steps is incorrect?
options: Using new threads to tie the ends of the umbilical cord
Wiping the baby’s eyes from medial to lateral corner
Bathing the child with warm water
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Bathing the child with warm water

The incorrect step is bathing the child with warm water immediately after birth. It is generally recommended to delay bathing in the immediate newborn period to help maintain the baby’s body temperature and prevent hypothermia.

Other options:

Option A: Using new threads to tie the ends of the umbilical cord is correct and helps prevent infection and ensure proper cord care.

Option B: Wiping the baby’s eyes from the medial to lateral corner is appropriate to prevent the spread of any potential infection from the eye’s inner to outer corners.

Option C: Skin-to-skin contact with the mother is beneficial as it helps stabilize the baby’s temperature, promotes bonding, and supports early breastfeeding.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old female patient has hypokalemia, hypertension and metabolic alkalosis. What is the most likely etiology?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Liddle's syndrome

Hypertension with hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis is seen in Liddle's syndrome.

Liddle's syndrome (pseudo aldosteronism) is an autosomal dominant condition that is caused due to the increased activation of ENaC channels. This causes increased reabsorption of Na+ exchanged for K+ causing hypokalemia. Increased Na absorption leads to hypertension, and there is also a loss of H+ ion with K+, leading to metabolic alkalosis. It is associated with low renin and low aldosterone levels.
questions.learning: Liddle's syndrome Hypertension with hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis is seen in Liddle's syndrome. Liddle's syndrome (pseudo aldosteronism) is an autosomal dominant condition that is caused due to the increased activation of ENaC channels.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Revised A 24-year-old primigravidae at 38 weeks gestation presents to the antenatal clinic with complaints of faintness on lying down for the past one week. She feels better when she turns to a side and while in sitting position. What is the reason for her symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. IVC compression

This is a case of IVC compression known as supine hypotension syndrome (postural hypotension).

* During late pregnancy, the gravid uterus produces a compression effect on the IVC when the patient is in supine position. In majority of pregnants, to compensate/avoid this effect there will be opening up of collaterals of paravertebral/Azygous veins.

* When there is failure of opening up of collaterals, venous return of the heart is curtailed leading to hypotension, tachycardia and syncope.

* The normal BP is quickly restored by turning the patient to lateral position.Hence pregnant females are adviced to lie in lateral positions (left lateral is better).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Oral hairy leukoplakia is associated with which of the following infections?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Epstein Barr virus

Oral hairy leukoplakia (OHL) is due to the reactivation of Epstein Barr Virus (EBV) infection and usually occurs in association with immunodeficiency due to HIV infection.

Oral hairy leukoplakia in HIV-infected patients presents with white corrugated plaque over the lateral border of the tongue, which cannot be rubbed off.

Other conditions associated with EBV infection are

* Glandular fever: fever, pharyngitis, and posterior cervical lymphadenopathy

* Rash triggered by Ampicillin

* Burkitt's Lymphoma

* Nasopharyngeal carcinoma

* EBV‐associated lymphoproliferative disease

* Age‐related EBV‐associated B‐cell lymphoma

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 17-year-old boy presents to the clinic with complaints of a painless lump on the lateral aspect of his left knee. The radiograph of the patient is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Osteochondroma

The given radiograph and clinical vignette suggests the diagnosis of osteochondroma.

Osteochondromas are benign bone tumors that present commonly in the adolescent age group. They usually present as painless masses in long bones like the femur or humerus. They are seen as well-defined bony protuberances which may be pedunculated or sessile. Pedunculated osteochondromas point away from the joint, towards the diaphysis. The cortex and cancellous bone of osteochondroma blend with that of the host bone. MRI shows a classical cartilaginous cap.

Osteochondromas usually grow with skeletal maturity and stop once growth stops. They rarely undergo malignant transformation.

Treatment is not indicated if the lesion does not produce symptoms. Excision can be done for large lesions with local pressure effects.

Other options:

Option A: Enchondroma is an intramedullary tumor of hyaline cartilage. They are asymptomatic and discovered incidentally. They are usually seen in individuals aged 20 to 50 years, in the tubular bones of the hands and feet. Radiographically, it appears as a central lesion with well-defined, rounded, edges and a thin rind of reactive sclerosis.

Option B: Chondroblastoma is a benign tumor and presents as a painful mass that causes effusion or stiffness. On x-ray, they are seen as round or oval lytic lesions in the epiphysis. The bony cortex is not breached but can appear expanded. The common sites are the ends of long bones. Microscopically, chondroblastoma consists of a sheet of chondroblasts embedded in the chondroid matrix. The calcification is often present and surrounds individual cells giving the appearance of ‘chicken wire.’

Option D:  Giant cell tumor, also known as osteoclastoma, is a benign bone tumor. However, it exhibits locally aggressive behaviour despite its benign nature. It usually affects young adults with a peak incidence in the age group of 20–45 years. It presents as a painful mass. A plain radiograph reveals an eccentric, expansile, lobulated lytic lesion (soap bubble appearance) in the epiphysis. There is minimal calcification within the tumor. Biopsy reveals osteoclast-like giant cells scattered among round or spindle-shaped mononuclear cells.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: “Leukemia”, as an occupational cancer, is most commonly related to the exposure to which one of the following industrial chemicals?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Benzol

Benzene (benzol) is a well-established occupational carcinogen associated particularly with leukemia, especially acute myeloid leukemia (AML).

Why not the other options?

• A. Mineral oil: Associated mainly with skin cancers after prolonged occupational exposure.
• B. Auramine: Associated with bladder cancer in occupational exposure.
• C. β-naphthylamine: Classically associated with urinary bladder carcinoma.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with polyuria, polydipsia, lethargy and abdominal pain. She also gives a history of mood disorders and recurrent kidney stones. Which of the following investigations would not be useful in arriving at a diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Angiography of renal arteries

The given clinical scenario of recurrent kidney stones, mood disorder and features of hypercalcemia (polyuria, polydipsia) is suggestive of primary hyperparathyroidism. Angiography of renal arteries is not a useful investigation for hyperparathyroidism.

Investigations in primary hyperparathyroidism: Ultrasonography of the neck is a safe and widely used technique for localising abnormal parathyroid glands.

Dual-energy radiographic absorptiometry (DEXA) is useful for demonstrating skeletal involvement in primary hyperparathyroidism. Nuclear medicine scanning with radiolabelled Sestamibi is also a widely used technique. Sestamibi accumulates in parathyroid adenomas. This radionuclide is concentrated in the thyroid and parathyroid tissue but usually washes out of normal thyroid tissue in under an hour. It persists in abnormal parathyroid tissue. The image given below shows a radiolabeled Sestamibi scan.

Clinical features of hyperparathyroidism:

* Bones:

* Pathological fractures Subperiosteal bone resorption - 2nd and 3rd digits, most common in radial aspect.

* Salt and pepper skull

* Osteitis fibrosa cystica or VonReckling Hausen’s disease

* Stones:

* Multiple and recurrent renal stones - most common

* Nephrocalcinosis

* Abdominal groans - colicky due to pancreatitis
Psychiatric overtones - raised PTH causing CNS depression and psychiatric symptoms
Band keratopathy
Features of hypercalcemia - vomiting, confusion, ECG changes: increased PR interval, shortened QT interval

The image given below shows a salt and pepper skull seen in hyperparathyroidism.
questions.learning: Angiography of renal arteries — The given clinical scenario of recurrent kidney stones, mood disorder and features of hypercalcemia (polyuria, polydipsia) is suggestive of primary hyperparathyroidism.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: For assessing the viral load in a test sample, which test utilizes the provided graph?
questions.explanation: The graph depicted is an "amplification curve" characteristic of Real-time Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT-PCR). This technique measures the increase in fluorescence (representing DNA amplification) during each cycle of the PCR process. The " value" (cycle threshold) is the point where the fluorescence crosses the background noise; a lower value indicates a higher initial "viral load" in the sample. Antigen tests (Option A) are rapid immunoassays that do not involve cycles or DNA amplification. While CBNAAT (Option C) and TruNat (Option D) are also molecular tests that use similar technology, "Real-time RT-PCR" is the broader, fundamental category that this specific type of cycle-fluorescence graph represents. During the COVID-19 pandemic, this graph became the global standard for identifying infected individuals and assessing how infectious they might be based on the value

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 34-year-old G3P2L2 woman with a past history of Caesarean section and a Dilatation and curettage , presents to the ER with hypotension, tachycardia, and severe abdominal pain. On examination, fetal parts are palpable in the abdomen and Fetal heart rate is weak. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Uterine rupture

The diagnosis of the given clinical scenario is uterine rupture.

Previous cesarean section and Dilatation and curettage are both potential risk factors for scar dehiscence and uterine rupture. Hypotension, tachycardia, dizziness, confusion, abdominal pain, scar site tenderness are all the signs of uterine rupture. Rarely, Hemoperitoneum can irritate the diaphragm and cause chest and shoulder tip pain.

CTG in uterine rupture will show non-reassuring variable fetal heart rate which might progress to late decelerations and bradycardia.

Differential diagnoses for uterine rupture:

* Pre-eclampsia

* Eclampsia

* Pulmonary embolism - amniotic fluid embolism / venous embolism

* Abruptio placenta

* Anaphylaxis to anesthesia

* Peripartum cardiomyopathy

Management of uterine rupture:

* confirm the fetal station and arrest of labor

* Stabilize the patient's vitals

* Immediate cesarean section should be performed, immediately/ as early as possible to avoid neurological or hypoxic sequelae in newborns.

* Depending on the extent of rupture and vitals on the table decision of uterine suturing or hysterectomy or sub-total hysterectomy may be taken.
questions.learning: Uterine rupture — The diagnosis of the given clinical scenario is uterine rupture. Previous cesarean section and Dilatation and curettage are both potential risk factors for scar dehiscence and uterine rupture.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A diabetic worker sustains a stab injury to the central part of his palm. Three days later, he develops swelling, severe pain, and inability to extend the middle and ring fingers. Pus collection in a palmar space is suspected. Which palmar space is most likely involved?
questions.explanation: A central palm stab injury followed by swelling, pain, and restricted movement of the middle and ring fingers indicates an infection of the midpalmar space (labeled B). This deep anatomical compartment is bounded anteriorly by the palmar aponeurosis and posteriorly by the metacarpals. The hypothenar space (Option A) is located on the ulnar side and primarily involves the little finger. The thenar space (Option C) is situated on the radial side, typically associated with infections of the thumb and index finger. The dorsal subaponeurotic space (Option D) is located on the back of the hand rather than the palm. Because the injury was central and the symptoms affect the third and fourth digits, the midpalmar space is the specific site of pus accumulation. Hand infections in diabetic patients are particularly serious due to impaired healing and increased susceptibility to deep-space abscesses
questions.learning: A central palm stab injury followed by swelling, pain, and restricted movement of the middle and ring fingers indicates an infection of the midpalmar space (labeled B).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 42-year-old man living in an endemic river basin area of Sub-Saharan Africa presents with generalized pruritus, subcutaneous nodules, and progressive visual impairment. What is the causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Onchocerca volvulus

Onchocerca volvulus is a filarial nematode that causes onchocerciasis (river blindness). It is transmitted by the bite of the female blackfly (Simulium species), which breeds in fast-flowing rivers and streams, making the disease endemic in Sub-Saharan Africa. The disease is characterized by intense pruritus, subcutaneous nodules (onchocercomas), skin depigmentation (“leopard skin”), and progressive ocular involvement leading to blindness.

Why not the other options?

• A. Loa loa: Causes loiasis (African eye worm), transmitted by the deer fly (Chrysops). It presents with Calabar swellings and migration of the adult worm across the conjunctiva, but does not typically cause river blindness.
• C. Wuchereria bancrofti: Causes lymphatic filariasis, presenting with lymphedema, hydrocele, and elephantiasis.
• D. Dracunculus medinensis: Causes Guinea worm disease, characterized by a painful skin blister from which the worm emerges, usually on the lower limb.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the following fracture.
options: Surgical neck humerus fracture with axillary nerve injury
Humerus shaft fracture with radial nerve palsy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Humerus shaft fracture with radial nerve palsy

The image shows a closed fracture of the shaft of the humerus in which the radial nerve is commonly damaged.

Holstein and Lewis associated a special type of fracture of the distal humerus, a simple displaced spiral fracture, with the distal end deviating toward the radial side occurring in about 7% of all humeral shaft fractures, with an increased rate of radial nerve palsy.

Injuries of ulnar and median nerves associated with humeral shaft fractures are not as frequent as injuries of the radial nerve.

It clinically manifests as an inability to dorsiflex the wrist and digits (wrist drop and finger drop).

Numbness occurs on the dorsoradial aspect of the hand and the dorsal aspect of the radial 3 1/2 digits.

Most cases of humerus shaft fractures can be managed conservatively using a hanging cast or U-slab for 2-3 weeks followed by functional bracing. Surgery is indicated in cases of open fractures, pathological fractures, simultaneous unstable humeral and forearm fractures (floating elbow), and in radial nerve palsy.  Surgical fixation can be performed by compression plating, interlocking intramedullary nail, semi-flexible pins or an external fixator.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents with recurrent infections arising from the lesion depicted in the image. Based on the clinical features and appearance of this lesion, which of the following statements regarding it is correct?
options: Derived from ectoderm of 1st and 2nd arch
Derived from the pouch of 1st and 2nd arch
Derived from mesoderm of 1st and 2nd arch
Derived from ectoderm of 3rd and 4th arch
questions.explanation: The clinical image depicts a preauricular sinus, a common congenital malformation. Developmentally, the external ear (pinna) is formed by the fusion of six auricular hillocks (of His) derived from the ectoderm of the first (Mandibular) and second (Hyoid) pharyngeal arches. A preauricular sinus results from the incomplete fusion of these hillocks, specifically between the first and second arches. Because it originates from the skin-forming layer, it is an ectodermal derivative lined with squamous epithelium. Pharyngeal pouches (Option B) are endodermal and give rise to structures like the Eustachian tube and tonsils. Mesodermal derivatives (Option C) include the cartilages and muscles of the arches. The third and fourth arches (Option D) contribute to the lower neck and laryngeal structures. These sinuses often remain asymptomatic unless they become infected, requiring antibiotics or surgical excision. They are frequently found anterior to the helix or the tragus

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: During a routine OPD visit, a 3-year-old child’s growth chart is reviewed and shows a Body Mass Index (BMI) between the 85th and 95th percentile for age and sex. How would you classify the nutritional status of this child?
questions.explanation: Nutritional status in children over the age of 2 is typically assessed using BMI-for-age growth charts. According to standardized CDC and WHO definitions, a child is categorized as overweight if their BMI is between the 85th and 95th percentile (Option C). If the BMI is at or above the 95th percentile, the child is categorized as obese (Option D). Moderate wasting (Option A) and Severe Acute Malnutrition (Option B) are categories used for children with low weight-for-height or low mid-upper arm circumference, representing undernutrition rather than excess weight. Identifying a child in the overweight category is important for implementing early lifestyle interventions to prevent progression to obesity and associated metabolic complications later in childhood. Therefore, based on the percentile range provided, overweight is the correct nutritional classification
questions.learning: Nutritional status in children over the age of 2 is typically assessed using BMI-for-age growth charts. According to standardized CDC and WHO definitions, a child is categorized as overweight if their BMI is between the 85th and 95th percentile (Option C).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 12-year-old girl with pigmented hair was noted. Which of the following amino acids is more likely to bind with keratin leading to this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cysteine

Cysteine is a sulfur-containing amino acid that is abundant in keratin, the principal structural protein of hair. During melanin synthesis, dopaquinone reacts with cysteine to form cysteinyldopa, which is the precursor of pheomelanin (yellow-red pigment). The incorporation of melanin into keratin gives hair its characteristic pigmentation.

Why not the other options?

• A. Methionine: A sulfur-containing essential amino acid involved in methylation reactions, but it is not the amino acid that directly combines with dopaquinone in melanin synthesis.
• B. Lysine: Important for collagen cross-linking and protein synthesis, but it has no specific role in hair pigmentation.
• D. Glycine: The most abundant amino acid in collagen, not keratin, and does not participate in melanin synthesis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following arteries passes in close proximity to the area marked by the arrow in the given image?
options: Anterior division of middle cerebral artery
Anterior division of the middle meningeal artery
Posterior division of middle cerebral artery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Anterior division of the middle meningeal artery

The area marked by an arrow in the given image is pterion and the artery that passes in close proximity to this area is the middle meningeal artery.

The pterion is an H shaped sutural junction between four bones of the skull:

• Frontal bone
• Squamous part of the temporal bone
• Greater wing of the sphenoid bone
• Parietal bone.

It is an important structure as it overlies the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery and lateral fissure of the cerebral hemisphere. The bone in this area is thin and any injury to this area may lead to rupture of the middle meningeal artery leading to extradural hematoma.
questions.learning: Anterior division of the middle meningeal artery — The area marked by an arrow in the given image is pterion and the artery that passes in close proximity to this area is the middle meningeal artery.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: An 18-year-old male presents with a two-month history of fever and gum bleeding. Examination shows pallor with no significant systemic findings. Laboratory investigations reveal severe anemia (Hb 3 g/dL), leukopenia (TLC 1,500/µL), thrombocytopenia (15,000/µL), macrocytosis on peripheral smear, and a low reticulocyte count of 0.5%. Bone marrow examination shows fatty infiltration with absence of megakaryocytes and no immature cells. What is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with symptoms of pancytopenia (Hb 3, TLC 1500, Platelets 15000) and clinical signs of failure in all cell lines: gum bleeding (thrombocytopenia), fever (neutropenia), and pallor (anemia). The key diagnostic findings are a low reticulocyte count (0.5), indicating a non-productive marrow, and a bone marrow biopsy showing hypocellularity with replacement by fat (fatty streaks) and an absence of megakaryocytes. The absence of immature cells (blasts) or dysplasia rules out Acute Leukemia or Myelodysplastic Syndrome (Option C). PNH (Option B) would typically show signs of hemolysis, such as high reticulocytes and dark urine. Tuberculosis (Option D) can cause pancytopenia but usually presents with granulomas in the marrow or other systemic signs. Therefore, the pathognomonic finding of a fatty, hypocellular marrow in a young patient with pancytopenia definitively confirms idiopathic acquired aplastic anemia
questions.learning: The patient presents with symptoms of pancytopenia (Hb 3, TLC 1500, Platelets 15000) and clinical signs of failure in all cell lines: gum bleeding (thrombocytopenia), fever (neutropenia), and pallor (anemia).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 14-year-old is brought to the opd with complaints that she is able to hear the sound of speech but has difficulty understanding words. Her PTA and BERA were inconsistent with each other, with PTA being more or less normal. Her middle latency and cortical responses were absent. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Auditory neuropathy

In the clinical scenario, the history of a child presenting with complaints of inability to understand words with abnormal BERA and normal PTA(Pure Tone Audiometry) is suggestive of auditory neuropathy.

Auditory neuropathy/auditory dyssynchrony is a condition that affects the neural processing of auditory stimuli.

Pathophysiology

• Injury to the synaptic junction between inner hair cells of the cochlea and dendrites of spiral ganglion neurons
• Direct damage to the dendrites of the spiral ganglion neurons
• Direct injury to the spiral ganglion neurons
• Direct axonal damage to the auditory nerve

Auditory neuropathy should be suspected in any child with severe speech and language delay out of proportion with the presumed hearing loss.

All of the following must be present in newborns to diagnose auditory neuropathy:

• Absent or severely abnormal ABR test results at maximal stimulus (100 dBnHL)
• Normal outer hair cell function as determined by OAEs(Otoacoustic emission)
• Absent or elevated stapedial reflex thresholds

In addition, adults with mildly to moderately abnormal pure tone thresholds and speech discrimination scores out of proportion with suspected hearing loss should undergo additional evaluation. Some patients may have normal or slightly elevated audiogram pure tone thresholds

Management includes conventional hearing aids. If a child does not progress with hearing aid devices and shows limited speech discrimination abilities, cochlear implantation is the next viable option.

Other options

Option A:

Michel aplasia: There is a complete absence of bone and a membranous labyrinth. Even the petrous apex is absent but external and middle ears may be completely unaffected. The child presents with congenital sensorineural hearing loss. No hearing aids or cochlear implantation can be used.

Option B:

Malingering(Nonorganic hearing loss)

In this type of hearing loss, there is no organic lesion. Usually, there is a motive to claim some compensation for being exposed to industrial noises, head injury, or ototoxic medication. The patient may present with any of the three clinical situations: Total hearing loss in both ears, total loss in only one ear, or exaggerated loss in one or both ears.

Investigations

Inconsistent results on Repeat Pure Tone and Speech Audiometry Tests: Normally, the results of repeat tests are within +5 dB. A variation greater than 15 dB is diagnostic of nonorganic hearing loss (NOHL).

Absence of Shadow Curve: Normally, a shadow curve can be obtained while testing bone conduction, if the healthy ear is not masked. This is due to the transcranial transmission of sound to the healthy ear. The absence of this curve in a patient complaining of unilateral deafness is diagnostic of NOHL.

Inconsistency in PTA and SRT: Normally, the pure tone average (PTA) of three speech frequencies (500, 1000, and 2000 Hz) is within 10 dB of the speech reception threshold (SRT). An SRT is better than PTA by more than 10 dB points to NOHL.

Stenger Test: It helps in identifying malingering

Acoustic Reflex: Threshold Normally, the stapedial reflex is elicited at 70-100 dB sensation level. If the patient claims total deafness but the reflex can be elicited, it indicates nonorganic hearing loss (NOHL).

Option C:

Otosclerosis is the disease of the bony labyrinth in which a normal dense endochondral layer of the bony otic capsule is replaced by irregularly laid spongy bone. It has a positive family history with an autosomal dominant trait. It is more commonly seen in females between 20-30 years of age and the hearing loss is aggravated during pregnancy and menopause. It may be associated with osteogenesis imperfecta and a viral infection like measles.

Stapedial otosclerosis is the most common type of otosclerosis. Here the lesion starts just in front of the oval window in an area called fissula ante fenestram.

Patients present with a bilateral conductive type of hearing loss, tinnitus (commonly in cochlear type and active stage), paracusis Willisii (better hearing in noisy surroundings than in a quiet place), vertigo, and a monotonous, well-modulated soft speech.

The tympanic membrane is quite normal and mobile. Eustachian tube function is also normal. Pure tone audiometry shows a dip at 2000 Hz in the bone conduction curve known as the Carhart's notch. Tympanometry shows an As type of tympanogram in which there is reduced compliance at or near the ambient air pressure.

On examination, Schwartz sign/flamingo flush showing a red blush of the tympanic membrane due to vascularity can be seen.

Treatment includes medical, surgical management, and hearing aids. Medical management with sodium fluoride is used in the active stage to speed up the maturity of the active focus and halt further cochlear loss. The treatment of choice is surgical management which includes stapedotomy/stapedectomy with the placement of a prosthesis. Hearing aids are used in patients who refuse or are unfit for the surgery.
questions.learning: Auditory neuropathy — In the clinical scenario, the history of a child presenting with complaints of inability to understand words with abnormal BERA and normal PTA(Pure Tone Audiometry) is suggestive of auditory neuropathy.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A militant presents with rashes all over his body sparing the palms and soles. On examination, he was febrile and lice were noted. Which of the following is responsible for his condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rickettsia prowazekii

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of epidemic or louse-borne typhus caused by Rickettsia prowazekii.

Pediculus corporis (human body louse) is the vector for the parasite, although the head louse may also transmit the disease. After the incubation period of 5 - 15 days, the disease typically starts with fever and chills. By around 4 - 5th day of fever, a characteristic rash appears, which starts on the trunk and spreads over the limbs but spares the face, palms, and soles.

The infection can be transmitted by

• Contaminated louse feces rubbed through abrasions caused by scratching
• Inhalation of aerosols of dried louse feces or directly through the conjunctiva

The disease is often severe with the fever lasting for over 2 weeks and is more fatal in patients older than 40 years of age.

Other options:

Option A: R. typhi causes murine (flea-borne) or endemic typhus. Rats are the reservoirs of infection and the parasite is transmitted by Xenopsylla cheopis (flea). The infection is transmitted when the flea feces is rubbed into the bite wound. The clinical features are similar to that of epidemic typhus but are milder and rarely fatal. Patients can present with fever, headache, myalgia, and rash.

Option C: R. akari causes rickettsial pox, which is a mild disease resembling varicella. The disease is transmitted by mites and the patients may present with fever, headache, and a vesicular rash.

Option D: R. conorii causes the Mediterranean spotted fever. The parasite is transmitted by ticks and the patients present with fever, headache, rash, and eschar (tache noire).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Single breath nitrogen method is used for measuring ____
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dead space volume

Anatomical dead space can be measured by the single-breath N2 curve (Fowler's method).

• Anatomical dead space is the respiratory system volume exclusive of alveoli.
• Alveolar dead space is the volume of gas not equilibrating with blood i.e. wasted ventilation.
• Physiological/total dead space is the sum of anatomical and alveolar dead space.
• The equation used for the calculation of total/physiological dead space is the Bohr’s equation.

The patient takes a deep breath of O2 From mid-inspiration, then exhales steadily. The changes in the N2 concentration of expired gas during expiration are plotted.

From I–II is a mixture of DS and alveolar gas.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient presents with hematuria and a mass in the right kidney on a CT scan, as shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Renal angiomyolipoma

The CT image showing renal lesions that has hypo-attenuating components consistent with macroscopic fat is highly suggestive of renal angiomyolipoma.

Angiomyolipomas are benign tumors that occur sporadically or in association with tuberous sclerosis. The mean age of presentation is 43 years and there is a female predilection. It can present as spontaneous retroperitoneal hemorrhage, especially with larger tumors. The patient can present with flank pain, palpable mass, hematuria, urinary tract infections, hypertension, or renal failure.

Imaging in renal angiomyolipoma: Demonstration of macroscopic fat is the main part of making a diagnosis. USG may show hyperechoic lesions in the cortex with posterior acoustic shadowing. In patients with tuberous sclerosis, the entire kidney is affected and produces an echogenic appearance with loss of normal corticomedullary junction.

CT findings:

• Cortical lesions that demonstrate macroscopic fat (less than -20 HU)
• Absence of ossification or calcification
• The presence of macroscopic fat is strongly suggestive of this condition, but not pathognomonic as RCC may rarely demonstrate macroscopic fat.
• Approximately 5% may be fat-poor.

MRI: It is an excellent tool to demonstrate intramural fat components. Two sequences are used:

• Fat-saturated techniques
• Phase-in and phase-out imaging that shows India ink artifacts at the junction between fat and non-fat components.

Digital subtraction angiography: They are hypervascular lesions showing a 'sunburst appearance' in the arterial phase and an 'onion peel appearance' in the venous phase.

They usually do not require any intervention. mTOR inhibitors like everolimus can be used to decrease the size of the lesion.

Other options:

Renal cell carcinoma (RCC): It is the most common malignant tumor of the kidney. It usually occurs in the age group 50-70 years and macroscopic hematuria is seen in about 60% of the cases. It is a differential for angiomyolipoma but it is important to note that macroscopic fat is almost always associated with ossification or calcification.

Renal oncocytoma: They are relatively benign in nature and usually present in the 6th to 7th decade. An important point regarding this tumor is its similarity with RCC and hence it is very difficult to differentiate between them preoperatively. A sharp central stellate scar may be seen in one-third of the cases. But RCC may also show this stellate scar appearance in some cases.

Renal cyst: It is a broader term that includes the cystic lesions of the kidney. They can be simple cysts that are benign. Complex or complicated cystic lesions needs evaluation and can be malignant. Bosniak classification of renal cysts is given above.
