questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the formula of crude birth rate?
options: (Total number of births / Estimated midyear Population) 1,000
(Number of live births / Estimated mid year women Population) 1,000
(Number of live births / Estimated midyear Population) 1,000
(Number of live births / Estimated midyear Population) 10,000
questions.explanation: The Crude Birth Rate (CBR) is a fundamental demographic measure used to quantify the fertility of a population. It is defined as the number of live births occurring in a given year per 1,000 of the estimated midyear population. Option A is incorrect because it uses "total number of births," which might include stillbirths; only live births are counted in CBR. Option B describes the General Fertility Rate, which restricts the denominator to the women of reproductive age. Option D is incorrect due to the use of 10,000 instead of the standard 1,000 multiplier. The midyear population is used as an estimate of the average population exposed to the risk of birth throughout the year. CBR is considered "crude" because it does not account for the age or sex structure of the population, but it is a vital starting point for evaluating demographic trends and population growth
questions.learning: The Crude Birth Rate (CBR) is a fundamental demographic measure used to quantify the fertility of a population. It is defined as the number of live births occurring in a given year per 1,000 of the estimated midyear population.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 12-year-old girl is being evaluated for pubertal development. She has onset of breast development, pubic hair has appeared, and she is at Tanner stage 2. Which of the following is the next likely event to occur according to Tanner staging?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Peak growth spurt

Sequence of pubertal development shows that after thelarche (onset of breast development, tanner stage 2) and pubarche (appearance of pubic hair, Tanner stage 2), the next most likely event is the peak height velocity (growth spurt). The growth spurt occurs early in female puberty, generally after Tanner stage 2 breast and pubic hair development.

In females at 10 to 11 years, the breast bud (thelarche) appears, which is the first sign of puberty, followed by the appearance of pubic hair (pubarche), growth spurt, and menarche. Thelarche > pubarche > growth spurt > menarche .

Tanner staging
Breast changes
Pubic hair changes

Stage 1

B1 - Denotes the prepubertal breast. At this infantile stage, only the papilla is elevated.

P1 - No pubic hair

Stage 2

B2 - Denotes thelarche. The breast buds are palpable, areola enlarges and the breast is elevated like a small mound.

P2 - The appearance of pigmented hair sparsely over the labia, either long or slightly curved.

Stage 3

B3 - There is further enlargement of the breast and its areola without separation of its contours.

P3 - Darker, coarser and curly hair

Stage 4

B4 - Preferential growth of the areola and nipple leads to formation of a secondary mound over the mound of the breast.

P4 - Preadult stage cover short inverted triangular distribution.

Stage 5

B5 - Formation of the mature adult breast.

P5 - Adult inverted triangular distributuion.

Other options:

Option B: Appearance of axillary hair – Axillary hair development occurs later, with stages A1 (no axillary hair), A2 (sparse axillary hair), and A3 (adult distribution). This follows pubic hair development and usually appears after the growth spurt.

Option C: Menarche is a late pubertal event, generally following thelarche by about 2 years.

Option D: Thelarche refers to the onset of breast development.
questions.learning: Peak growth spurt Sequence of pubertal development shows that after thelarche (onset of breast development, tanner stage 2) and pubarche (appearance of pubic hair, Tanner stage 2), the next most likely event is the peak height velocity (growth spurt).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Identify the type of inhibition shown in the graph.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Non-competitive inhibition

The above graph is called a 'Lineweaver-Burk plot' or 'double reciprocal' plot, and it represents non-competitive inhibition.

Non-competitive inhibition: When the substrate and the inhibitor are chemically not similar and have different shapes, the inhibitor binds away from the active site, i.e., at the allosteric site. This type of inhibition is known as non-competitive inhibition.

In non-competitive inhibition,

* Vmax decreases.(1/Vmax increases)

* Km remains constant.

In a Lineweaver-Burk Plot, the addition of a non-competitive inhibitor causes plots with the same x-intercept (Km is unaffected) but different slopes and y-intercepts.

Competitive inhibition - Here, the inhibitor is a structural analog of the substrate. Inhibitor molecules are competing with the normal substrate molecules for binding to the active site of the enzyme. Here, Vmax is unchanged (same y-intercept), and Km is increased (− 1/Km moves closer to zero from a negative value).

Uncompetitive inhibition  - Here, the inhibitor does not have any affinity for the free enzyme. The inhibitor binds to the enzyme-substrate complex, but not to the free enzyme. Here, both Vmax and Km are decreased.

Pearl PF0696: Difference between Competitive & Non-Competitive inhibitors

Reversible inhibitors are of two types:

* Competitive inhibitors

* Non-Competitive inhibitors

Difference between Competitive & Non-Competitive inhibitors

Competitive inhibitors

Non-Competitive inhibitors

Succinate dehydrogenase is inhibited by Malonate

Pyruvate kinase is inhibited by alanine

Substrate & inhibitor are chemically similar & have same shape

Substrate & inhibitor are chemically not similar & have different shape

Inhibitor binds to active site

Inhibitor binds away from active site, i.e., at allosteric site

Inhibitor does not change the shape of the active site

Inhibitor changes the shape of the active site

Increase in substrate concentration reduces the inhibition

Increase in substrate concentration does not affect the inhibition

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with a chest x-ray finding of pneumothorax. Which of the following is not a boundary of the triangle of safety for ICD insertion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mid-clavicular line

The mid-clavicular line is not a boundary of the triangle of safety for chest tube insertion.

Chest tube insertion is carried out in the 5th intercostal space (ICS) anterior to the midaxillary line in the triangle of safety (image below).

Boundaries of Triangle of Safety:

• Anteriorly (red line) : Below and lateral to the pectoralis major muscle
• Posteriorly(yellow line) : Anterior to the mid-axillary line (some references mention the lateral border of latissimus dorsi)
• Inferiorly (blue line) : Above the horizontal level of the nipple at the level of the 5th ICS

Chest tube insertion/ thoracostomy is indicated in pneumothorax, hemothorax, chylothorax, pleural effusion, etc. Contraindications include pulmonary adhesions, pulmonary trauma, coagulopathy, and diaphragmatic hernia.

Possible complications of this procedure include:

• Clogging of the tube (most common)
• Incorrect placement
• Intercostal nerve/ vessel injury
• Subcutaneous hematoma/ emphysema
• Pain

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient with COPD presented with ARDS symptoms. What is the role of IL-8 in inflammation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Recuritement of neutrophils

IL-8 (CXCL8) is secreted by activated macrophages and endothelial cells which causes activation and recruitment of neutrophils.

Once leukocytes have exited the circulation, they move towards the inciting stimulus by chemotaxis. This process is mediated by:

Exogenous chemoattractants, such as bacterial products as well as endogenous chemoattractants: cytokines of the chemokine family (e.g., IL-8), components of the complement system (particularly C5a), and arachidonic acid (AA) metabolites (mainly leukotriene B4).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman presents with a palpable mass in the upper outer quadrant of the breast. Histopathological examination reveals tumor cells with a characteristic signet-ring appearance. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: In breast pathology, "signet ring cells" are characterized by a large cytoplasmic vacuole containing mucin that displaces the nucleus to the periphery. While classically associated with lobular carcinoma, signet ring cells are also a prominent feature of "Colloidal" or mucinous carcinoma of the breast. Colloidal carcinoma typically occurs in slightly older women and has a relatively favorable prognosis compared to invasive ductal carcinoma. Papillary carcinoma (Option B) is characterized by finger-like projections and lacks mucinous signet ring cells. Medullary carcinoma (Option C) features a dense lymphocytic infiltrate and large pleomorphic cells, but not signet ring morphology. Phyllodes tumors (Option D) are fibroepithelial lesions characterized by leaf-like stromal growth rather than specialized signet ring adenocarcinoma cells. The identification of signet ring morphology is critical as it indicates mucin production. Clinicians must distinguish whether these cells represent a primary breast malignancy or metastasis from the gastrointestinal tract, though given the options, colloidal carcinoma is the intended diagnosis
questions.learning: In breast pathology, "signet ring cells" are characterized by a large cytoplasmic vacuole containing mucin that displaces the nucleus to the periphery.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the instrument given below:
questions.explanation: The instrument shown in the image is a linear stapler, often specifically a linear cutter used in various abdominal and thoracic surgeries. These devices are designed to place two or more staggered rows of staples and then cut the tissue between them, allowing for the simultaneous resection and closure of organs like the stomach or intestines. A circular stapler (Option C) has a distinct round head and is used primarily for end-to-end anastomoses, such as after a low anterior resection of the rectum. Skin staplers (Option B) are much smaller, handheld devices used only for external skin closure. Curved staplers (Option D) have a specific contoured head to assist in deep pelvic closures but do not match the straight, elongated profile of the linear stapler shown. Therefore, based on the straight design and the typical appearance used in stapled anastomoses, the linear stapler is the correct identification for this common surgical tool

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 49-year-old female from Nagaland presented with right-sided hearing loss. On examination, a dull right tympanic membrane is noted. Enlarged lymph nodes are seen in the posterior triangle of the neck. Which of the following is the management of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Radiotherapy

The given clinical scenario of a patient presenting with right-sided hearing loss, dull tympanic membrane (middle ear effusion leading to a conductive hearing loss) and enlarged lymph nodes in the posterior triangle of the neck (cervical lymphadenopathy) is indicative of nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Radiotherapy is the treatment of choice.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is extremely radiosensitive, hence treatment of local and regional disease is invariably radiotherapy.

* Stage I and II are treated by radiotherapy alone while

* Stage III and IV require concomitant radiation and chemotherapy or radiation followed by chemotherapy.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is a malignant tumor of the nasopharynx. The theories for etiology include genetics, infection with Epstein-Barr virus, air pollution, and smoking.

It has three types -

* Keratinizing carcinoma

* Nonkeratinizing differentiated carcinoma

* Nonkeratinizing undifferentiated carcinoma.

The most common presenting symptom is cervical lymphadenopathy, occurring in 60-90% of cases. The most common site of origin of nasopharyngeal carcinoma is the fossa of Rosenmuller. From here, it can spread extensively in any direction locally. It also can spread lymphatically to the cervical, retropharyngeal, or parapharyngeal lymph nodes.

Symptoms include:

* Nasal- Nasal obstruction, denasal speech, nasal discharge, epistaxis.

* Otologic- unilateral conductive hearing loss, and serous or suppurative otitis media.

* Facial pain and reduced corneal reflex- cranial nerve V. (most common cranial nerve to be involved)

* Squint and diplopia- involvement of cranial nerve VI.

* Exophthalmos and blindness- cranial nerve II.

* Horner's syndrome

* Cervical lymphadenopathy is the most common presenting symptom.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma can present with Trotter's triad, which includes:

* Conductive deafness (eustachian tube blockage),

* Ipsilateral temporoparietal neuralgia due to involvement of CN V and

* Palatal paralysis due to involvement of CN X

Enlarged lateral retropharyngeal nodes compress the cranial nerve IX, X, and XI causing jugular foramen syndrome. High-resolution contrast-enhanced CT (HR-CECT) of nose and nasopharynx is the investigation of choice.

Other Options:

Option A: Grommet insertion + steroids would only treat the middle ear effusion symptomatically without addressing the underlying nasopharyngeal malignancy.

Option C: "Wait and watch" would be inappropriate for a suspected malignancy, as delayed treatment could lead to disease progression.

Option D: Radical neck dissection alone would be incorrect as it doesn't address the primary tumor in the nasopharynx, and NPC is primarily treated with radiotherapy rather than surgery due to its anatomical location and radiosensitivity.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient presents with obstructed labor, and abdominal examination reveals a palpable groove or band across the uterus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A Bandl’s ring is a pathological retraction ring that develops during obstructed labor. It forms at the junction between the upper contractile segment of the uterus and the lower, pathologically thinned and stretched segment. On physical examination, it is felt as a palpable groove or band running transversely across the abdomen, and it is a grave warning sign of impending uterine rupture. Constriction rings (Option A) are localized muscle spasms that occur around the fetus rather than at the segment junction. Schroeder's ring (Option B) is a pathological ring often associated with oxytocin misuse and atony. A contraction ring (Option C) is the normal physiological boundary between segments that is not palpable in a healthy labor. Immediate cesarean section is required when a Bandl's ring is identified to prevent rupture
questions.learning: A Bandl’s ring is a pathological retraction ring that develops during obstructed labor. It forms at the junction between the upper contractile segment of the uterus and the lower, pathologically thinned and stretched segment.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 26-year-old man presents with chronic rhinitis, recurrent respiratory tract infections, and infertility, raising suspicion of Kartagener syndrome. A defect in which structural component (as shown in the image) is most commonly associated with Kartagener syndrome?
questions.explanation: Kartagener Syndrome, a subtype of Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia (PCD), is caused by a structural or functional defect in the cilia. The classic triad includes situs inversus, bronchiectasis (due to recurrent infections), and chronic sinusitis. The defect most commonly involves the dynein arms of the ciliary axoneme, which are responsible for generating the force for ciliary beating. Without functional cilia, the respiratory tract cannot clear mucus, leading to recurrent infections (Option A/B are incorrect). Furthermore, sperm motility is impaired because the flagella (which share the same structural components as cilia) are non-functional, resulting in male infertility. Microvilli (Option A) are involved in absorption and lack the 9+2 microtubule arrangement of cilia. Microfilaments (Option D) are composed of actin and are part of the general cytoskeleton. Diagnosis is supported by low nasal nitric oxide levels and confirmed by electron microscopy showing absence of outer or inner dynein arms. Management centers on chest physiotherapy, aggressive antibiotic treatment for infections, and assisted reproductive techniques for infertility
questions.learning: Kartagener Syndrome, a subtype of Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia (PCD), is caused by a structural or functional defect in the cilia. The classic triad includes situs inversus, bronchiectasis (due to recurrent infections), and chronic sinusitis.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The fallopian tube is lined by ______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ciliated columnar epithelium

The lining epithelium of the fallopian tube is a single layer of ciliated columnar epithelium.

The ciliated epithelial cells are predominant in the distal part of the fallopian tube. There is an increase in the height and number of cilia in these cells during the estrogenic phase of the menstrual cycle.

Other cells in the fallopian tube epithelium include:

* Secretory or peg cells - maximally located in the proximal portion of the tube. These cells are active around the time of ovulation, and their secretions help in the capacitation of sperms.

* Intraepithelial lymphocytes - may present occasionally.

Pearl PF1615: Fallopian tube

Gross anatomy:

The fallopian tube is divided into the following parts:

* Intramural/Interstitial portion:

* Intrauterine

* The narrowest and shortest part

* Isthmus:

* The most common site for tubectomy

* Ampulla:

* The longest part

* The most common site for - fertilization and ectopic pregnancy

* Infundibulum:

* The widest part

Histology:

The ampulla, isthmus and infundibulum are extrauterine. They're covered by three layers:

* Mesosalpinx - It is the peritoneal layer. Also called serosa.

* Myosalpinx - It contains smooth muscle and has 2 layers:

* Inner circular

* Outer longitudinal

* Endosalpinx - It is the mucosal layer. It has the following features:

* Numerous branching folds, filling the entire lumen

* Basement membrane

* Ciliated, columnar epithelium

* Peg cells - non-ciliated epithelium. They help in the capacitation of sperms.

Pearl PF1699: Various Types of Epithelium, Their Location and Functions
questions.learning: Ciliated columnar epithelium — The lining epithelium of the fallopian tube is a single layer of ciliated columnar epithelium. The ciliated epithelial cells are predominant in the distal part of the fallopian tube.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman with a history of hypertension presented to the emergency room with loss of consciousness, chest pain, and diaphoresis. On examination, she was grossly unstable and the bilateral pulses were unequal. ECG showed nonspecific ST-T changes. What is the next best investigation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Transesophageal echocardiography

The clinical presentation and ECG showing nonspecific ST-T changes are highly suggestive of aortic dissection. As the patient is hemodynamically unstable the next best investigation is transesophageal ECHO.

Aortic dissection:

This occurs when a defect or flap occurs in the intima of the aorta. It results in blood tracking into the aortic tissues and splitting of the medial layer of the aorta.

Predisposing factors:

• Age
• Hypertension
• Marfan syndrome
• Pregnancy
• Other connective tissue disorders, for example, Ehlers–Danlos syndrome, giant cell arteritis, systemic lupus erythematosus
• Coarctation of the aorta
• Turner or Noonan syndromes
• Aortic cannulation site (iatrogenic)

Clinical features:

The most typical presentation of aortic dissection is a tearing interscapular pain. It is associated with diaphoresis. Other symptoms are syncope, weakness, and dyspnea. On examination, there can be hypertension or hypotension, loss of pulses, findings of aortic regurgitation, pulmonary edema, or neurological manifestations. Unequal pulses or blood pressure in the extremities may be seen due to changes of flow in the true and false lumens.

ECG findings: An ECG that shows no findings of acute myocardial infarction helps to differentiate aortic dissection from myocardial infarction.

Imaging:

In hemodynamically stable patients the diagnosis is established with a contrast-enhanced CT scan. The characteristic diagnostic finding is a double lumen aorta.

Transesophageal ECHO(TEE) is the investigation of choice in a hemodynamically unstable patient.

Treatment:

The initial management is with beta-blockers to control hypertension, along with pain management. The preferred beta-blocker is esmolol. These reduce cardiac contractility and blood pressure.

Isolated use of a direct vasodilator such as hydralazine is contraindicated in acute dissection because these agents can increase hydraulic shear and worsen the dissection. CCBs like verapamil and diltiazem may be used intravenously if nitroprusside or beta-blockers cannot be employed.

Once hypertension is controlled, definitive surgical repair of aortic dissection is done. Treatment options depend on the classification.

• Stanford Type A (DeBakey types I and II) requires surgical intervention once the patient's blood pressure is stabilized.
• Stanford Type B (DeBakey type III) is best managed by antihypertensive drugs. Surgical intervention is indicated in complicated cases if the pain increases (signaling impending rupture) or when there is evidence of malperfusion of organs or neurological symptoms.
questions.learning: Transesophageal echocardiography — The clinical presentation and ECG showing nonspecific ST-T changes are highly suggestive of aortic dissection. As the patient is hemodynamically unstable the next best investigation is transesophageal ECHO.

questions.text: An intern has to study the relationship between ordering food online and development of obesity using a case control study. What are the best study groups to be selected ?
options: Online food eaters and Non online food eaters

Pearl PF0221: Case Control Study

* In a case control study, progression is from effect to cause as outcome or disease has already occurred.

* It is also called retrospective study.

* Design of Case Control Study

* Steps of Case Control Study

* Selection of cases and controls

* Matching

* Measurement of exposure

* Analysis in the form of exposure rates, risk ratio, and odds ratio

* Advantages and Disadvantages

Advantages

Easy to carry out

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the population norm for an ASHA worker?
questions.explanation: Under the National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) in India, the Accredited Social Health Activist (ASHA) serves as a vital link between the community and the public health system. The standard population norm for an ASHA is one worker for every 1,000 people in plain areas. However, in tribal, hilly, or difficult-to-reach areas, this norm is flexible and can cover populations up to 2,500. Option A (700-1000) is incorrect as 1,000 is generally the lower threshold. Option B (1000-1500) and Option D (2000-2500) do not reflect the full standard range utilized by health planners. The ASHA is primarily a woman from the village itself, trained to promote immunization, institutional delivery, and basic nutrition. This population ratio ensures that health services are accessible and that the worker is not overburdened while maintaining close ties with her community
questions.learning: Under the National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) in India, the Accredited Social Health Activist (ASHA) serves as a vital link between the community and the public health system.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 20-year-old male presents with sudden onset severe headache and vomiting. On examination, he has neck stiffness. A CT scan of the brain shows hydrocephalus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Subarachnoid Haemorrhage

The classic triad here is:

• Sudden onset severe headache ("thunderclap headache" — worst headache of life)
• Neck stiffness (meningeal irritation)
• Young patient (20-year-old)

This points strongly to SAH, most commonly caused by rupture of a berry (saccular) aneurysm.

Why the other options are wrong

| Option | Why eliminated

| ------ | --------------

| A - Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus | Occurs in elderly with classic triad: dementia, gait disturbance, urinary incontinence — not sudden headache

| B - Bacterial Meningitis | Can cause neck stiffness, but headache is gradual, fever is prominent, and CT rarely shows hydrocephalus acutely

| C - Viral Encephalitis | Presents with altered consciousness, fever, seizures — not sudden thunderclap headache

Key Exam Points

• SAH = "worst headache of life" + neck stiffness + young patient
• CT shows hyperdense (white) blood in basal cisterns
• If CT negative → do lumbar puncture (xanthochromia)
• Most common cause: berry aneurysm (Circle of Willis)
questions.learning: Subarachnoid Haemorrhage — The classic triad here is: • Sudden onset severe headache ("thunderclap headache" — worst headache of life) • Neck stiffness (meningeal irritation) • Young patient (20-year-old) This points strongly to SAH, most commonly caused…

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A man was found dead due to starvation. Which of the following findings will be seen on autopsy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Distended gall bladder

In starvation, the gall bladder is distended.

In starvation, bile does not get secreted into the duodenum due to the absence of food entering the stomach and intestine. So bile gets accumulated in the gall bladder and gets distended.

Starvation:

* Feeling of intense hunger lasts for 30–48 hours.

* Person can survive for 10–12 days without food and water and for 6–8 weeks without food alone.

* Loss of 40% of body weight is usually fatal.

* Loss of 70–90% of body fat and 20% of body protein is fatal.

* There is reduction in weight and size of all organs except brain.

Other features of starvation:

* Dry, lustreless hair

* Brittle nails

* Pale skin with edema around ankles

* Loss of fat in subcutaneous tissue, in the omentum
(sparing of fat in female breast and orbit till later)

* Atrophy of muscles and darkening due to lipochrome

* The heart is atrophied with empty chambers

* Pale and collapsed lung

* Shrunken liver with necrosis

* Tissue paper-like intestinal mucosa

* Empty bladder
questions.learning: Distended gall bladder — In starvation, the gall bladder is distended. In starvation, bile does not get secreted into the duodenum due to the absence of food entering the stomach and intestine.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 67-year-old patient with diabetes presents with knee swelling, restricted joint movement, and minimal pain. An X-ray of the knee is shown. Based on the clinical features and radiographic findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical scenario of a diabetic patient with a "severely swollen joint" that is "painless" (out of proportion to its appearance) is the classic presentation of "Charcot arthropathy" or neuropathic joint. Chronic diabetic neuropathy leads to a loss of protective sensation, resulting in repetitive microtrauma and progressive, painless joint destruction. The provided X-ray shows the "6 Ds" of Charcot joints: Distension, Density (sclerosis), Disorganization, Debris (fragmentation), Dislocation, and Destruction. Rheumatoid arthropathy (Option A) typically involves symmetric, painful, small joint inflammation. Osteoarthritis (Option B) involves asymmetric joint space narrowing and osteophytes but not massive bone destruction and fragmentation. Psoriatic arthropathy (Option D) is characterized by "pencil-in-cup" deformities and skin lesions. Charcot arthropathy is a debilitating condition that can lead to limb deformity and amputation if not managed early with strict offloading (e.g., total contact casting). Maintaining tight glycemic control is also essential to slow the progression of underlying neuropathy
questions.learning: The clinical scenario of a diabetic patient with a "severely swollen joint" that is "painless" (out of proportion to its appearance) is the classic presentation of "Charcot arthropathy" or neuropathic joint.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A young patient presents with recurrent seasonal conjunctivitis marked by intense itching and excessive watering of the eyes. Given that this is an immediate hypersensitivity reaction, which cell type primarily mediates these symptoms?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of seasonal conjunctivitis, characterized by recurring intense itching and tearing, is a classic Type I hypersensitivity reaction. Mast cells are the primary mediators in this immediate allergic response. When a sensitized individual is exposed to seasonal allergens like pollen, IgE antibodies already bound to the surface of mast cells trigger degranulation. This release of pre-formed inflammatory mediators, most notably histamine, causes the characteristic symptoms of redness, itching, and chemosis. While eosinophils (Option A) are often recruited later in the allergic cascade and contribute to chronic inflammation, they are not the primary cells responsible for the immediate, acute symptoms. Neutrophils (Option C) are typically associated with acute bacterial infections and are not central to the allergic pathway. Lymphocytes (Option D), particularly T-cells, play roles in delayed hypersensitivity but are not the primary drivers of the rapid, IgE-mediated symptoms seen in seasonal allergic conjunctivitis. Therefore, mast cell stabilization and histamine blocking are key therapeutic strategies for these patients
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of seasonal conjunctivitis, characterized by recurring intense itching and tearing, is a classic Type I hypersensitivity reaction.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with a fish bone lodged in the pyriform sinus. During attempted removal, which nerve is most at risk of injury?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Internal laryngeal nerve (ILN)

A fish bone in the pyriform sinus puts the internal laryngeal nerve (ILN) at risk during removal because it provides sensory innervation to the supraglottic larynx and pyriform fossa.

• Internal laryngeal nerve (branch of superior laryngeal nerve):

• Purely sensory above the vocal cords
• Supplies pyriform sinus, epiglottis, laryngeal inlet

• It pierces the thyrohyoid membrane → lies close to the pyriform fossa

• Injury leads to:

• Loss of protective cough reflex
• Risk of silent aspiration

Why not other options:

• External laryngeal nerve (ELN): Motor to cricothyroid, not in pyriform sinus
• Recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN): Supplies below vocal cords, deeper course

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: α1-antitrypsin is the major inhibitor of the enzyme ________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Elastase

α1-antitrypsin is the major inhibitor of the enzyme neutrophil elastase.

• Lysosomal enzymes, if unchecked, can potentiate further inflammation by damaging tissues.
• These harmful proteases, however, are normally controlled by a system of antiproteases in the serum and tissue fluids.
• α1-antitrypsin is the prototype member of the serine protease inhibitor (serpin) superfamily of proteins.

Clinical correlate:

• Alpha 1 anti-trypsin deficiency (α1-ATD) is caused by mutations in the SERPINA1 gene located in the long arm of chromosome 14.
• This genetic defect alters the configuration of the α1-antitrypsin molecule and prevents its release from hepatocytes.
• As a result, serum levels of α1-antitrypsin are decreased, leading to low alveolar concentrations, where the α1-antitrypsin molecule normally would provide protection against proteases such neutrophil elastase.
• The resulting protease excess in alveoli destroys alveolar walls and causes emphysema.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A given drug has a bioavailability of 30%. What does this mean?
options: 30% percent of the drug reaches the systemic circulation in unchanged form
The drug is 30 percent potent in producing therapeutic effec
30 percent of the drug undergoes first pass metabolism in Liver
The drug is 30 percent pure in its chemical composition
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 30% percent of the drug reaches the systemic circulation in unchanged form

If a drug has a bioavailability of 30%, it means that only 30% of the drug reaches the systemic circulation in its original, unchanged form after it is administered. The remaining 70% of the drug may undergo various processes such as metabolism, degradation, or excretion before it reaches the bloodstream.

Bioavailability is defined as the fraction of a drug reaching systemic circulation in an unchanged form after administration by any route. The area under the blood concentration-time curve (AUC) is proportional to the dose and the extent of bioavailability for a drug.

Bioavailability (F) = Quantity of drug reaching systemic circulation/Quantity of drug administered

Bioavailability depends on two factors, absorption and 1st pass metabolism. The bioavailability of the drug injected intravenously is 100%. However it is lower after oral ingestion because of incomplete absorption and first-pass metabolism in the intestinal wall or liver and lies between 5% to <100%. The bioavailability of subcutaneous and intramuscular routes lies between 75% to ≤100%.

The image given below shows the difference between the bioavailability of drugs injected intravenously (IV) and administered per orally (PO). Note the area under the respective curves shaded in red and blue colors which represent the absorption of the drug.
questions.learning: 30% percent of the drug reaches the systemic circulation in unchanged form If a drug has a bioavailability of 30%, it means that only 30% of the drug reaches the systemic circulation in its original, unchanged form after it is administered.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presents with severe eye pain following an injury involving vegetative material. Examination and microscopy reveal septate hyphae with acute-angle branching. Which organism is most likely responsible for this ocular infection?
questions.explanation: A history of ocular trauma with vegetative matter (such as a leaf, twig, or branch) is a classic red-flag history for fungal corneal ulcer (mycotic keratitis). The definitive laboratory finding of septate hyphae branching at acute angles (≈45°) is characteristic of filamentous fungi, most commonly Aspergillus or Fusarium species. Bacterial corneal ulcers (Option C) usually present with an acute onset, marked purulent discharge, and a wet-looking infiltrate. Viral keratitis (Option B), most commonly due to herpes simplex virus, typically shows dendritic or geographic ulcers on fluorescein staining. Acanthamoeba keratitis (Option D) is strongly associated with contact lens use, severe pain out of proportion to clinical findings, and a characteristic ring-shaped stromal infiltrate. Fungal corneal ulcers classically have feathery margins, satellite lesions, and a dry, grayish-white infiltrate. Management is an ophthalmic emergency and requires prompt initiation of topical antifungal therapy, most commonly natamycin 5%. In cases with deep stromal involvement or poor response to medical treatment, therapeutic penetrating keratoplasty may be required to prevent corneal perforation and preserve vision
questions.learning: A history of ocular trauma with vegetative matter (such as a leaf, twig, or branch) is a classic red-flag history for fungal corneal ulcer (mycotic keratitis).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text:
The following are the disease frequencies in a population. Based on the number of cases which of the following is the correct match?

Disease 1: Number of cases last week 42 this week 43
Disease 2: Number of cases last week 2 and present week 42
Disease 3: Number of cases last week 6 and present week 1
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Endemic, epidemic, sporadic

Disease 1- the cases have been almost the same so it has to be endemic.
Disease 2- there is an alarming increase in the number of cases. It has to be an epidemic.
Disease 3- the number of cases has decreased without any explanation so it has to be sporadic.

Epidemic refers to the occurrence of a disease in excess of expected frequency.

A pandemic is an epidemic affecting a large population over a large geographical area crossing international boundaries.

An endemic disease is a regularly occurring disease in a population in expected frequency without any importation from outside.

Sporadic diseases present as scattered cases of infection without relation temporally/spatially.
questions.learning: Endemic, epidemic, sporadic Disease 1- the cases have been almost the same so it has to be endemic. Disease 2- there is an alarming increase in the number of cases.

options: It integrates HBNC and HBYC into a single continuum from birth to 36 months

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A young male weighing 46 kg was treated with a drug. It has a Vd of 6 L/kg and clearance of 4.6 L/hour. What is the approximate half-life of this drug?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 40 hours

Given:

• Vd = 6 L/kg
• Weight = 46 kg

Total Vd = 6 L/kg × 46 kg = 276 L.

Half-life t½ = 0.693 × Vd / Clearance = 0.693 × 276 / 4.6 ≈ 0.693 × 60 ≈ 41.6 hours.

Thus the approximate half-life is \~40 hours.

This uses the standard pharmacokinetic half-life equation.

| Factor | Effect

| ------ | ------

| Vd ↑ | Drug stored in tissues → longer half-life

| Clearance ↓ | Drug removed slowly → longer half-life

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 30-year-old man presents with a slowly progressive swelling around the wrist joint that has been increasing over the past three months. An X-ray image of the wrist is provided. Based on the clinical history and radiographic findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Osteoclastoma, also known as Giant Cell Tumor (GCT) of the bone, is the most likely diagnosis. It typically occurs in young adults (aged 20–40) and is characteristically located in the epiphysis of long bones, most commonly the distal radius or distal femur. The X-ray shows the classic "soap bubble appearance"—an eccentric, purely lytic lesion that extends to the subchondral bone without a sclerotic rim. Ewing’s sarcoma (Option A) is a pediatric tumor that appears in the diaphysis with an "onion-skin" periosteal reaction. Osteosarcoma (Option B) usually presents with a "sunburst" appearance and Codman's triangle in the metaphysis. Osteochondroma (Option D) is a benign, bone-capped growth that protrudes from the bone surface (exostosis). GCT is locally aggressive and can occasionally metastasize to the lungs. Treatment usually involves thorough curettage of the tumor followed by bone grafting or the use of bone cement (polymethylmethacrylate) to reduce the risk of recurrence
questions.learning: Osteoclastoma, also known as Giant Cell Tumor (GCT) of the bone, is the most likely diagnosis. It typically occurs in young adults (aged 20–40) and is characteristically located in the epiphysis of long bones, most commonly the distal radius or distal femur.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: During strenuous exercise, ventilation remains elevated for a short period even after cessation of exercise. This persistence of increased ventilation is best explained by the overdrive mechanism mediated primarily by which of the following?
options: Dorsal respiratory group activation by peripheral chemoreceptors
Ventral respiratory group–mediated recruitment of expiratory muscles
Pneumotaxic center–mediated shortening of inspiratory time
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ventral respiratory group–mediated recruitment of expiratory muscles

During strenuous exercise, ventilation increases due to activation of the ventral respiratory group (VRG) in the medulla.

Mechanism:

• The VRG becomes active during forced breathing.
• It recruits accessory inspiratory muscles and expiratory muscles (e.g., abdominal muscles, internal intercostals).
• This produces active expiration and increased ventilation.

Even after exercise stops, the central respiratory drive (overdrive) may persist briefly, maintaining elevated ventilation.
questions.learning: Ventral respiratory group–mediated recruitment of expiratory muscles During strenuous exercise, ventilation increases due to activation of the ventral respiratory group (VRG) in the medulla.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presenting with bleeding gums and easy bruisability was diagnosed with scurvy. What is the biochemical basis of scurvy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Defective collagen formation

Scurvy is caused by vitamin C (ascorbic acid) deficiency, leading to defective collagen synthesis. Vitamin C is required for hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues in collagen via prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase. This hydroxylation is essential for:

• Stabilization of collagen triple helix
• Proper cross-linking of collagen fibers

Clinical features explained:

• Bleeding gums & petechiae → weak vascular connective tissue
• Poor wound healing
• Bone pain (in children)

Why other options are incorrect:

• Low calcium: Causes bone disorders (rickets/osteomalacia)
• Inhibition of clotting factors: Seen in vitamin K deficiency
• Increased keratinization: Seen in vitamin A deficiency
questions.learning: Defective collagen formation Scurvy is caused by vitamin C (ascorbic acid) deficiency, leading to defective collagen synthesis. Vitamin C is required for hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues in collagen via prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old man is intubated for surgery. What is the best method to confirm correct placement of the endotracheal tube?
questions.explanation: In modern anesthesia, Capnography (measuring the concentration of carbon dioxide in the exhaled air) is considered the "gold standard" and best method to confirm the correct placement of an endotracheal (ET) tube in the trachea. The presence of a persistent CO2 waveform (a "capnograph") definitively proves that the tube is in the respiratory tract and not the esophagus. Auscultation of breath sounds (Option B) and observing chest expansion (Option D) are important secondary checks, but they can be misleading (e.g., in obese patients or if the tube is in the esophagus but air is being pushed into the stomach). A Chest X-ray (Option A) is the best way to confirm the depth of the tube (ensuring it is not in the right mainstem bronchus) but is not practical for the immediate confirmation of tracheal versus esophageal intubation in the operating room. Failure to recognize esophageal intubation is a major cause of preventable anesthetic death and brain damage
questions.learning: In modern anesthesia, Capnography (measuring the concentration of carbon dioxide in the exhaled air) is considered the "gold standard" and best method to confirm the correct placement of an endotracheal (ET) tube in the trachea.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following is true about perimetry?
options: Kinetic perimetry is used in quantification and tracking of visual changes in established glaucoma
In Static perimetry, stimulus intensity is held constant and moved centrally with detection
Visual field defect to be classified as glaucoma, it should have the corresponding optic nerve head abnormalities
Early signs include generalised constriction of isopters and baring of blind spot
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Early signs include generalised constriction of isopters and baring of blind spot

Early signs of glaucoma in perimetry include generalized constriction of isopters and baring of blind spot.

Progression of visual field changes seen in glaucoma:

Early non-specific changes

Isopter contraction

Baring of blind spot: Exclusion of blind spot from the central field

Early significant changes

Peripheral nasal step (may be early or late)

Paracentral scotoma in Bjerrum's area.

Siedel’s  scotoma: Paracentral scotoma joins the blind spot

Late significant changes

Arcuate or Bjerrum scotoma

Ring or Double arcuate scotoma: When 2 arcuate scotomas join together

Roenne’s central nasal step

Advanced glaucomatous field defects

Tubular vision

No light perception: Complete visual field defect.

Perimetry is the procedure of estimating the extent of the visual fields. There are 2 types of perimetry - kinetic and static. In kinetic perimetry, a target of given luminance is moved from a non-seeing area in the periphery towards the center where it is perceived. In the static method, the location of a stimulus remains fixed, with the intensity increased until it is seen by the subject (threshold is reached) or decreased until it is no longer detected.

Charting of the visual fields is useful in the diagnosis of many disease conditions such as glaucoma, neurological disorders, and retinal diseases (e.g. retinitis pigmentosa) as well as following laser treatment of diabetic retinopathy.

Other options-

Option A: Static perimetry (not kinetic perimetry) is used in the quantification and tracking of visual changes in established glaucoma.

Option B: In Kinetic perimetry (not static perimetry), stimulus intensity is held constant and moved centrally with detection.

Option C: Optic disc changes are much greater than visual field changes. Therefore, visual field defects need not correspond to optic nerve head abnormalities to be classified as glaucoma.
questions.learning: Early signs include generalised constriction of isopters and baring of blind spot Early signs of glaucoma in perimetry include generalized constriction of isopters and baring of blind spot.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following amino acid is necessary for the conversion of nor-epinephrine to epinephrine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Methionine

Methionine is necessary for the conversion of nor-epinephrine to epinephrine.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An abdominal mass in a patient with congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is best seen _________.
options: During palpation over the left hypochondrium
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. During feeding

In a child with congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (CHPS), the abdominal mass is best seen during test feed in the right upper quadrant.

Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis most presents with non-bilious projectile vomiting. It is common between 2 and 8 weeks of age. Hypertrophy of the circular muscle of the pylorus results in constriction and obstruction of the gastric outlet. Male infants are at a higher risk.

Clinically, when the infant is given a test feed, an olive-shaped mass is palpable in the right upper quadrant and visible peristalsis is usually observed moving from left to right across the abdomen.

Infants with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis develop a characteristic metabolic abnormality- hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Persistent vomiting results in loss of hydrochloric acid leading to the development of metabolic alkalosis (due to loss of H+) and hypochloremia (due to loss of Cl-).

All infants with congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis are evaluated with an ultrasound (investigation of choice). It confirms the diagnosis in the majority of cases.

Management: Rehydration and metabolic correction prior to definitive surgery - Ramstedt's pyloromyotomy.
questions.learning: During feeding — In a child with congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (CHPS), the abdominal mass is best seen during test feed in the right upper quadrant.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A patient presented with cheilitis, stomatitis, and a glove and stocking pattern of neuropathy. Which vitamin deficiency is most likely responsible for this clinical presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vitamin B12

The clinical presentation described, including cheilitis, stomatitis, and glove and stocking pattern neuropathy, is most consistent with Vitamin B12 deficiency. This deficiency can lead to a condition known as pernicious anemia which presents with a variety of symptoms including those described.

Vitamin B12 deficiency can cause a wide range of symptoms, including neurological manifestations such as peripheral neuropathy (glove and stocking pattern), as well as gastrointestinal symptoms like diarrhea. Additionally, vitamin B12 deficiency can lead to megaloblastic anemia, which may present with cheilitis and stomatitis.

Other options:

(a) Niacin (B3) deficiency: Niacin deficiency can lead to a condition called pellagra, which is characterized by the "3 Ds": dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia. Cheilitis and stomatitis are common manifestations of pellagra, but glove and stocking pattern neuropathy are not typically associated with niacin deficiency.

(b) Thiamine (B1) deficiency: Thiamine deficiency can cause a condition known as beriberi, which can manifest with neurological symptoms such as peripheral neuropathy, but it usually does not present with dermatological symptoms like cheilitis and stomatitis.

(d) Riboflavin (B2) deficiency: Riboflavin (vitamin B2) deficiency can cause glossitis (inflammation of the tongue) and cheilosis (cracks or sores at the corners of the mouth). While riboflavin deficiency can cause dermatological symptoms, it is less likely to cause rashes in sun-exposed areas and peripheral neuropathy.
questions.learning: Vitamin B12 — The clinical presentation described, including cheilitis, stomatitis, and glove and stocking pattern neuropathy, is most consistent with Vitamin B12 deficiency.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presents with fever, mild headache, dysphagia, cervical lymphadenopathy, and a thick, whitish tonsillar membrane that bleeds on scraping. Considering these clinical features and Gram stain findings from the lesion, which organism is most likely responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a thick, whitish-gray pseudomembrane on the tonsils that bleeds upon scraping is pathognomonic for Diphtheria. The provided Gram stain confirms the diagnosis, showing Gram-positive, club-shaped rods typically arranged in "Chinese letter" patterns ( or shapes). Parvovirus (Option A) and HHV6 (Option B) are viruses that cause viral rashes, not tonsillar membranes. Beta-hemolytic streptococci (Option D) cause acute tonsillitis, which features exudates that can be wiped away easily without bleeding, and the bacteria appear as cocci in chains. Corynebacterium diphtheriae produces a powerful exotoxin that causes both the local membrane and potentially lethal systemic effects on the heart and nerves. Therefore, the combination of the adherent bleeding membrane and the classic microscopic rod morphology confirms Diphtheria as the causative agent

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Two construction workers were working together when a hammer slipped from one worker's hand and struck the other on the head. An X-ray revealed a fracture. What type of fracture could this be?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Depressed skull fracture

The clinical history and the X-ray image are suggestive of a depressed skull fracture of the frontal bone.

A depressed skull fracture happens when a section of the skull bone is driven inward following a traumatic impact. This injury creates a noticeable indentation or depression in the skull and typically results from a direct blow to the head.

The management of depressed skull fractures:

* The first step is to order a CT scan to know the degree of depression and to exclude the presence of an intracranial hematoma or contusion.

* The depressed fracture is elevated and managed as an open fracture (surgery) if:

* The degree of depression is greater than the thickness of the adjacent skull.

* The wound is open and grossly contaminated.

* There are focal neurological deficits.

* Less severe depressed fractures are managed by the closure of the overlying scalp laceration, if present.

Other options:

Option A: A Linear fracture is a type of skull fracture where the bone breaks in a thin, straight line without displacement. It is often caused by blunt force trauma and typically does not involve significant damage to surrounding tissues.

Option B: A Hinge fracture is a type of skull base fracture where the skull splits along the base, resembling an open hinge. It is usually caused by severe trauma and can be associated with brain injury and damage to vital structures.

Option C: A Ring fracture is a circular fracture around the base of the skull, typically occurring in the posterior fossa around the foramen magnum. It is often caused by severe trauma, such as a fall from a height or forceful impact on the head. These occur If the kinetic energy of the fall is not absorbed by fractures of the legs, pelvis, or spine, the impact is transmitted up the cervical spine. This force may be rammed into the skull, carrying a circle of occipital bone with it.

Pearl PF0368: Types of skull vault fracture

Diastatic fracture - Separation of sutures due to blow with blunt weapon or from cerebral edema. It is also called sutural fracture.

Fissured fracture/Linear fracture:

* Linear skull fractures are breaks in the bone that traverse the full thickness of the skull from the outer to inner table.

* They are usually fairly straight with no bone displacement.

* The common cause of injury is blunt force trauma where the impact energy transferred over a wide area of the skull.

Pond fracture - Occurs in children due to elasticity of bones. It is also known as indented fracture.

Depressed fracture - Caused by a heavy weapon with a small striking surface. Its shape indicates the type of weapon which is produced. So it is also called 'signature fracture'.

Comminuted fracture - It is also called spider web fracture and has a stellate appearance where there is no displacement of fracture.
questions.learning: Depressed skull fracture — The clinical history and the X-ray image are suggestive of a depressed skull fracture of the frontal bone. A depressed skull fracture happens when a section of the skull bone is driven inward following a traumatic impact.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 60-year-old postmenopausal female patient with a previous history of Colle's fracture came with complaints of lower backache. On evaluation, her T score was -2.5. Which of the following statements are false about the management of her condition?
options: Teriparatide should be started before supplementing with bisphosphonates
Bisphosphonates are not given for more than a year
Calcium requirement is 1200 mg per day
Oral vitamin D3 is given along with oral calcium
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bisphosphonates are not given for more than a year

Bisphosphonates are given for periods of more than one year (Option B is false). In this case, as the patient is having a history of osteoporotic fracture, teriparatide can be given before bisphosphonates.

Pharmacologic management of osteoporosis:

Bisphosphonates: These are pyrophosphate analogs that act by directly inhibiting bone resorption. The antiresorptive action is mainly due to its direct inhibitory effect on osteoclasts. It causes osteoclast apoptosis as well as the prevention of hydroxyapatite dissolution. Long-term bisphosphonates therapy is given for durations of 3-5 years, depending on the fracture risk of the patient. Since they are associated with osteonecrosis of the jaw and atypical femur fractures, a drug holiday may be advised after long-term management.

Teriparatide is a recombinant PTH analog that has an anabolic effect on bone homeostasis by increasing osteoblastic activity. It increases bone mineral density and decreases the risk of fractures in postmenopausal women. Indications of teriparatide therapy include the history of osteoporotic fracture, multiple risk factors for fracture, intolerance, or failure of previous osteoporosis therapy. It is only approved for 2 years of use. Clinical trials that used teriparatide prior to bisphosphonate have been proven effective.

Denosumab is a human monoclonal antibody with a mechanism of action similar to that of osteoprotegerin (OPG). It binds to RANK Ligand (RANKL), thereby inhibiting its binding to the RANK receptor of the surface of osteoclasts. This prevents RANK receptor activation and subsequent bone resorption.

Selective estrogen receptor modulators (SERMs) - Estrogen has a protective effect that prevents accelerated bone loss. This is carried out by reducing the bone resorption effects of parathyroid hormone (PTH). Keeping in line with these effects, osteoporosis prevention in postmenopausal women has been attributed to the use of SERMs such as raloxifene. It acts as an estrogen agonist on the bone and liver.

Calcium and Vitamin D supplementation: Calcium supplementation in the elderly suppresses bone turnover and improves bone mineral density. 1200mg of calcium is daily required in adults of more than 50 years of age. Vitamin D supplementation with 400-800IU/day improves intestinal calcium absorption, suppresses bone remodeling, and improves bone mineral density.
questions.learning: Bisphosphonates are not given for more than a year Bisphosphonates are given for periods of more than one year (Option B is false). In this case, as the patient is having a history of osteoporotic fracture, teriparatide can be given before bisphosphonates.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman presented with menorrhagia. A hysterectomy was performed, and the specimen is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Intramural Fibroid

The given clinical scenario as well as the specimen suggests that this is a case of leiomyoma uteri or fibroid uterus. The specimen is of a leiomyoma.

Gross specimen appearance:

• The uterine body/corpus is enlarged and deformed.
• The cut surface shows multiple nodules, well-circumscribed, firm, and white-greyish with a whorled appearance formed by the intersecting bundles of brown muscle fibres and white fibrous tissue.
• Leiomyomas can also present bleeding areas, cystic degeneration, and calcifications. The uterine cavity is compressed.
• A typical myoma is a well-circumscribed tumor with a pseudo capsule and firm inconsistency. The cut surface has a whorled appearance.
• The vessels that supply blood to the tumor lie in the capsule and send radial branches into the tumor.
• Therefore, the central portion of the tumour receives the least blood supply and degeneration is noticeable early in this part of the tumour.
• On the other hand, calcification begins at the periphery and spreads inwards along the vessels.

Risk factors:

Increased risk of leiomyomas is seen in nulliparous women, those with obesity, and individuals in a hyper-estrogenic state, such as in conditions like endometriosis, endometrial hyperplasia, or endometrial carcinoma. Black women are also at higher risk.

Conversely, the risk is decreased in multiparous women. Recent studies have shown no significant correlation between smoking and the development of leiomyomas.

Symptoms of fibroid uterus:

Most women with leiomyomas are asymptomatic, but those affected may experience bleeding, pain, pressure, or infertility. Symptom risk increases with the size and number of myomas. Heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB) is common, linked to dilated endometrial venules and dysregulated vasoactive growth factors. When these engorged venules are disrupted during menstruation, bleeding can overwhelm normal hemostatic mechanisms, causing HMB.

Treatment:

Medical therapy for fibroids includes mifepristone, GnRh analogs, Aromatase inhibitors

Drugs to reduce the size of the fibroid

• Antiprogesterone – Mifepristone/RU-486
• Danazol (Usually not used due to androgenic side effects)
• GnRH analogs

• Agonists – goserelin, leuprorelin, nafarelin, buserelin
• Antagonists – cetrorelix, ganirelix

• Levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system
• Selective progesterone receptor modulator (SPRM’s) – Asoprisnil

Other management options

• Uterine artery embolization
• Myomectomy
• Hysterectomy

Other Options:

Option B: Myomatous Polyp: They are typically found on the endometrial lining and would not present as a fibroid embedded in the wall of the uterus.

Option C: Endometrioma: An endometrioma is an ovarian cyst filled with endometrial tissue. It would not be found within the uterine wall but rather on the ovaries.

Option D: Adenomyoma: Adenomyoma is a localized area of endometrial tissue within the myometrium (muscle layer) of the uterus. While it can cause similar symptoms, it does not typically present as a discrete mass protruding from the uterine wall like an intramural fibroid.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which drug is known to elevate the levels of uric acid in urine?
questions.explanation: Probenecid is a uricosuric agent, meaning its primary mechanism of action is to elevate the levels of uric acid in the urine. It achieves this by inhibiting the reabsorption of uric acid in the proximal convoluted tubules of the kidney, thereby increasing its renal excretion and lowering the concentration of uric acid in the blood. In contrast, Allopurinol (Option D) and Febuxostat (Option B) are xanthine oxidase inhibitors that lower blood uric acid by decreasing its production; consequently, they actually reduce the total amount of uric acid excreted in the urine over time. Colchicine (Option A) is an anti-inflammatory drug used for acute gout flares and does not significantly affect uric acid levels in the blood or urine. Probenecid is used for chronic gout management but is contraindicated in patients with a history of renal stones, as the high urinary uric acid concentration can promote stone formation. Understanding this "production vs. excretion" distinction is vital for choosing the appropriate gout therapy

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A neonate presents with features of congestive heart failure. On examination, there is an enlarged fontanelle and a bruit is heard on auscultation. Ultrasound reveals a midline hypoechoic lesion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a neonate with high-output congestive heart failure, enlarging fontanelles (hydrocephalus), and a cranial bruit heard on auscultation is pathognomonic for a Vein of Galen Malformation (VOGM) (Option A). VOGM is a direct arteriovenous shunting from cerebral arteries into the great cerebral vein, which dilates into a massive aneurysmal sac. The USG midline hypoechoic lesion represents this dilated venous sac. Aqueduct stenosis (Option B) and arachnoid cysts (Option C) cause hydrocephalus but would not cause heart failure or a bruit. Medulloblastoma (Option D) is a malignant posterior fossa tumor that typically presents in older children, not as a neonate in heart failure. The shunt in VOGM acts as a low-resistance path for blood, forcing the heart to work excessively to maintain systemic circulation. Therefore, VOGM is the only diagnosis that accounts for both the neurological and cardiovascular findings
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of a neonate with high-output congestive heart failure, enlarging fontanelles (hydrocephalus), and a cranial bruit heard on auscultation is pathognomonic for a Vein of Galen Malformation (VOGM) (Option A).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 56-year-old multipara woman presented with grade II/III uterine prolapse with cystocele. She complains of passing urine on coughing and sneezing. What is the type of urinary incontinence seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Stress incontinence

The type of urinary incontinence present in a patient with prolapse and cystocele experiencing urination on coughing and sneezing is stress incontinence.

Stress incontinence refers to the involuntary leakage of urine when there is increased intra-abdominal pressure (eg, coughing, sneezing, laughing, Valsalva maneuver). Absence of detrusor muscle contraction is seen in urodynamic studies.

Causes:

• Age and menopause - due to estrogen deficiency
• Multiparity - due to loss of pelvic muscle tone
• Obesity
• Smoking
• Constipation, chronic cough
• Pelvic organ prolapse
• Pregnancy - due to the effect of progesterone and pressure of the gravid uterus on the bladder neck.
• Puerperium - due to descent of the bladder neck, loss of urethro-vesical angle, and reduced pelvic muscle tone
• Surgical repair of vesicovaginal fistula

Grading of genuine stress incontinence (GSI) :

• Grade I: Incontinence with only severe stress, such as coughing, sneezing, and jogging.
• Grade II: Incontinence with moderate stress, such as fast walk, going up and down the stairs.
• Grade III: Incontinence with mild stress such as standing.

Investigations are only done prior to surgery to confirm the diagnosis. They include:

• Stress test
• Cotton swab or Q-tip test
• Marshall and Bonney’s test
• Urethroscopy
• Urodynamic studies.

These are not required prior to conservative management.

Conservative management includes Kegel's pelvic exercises, electric nerve stimulation, devices like pessaries, vaginal cones, and artificial sphincters. Medical treatment with estrogen creams, alpha agonists, venlafaxine, and imipramine may be useful.

Other options:

Option A: Overflow incontinence is an old term that refers to the inability to empty the bladder, with involuntary, continuous urinary dribbling. Currently, it refers to another presentation of urge incontinence.

Option B: Urge incontinence is the involuntary escape of urine when there is an imminent need to urinate. It occurs due to detrusor muscle overactivity or detrusor instability. It is seen more commonly in old women with decreased bladder capacity, decreased sensation, and CNS inhibition.

Option D: Neurogenic bladder occurs in patients with neurogenic dysfunction leading to detrusor hyperreflexia. Conditions such as multiple sclerosis, stroke, Parkinson's disease, and spinal injury give rise to this. They present with urgency or urge incontinence.
questions.learning: Stress incontinence — The type of urinary incontinence present in a patient with prolapse and cystocele experiencing urination on coughing and sneezing is stress incontinence.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 42-year old alcoholic and a chronic smoker presented with bouts of vomiting and stabbing pain in the epigastrium. He was binge drinking shortly before the symptoms started. He is febrile and tachycardic. The given findings were seen on bedside radiological imaging. Which among the following is a likely cause of this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Peptic ulcer perforation

In the given case scenario, the supine abdominal x-ray shows air beneath the diaphragm along with Rigler's double-wall sign indicating pneumoperitoneum. The likely cause for this would be peptic ulcer perforation. Consumption of alcohol and chronic tobacco smoking are high-risk factors for developing peptic ulcers. Fever and tachycardia suggest peritonitis from the perforated ulcer.

Gastric ulcers are more prone to perforate than bleed. Thus, these perforations lead to pneumoperitoneum which is an emergency and warrants immediate surgical intervention.

Other options:

A. Tension pneumothorax - presents with a rapid hemodynamic compromise with absent breath sounds. Pneumoperitoneum rarely is caused by pneumothorax, and downward displacement of air is more likely seen in retroperitoneal spaces.

C. Boerhaave syndrome or spontaneous esophageal rupture - occurs in alcoholics after binge drinking, due to forced vomiting from the closed glottis.  Pneumomediastinum and subcutaneous emphysema are seen here.

D. Mallory Weis tear - longitudinal mucosal tear resulting in upper GI bleeding. It is commonly seen in alcoholics.
questions.learning: Peptic ulcer perforation — In the given case scenario, the supine abdominal x-ray shows air beneath the diaphragm along with Rigler's double-wall sign indicating pneumoperitoneum.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A patient from a North-Eastern state was diagnosed to have an infection with P. falciparum malaria. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Artemether plus lumefantrine

The most appropriate treatment for Plasmodium falciparum infection in North-Eastern states is artemether (20 mg) plus lumefantrine (120 mg).

As per National Vector Borne Disease Control Program (NVBDCP):

* Plasmodium malariae: treat as Plasmodium falciparum

* Plasmodium ovale: treat as Plasmodium vivax

* Severe and complicated malaria

-Intial parenteral treatment x 24-48 hr:  quinine/artemether/artesunate/arteether

-Oral treatment after 48 hrs-after parenteral quinine: quinine + doxycyclinex 7 days or quinine + clindamycin x 7 days (pregnancy and chidren<8yrs)

-After parenteral artimisin derivates: in NE states: ACT -AL X 3 days+primaquine (day2) , in other states:ACT-SPX 3 days+primaquine (day 2)

* Chemoprophylaxis

Short-term, less than or equal to 6 weeks: Doxycycline OD (start one day before travel and continue for 4 weeks after return)

Long-term, more than 6 weeks: mefloquine weekly (start 2 weeks before travel and 4 weeks after return).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with a history of recurrent vomiting undergoes arterial blood gas analysis, which shows a pH of 7.5, PaCO₂ of 48 mm Hg, and HCO₃⁻ of 30 mm Hg. Based on these findings, what is the most likely acid–base disorder?
questions.explanation: The blood gas findings show an elevated pH (7.5), confirming alkalosis. The primary cause is an elevated bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) of 30 mEq/L, which results from the loss of gastric hydrochloric acid (HCl) during vomiting. The body responds through respiratory compensation—hypoventilation to retain —which explains the elevated of 48 mm Hg. Metabolic acidosis (Option B) would feature a low pH and low . Respiratory acidosis (Option C) is characterized by a low pH and high . Respiratory alkalosis (Option D) involves a high pH with a low due to hyperventilation. Thus, the clinical context of vomiting combined with the metabolic laboratory values clearly points to metabolic alkalosis with partial respiratory compensation as the most likely acid-base disturbance in this patient
questions.learning: The blood gas findings show an elevated pH (7.5), confirming alkalosis. The primary cause is an elevated bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) of 30 mEq/L, which results from the loss of gastric hydrochloric acid (HCl) during vomiting.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What is the most common cause of ventriculomegaly in newborns?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Aqueductal stenosis

Aqueductal stenosis is the most common cause of ventriculomegaly and hydrocephalus in newborns.

Ventriculomegaly is the dilation of the ventricles. When ventriculomegaly occurs in association with raised cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pressure, it is called hydrocephalus.

Pathologic etiologies can be congenital or acquired. Congenital causes include structural abnormalities such as aqueductal stenosis, agenesis of the corpus callosum, Dandy-Walker malformations, Chiari malformations, and neural tube defects. Acquired causes are intracranial infections(cytomegalovirus, toxoplasmosis), intracranial hemorrhage, ischemic injury, and brain parenchymal tumors.

Aqueductal stenosis is the narrowing or obstruction of the cerebral aqueduct, a narrow channel that connects the third and fourth ventricles in the brain. As a result, the fluid accumulates within the ventricles, causing them to enlarge.

Treatment for aqueductal stenosis includes ventriculostomy, diuretics, serial lumbar punctures in specific cases, and CSF diversion. In severe cases, CSF diversion procedures (shunting), may be necessary to redirect the flow of CSF and relieve pressure on the brain.
questions.learning: Aqueductal stenosis Aqueductal stenosis is the most common cause of ventriculomegaly and hydrocephalus in newborns. Ventriculomegaly is the dilation of the ventricles.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text:
The drug 'X' is a GHRH analogue that is FDA-approved for the treatment of HIV-associated lipodystrophy and not used for Growth hormone deficiency. Identify the drug 'X'.

GHRH- Growth Hormone Releasing Hormone
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tesamorelin

Tesamorelin is approved for use in HIV-associated lipodystrophy but not for GH deficiency. It is a synthetic N-terminal modified form of human GHRH. It does not get degraded by dipeptidyl peptidase 4 and therefore has a longer duration of action.

It increases the levels of growth hormone (GH) and insulin-like growth factor (IGF-1) but reduces visceral fat accumulation.

Tesamorelin is approved for use in HIV-associated lipodystrophy but not for GH deficiency.

Other options:

Option A: Octreotide is a somatostatin analogue that decreases growth hormone levels. It is used in the treatment of acromegaly, variceal bleeding, diarrhoea due to adenomas secreting VIP (vasoactive intestinal peptide), and sulfonylurea toxicity. One of its adverse effects is gallstone formation.

Option B: Somatropin is a growth hormone analogue. It is used in growth hormone deficiency and other short-stature conditions like Turner's syndrome, Noonan syndrome, and Prader-Willi syndrome. Their use is contraindicated in acute critical illness, active malignancy, and proliferative retinopathy.

Option D: Mecasermin is a recombinant human IGF-1. It is used in IGF-1 deficiency, growth hormone receptor defects, and antibodies against growth hormone receptors. Adverse effects include hypoglycemia and lipohypertrophy. Another recombinant human IGF-1 with its IGFBP-3, mecasermin rinfabate has been FDA-approved for HIV-associated adipose redistribution syndrome.
questions.learning: Tesamorelin Tesamorelin is approved for use in HIV-associated lipodystrophy but not for GH deficiency. It is a synthetic N-terminal modified form of human GHRH.

questions.text: All of the following conditions are known to be associated with chronic Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Gianotti-Crosti syndrome

Chronic hepatitis C infection is associated with multiple immune-complex mediated extrahepatic manifestations, including:

• Mixed cryoglobulinemia
• Leukocytoclastic vasculitis
• Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN)

These occur due to circulating immune complex deposition.

Gianotti–Crosti syndrome is classically associated with hepatitis B infection (and some viral infections in children like EBV), not chronic hepatitis C.

A self-limiting, childhood exanthem characterized by a symmetric papular or papulovesicular eruption on the face, buttocks, and extremities, typically following a viral infection. Also called: Papular Acrodermatitis of Childhood (PAC)
