questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: During analysis of an aortic pressure tracing, a small notch is observed on the descending limb of the pressure curve immediately after ventricular ejection. Which event is responsible for this dicrotic notch?
options: Rapid filling of the left ventricle
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Closure of the aortic valve

• The dicrotic notch (incisura) on the aortic pressure tracing occurs immediately following closure of the aortic valve.
• At the end of ventricular systole, left ventricular pressure falls below aortic pressure. This produces a brief tendency for blood to flow backward toward the left ventricle, causing the aortic valve to close. The combination of transient retrograde flow and elastic recoil of the aorta produces the characteristic dicrotic notch.

The dicrotic notch therefore marks:

• End of ventricular ejection → Aortic valve closure → Beginning of isovolumetric relaxation
questions.learning: Closure of the aortic valve • — The dicrotic notch (incisura) on the aortic pressure tracing occurs immediately following closure of the aortic valve. • At the end of ventricular systole, left ventricular pressure falls below aortic pressure.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 40-year-old patient accidentally swallowed a fish bone and presented with choking. On examination, the bone was found to be impacted in the esophagus at the level of T4 vertebra. Which of the following structures is responsible for the obstruction at this level?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Arch of aorta

The esophagus has physiological constrictions, one of which occurs at the T4 vertebral level due to the arch of aorta crossing anterior to the esophagus.

This site is a common location for foreign body impaction, especially fish bones.

The cricopharyngeal junction lies at C6, the left bronchus crosses at T5–T6, and the diaphragm constriction is at T10.
questions.learning: Arch of aorta — The esophagus has physiological constrictions, one of which occurs at the T4 vertebral level due to the arch of aorta crossing anterior to the esophagus.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: An auxiliary nurse midwife is tasked with organizing a vaccination camp within a rural community. She has been provided with 2 vials that have been unsealed. Among these, one contains a pentavalent vaccine, while the other holds an MR vaccine. What options does she have in terms of effectively using these vials?
options: Use MR vaccine and discard pentavalent vaccine
Use pentavalent vaccine and discard MR vaccine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Use pentavalent vaccine and discard MR vaccine

This scenario is governed by the Open Vial Policy (OVP) under the Universal Immunization Programme.

However, lyophilized (freeze-dried) vaccines must be discarded after reconstitution.

Pentavalent vaccine is a liquid, non-live, multi-dose vaccine that can be reused if the vial has been opened, provided cold chain is maintained, VVM is valid, expiry date not crossed, and aseptic technique was followed.

Exceptions to open vial policy: MMR, BCG, JE (Live), Yellow fever, COVID-19
questions.learning: Use pentavalent vaccine and discard MR vaccine — This scenario is governed by the Open Vial Policy (OVP) under the Universal Immunization Programme. However, lyophilized (freeze-dried) vaccines must be discarded after reconstitution.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A child is infected with a negative sense RNA virus which also contains neuraminidase receptors. What is the causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Influenza virus

Influenza virus is a segmented, negative-sense/negative-strand RNA virus with neuraminidase receptors/peplomers projecting from the envelope. It belongs to the family of orthomyxoviruses. The hemagglutinin and neuraminidase receptors are present as two different spikes on the envelope.

Parainfluenza virus, Newcastle disease virus, and Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) are negative-sense single-stranded RNA viruses with a linear genome. No neuraminidase is seen.
questions.learning: Influenza virus Influenza virus is a segmented, negative-sense/negative-strand RNA virus with neuraminidase receptors/peplomers projecting from the envelope.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: 42-year-old woman comes to the office due to worsening double vision and gait unsteadiness. She states she had cramping abdominal pain and diarrhoea 2 weeks ago after an outdoor picnic which spontaneously resolved after 3 days. The double vision began 4 days ago and is persistent and progressive. She has had no fever, headache, neck pain, photophobia, or bowel or bladder dysfunction. On physical examination, she is fully alert and oriented with normal memory, speech, and language comprehension. There is mild ptosis of the right eye with weakness of the medial and upward gaze. Left eye movements are normal. Bilateral lower-extremity weakness with loss of deep tendon reflexes is present. Bilateral upper-extremity muscle strength, reflexes, and coordination are normal. Sensation to touch and pinprick is normal throughout. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's current condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Immune-mediated nerve injury

Progressive ascending symmetrical weakness with areflexia following a recent diarrheal illness suggests Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS), caused by immune-mediated nerve injury.

Pathogenesis:

• Often follows infection (classically Campylobacter jejuni)
• Molecular mimicry → antibodies attack peripheral nerve myelin or axons
• Results in acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy

Why not others (short):

A. Botulism: Descending paralysis, dilated pupils, autonomic signs → not ascending areflexic weakness.

B. Thiamine deficiency: Confusion + ataxia (Wernicke), not acute limb weakness with areflexia.

D. Neuroinvasive viral infection: Fever, encephalitis/meningitis signs expected.
questions.learning: Immune-mediated nerve injury Progressive ascending symmetrical weakness with areflexia following a recent diarrheal illness suggests Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS), caused by immune-mediated nerve injury.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 19-year-old male, chronic smoker, presented with fever, a painful lump over his left cheek just below the ear, and difficulty in swallowing or talking. The patient also complained of mild testicular pain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mumps

The clinical features of painful swelling in the parotid region (parotitis) together with testicular pain (orchitis) is most likely suggestive of mumps.

Mumps is a paramyxoviral disease, which spreads by respiratory droplets. It usually affects children. However, there has been an increasing trend in the incidence of mumps in adolescents and young adults. The disease is more serious in adults than in children.

Clinical features:

* Parotitis is the most common presentation. It is often bilateral. Other salivary glands such as submaxillary and sublingual glands may also be involved, but are less likely than parotid.

* Patients complain of earache and find it difficult to eat, swallow, or talk.

* Epididymo-orchitis is the next common presentation. The testis is painful and tender and may enlarge up to several times its normal size.

Complications of Mumps:

* Meningitis or Meningoencephalitis

* Other complications include: Arthritis, oophoritis, nephritis, pancreatitis, thyroiditis and myocarditis.

Diagnosis is made by detection of viral RNA by reverse-transcriptase PCR (RT-PCR) or on serology.

Treatment: The disease is self-limiting. Analgesics and application of warm or cold compress over the parotid and testicular swellings may help relieve the symptoms.
questions.learning: Mumps — The clinical features of painful swelling in the parotid region (parotitis) together with testicular pain (orchitis) is most likely suggestive of mumps.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Choose the correct statements from the following options: a. Widal test done in first week of illness b. Microscopic agglutination test in Leptospira c. Weil Felix test in typhus fever d. Standard agglutination test in Brucellosis e. VDRL used for Treponema pallidum
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. b, c, d, e

Understanding the appropriate serological tests for different infections is essential for diagnosis and exam questions.

Correct associations:

• Leptospira → Microscopic agglutination test (MAT)
• Typhus (rickettsial infections) → Weil-Felix test
• Brucellosis → Standard agglutination test (SAT)
• Treponema pallidum → VDRL (non-treponemal screening test)

Incorrect statement:

• Widal test is not useful in the first week of illness; it becomes positive only after 7–10 days
questions.learning: b, c, d, e Understanding the appropriate serological tests for different infections is essential for diagnosis and exam questions. Correct associations: • Leptospira → Microscopic agglutination test (MAT) • Typhus (rickettsial infections) → Weil-Felix test…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young man has the following hepatitis B serological profile: HBsAg positive, IgM anti- HBc negative, IgG anti-HBc positive, and HBeAg positive. Based on this serological status, what is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: The serological profile indicates chronic active Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection. HBsAg positivity indicates ongoing infection, while negative IgM anti-HBc and positive IgG anti-HBc confirm that the disease is in the chronic phase rather than acute. The presence of HBeAg signifies high viral replication and increased infectivity. Antiviral therapy is required to suppress viral replication and prevent liver damage. Lamivudine is an oral nucleoside analog that inhibits HBV DNA polymerase and is an effective (though older) treatment option for chronic HBV. Ombitasvir (Option B) is used for Hepatitis C (HCV), not HBV. Ritonavir (Option C) and Abacavir (Option D) are components of antiretroviral therapy (ART) for HIV and are not standard treatments for HBV monoinfection. While tenofovir and entecavir are now preferred first-line due to lower resistance rates, Lamivudine is the only appropriate HBV drug listed
questions.learning: The serological profile indicates chronic active Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection. HBsAg positivity indicates ongoing infection, while negative IgM anti-HBc and positive IgG anti-HBc confirm that the disease is in the chronic phase rather than acute.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 70-year-old patient who was using presbyopic glasses for the past few years is now able to comfortably read the newspaper without the glasses. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Index myopia

The clinical scenario of improvement in near vision of a presbyopic patient is termed the second sight phenomenon. This is seen due to index myopia caused by the formation of nuclear cataracts.

Presbyopia, also known as the eyesight of old age, is a condition of physiological insufficiency of accommodation leading to a progressive fall in near vision. The treatment of presbyopia is the prescription of appropriate convex glasses for near work.

In nuclear cataracts, nuclear sclerosis occurs leading to an increase in refractive index. This leads to progressive myopia known as index myopia. When a presbyopic patient develops a nuclear cataract, this increase in the refractive index of the lens compensates for the physiological insufficiency of accommodation that the patient has.

Thus, a patient with presbyopia may be able to read again, without the aid of spectacles due to this improvement in near vision, termed second sight. At the same time, this increased refractive index causes a deterioration in far vision.

Option B: Index hypermetropia occurs in cortical cataracts and sclerosis that lead to a decrease in the refractive index of the lens in old age. In such patients, there will be worsening of the near vision which does not align with the history of a presbyopic being able to read with his glasses.

Option C: Presbyopia occurs due to a decrease in the accommodative power of the crystalline lens with increasing age, and thus does not regress spontaneously. It can however be easily corrected with the prescription of appropriate convex glasses for near work.
questions.learning: Index myopia — The clinical scenario of improvement in near vision of a presbyopic patient is termed the second sight phenomenon. This is seen due to index myopia caused by the formation of nuclear cataracts.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: DNA packing is done by which of the following ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Histone

The proteins involved in DNA packing are histones.

Chromatin contains double-stranded DNA molecules and small basic proteins known as histones. In addition, nonhistone proteins are present that are involved in DNA replication and repair, and RNA synthesis. Histones play a role in condensing the DNA.

Nucleosomes are the organizational unit of chromatin and contain an octamer of histones around which 150 base pairs of DNA are packed. There are various types of histone proteins. H2A, H2B, H3, and H4 groups are components of nucleosomes and are known as core histones. They undergo post-translational modifications such as acetylation and methylation. This plays a critical part in chromatin structure and function.

The DNA in the nucleosome is arranged in a left-handed helical configuration over the histone octamer.

Other options:

Option B - Glycoproteins are proteins with oligosaccharide chains (glycans) bound to amino acids. Certain plasma proteins, peptide hormones, and cell membrane proteins are examples. Structural changes in the glycoproteins present in cancer cells may play a role in metastasis.

Option C - Nucleic acids can be either DNA or RNA. DNA is thought to be arranged in a double-stranded helix model. RNA on the other hand exists as a single strand. There are different types of RNA such as mRNA (messenger RNA), tRNA (transfer RNA), and rRNA (ribosomal RNA).

Option D - Adenine is a purine base that when linked to ribose forms adenosine, a nucleoside. When a nucleoside is esterified with a phosphate group a nucleotide is formed. Guanine is the other purine base. Cytosine is the pyrimidine base common to DNA and RNA. Thymine is present only in DNA and Uracil in RNA.
questions.learning: Histone — The proteins involved in DNA packing are histones. Chromatin contains double-stranded DNA molecules and small basic proteins known as histones.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following conditions gives the haematological picture as shown below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Saturnism

The given haematological picture showing basophilic stippling with Cabot's ring is suggestive of chronic lead poisoning also called as plumbism or saturnism.

Clinical features of lead poisoning include

* A - Anemia with basophilic stippling.

* B - Burtonian line (blue stippled line on gums).

* C - Constipation & Abdominal Colic

* D - wrist Drop & foot Drop

* E - Encephalopathy

* F - Facial pallor -earliest sign.

Other Options:

Option A : Minamata disease is chronic mercury poisoning can show anemia secondary to GI hemorrhage.

Option C : Chronic iron toxicity, can present with leucocytosis and anemia (due to blood loss).

Option D : Arsenic poisoning can induce microcytic hypochromic anemia or hemolytic anemia.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The students of a boarding school eat from the same canteen. One of the students developed abdominal pain, jaundice, and fever following which other students also presented with similar symptoms. Which of the following investigations should the Medical Officer of the area check for to reach a diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. IgM for Hepatitis A

The given scenario is of a Hepatitis A outbreak that is spread via the fecal-oral route and the investigation of choice is IgM for Hepatitis A.

Hepatitis A:

Modes of transmission

* Fecal-oral route: This is the major route of transmission. It can occur directly (handshake after toilet) or indirectly via contaminated food, water, or milk.

* Parenteral route: This is very rare and occurs during the viral dissemination phase. It occurs during the prodromal phase and not when patients are symptomatic and admitted to the hospital. As a result, healthcare workers are not at increased risk.

* Sexual transmission may occur in individuals practicing oro-anal methods (usually homosexual men). It however would not cause an outbreak.

Incubation period:

* 10 to 50 days (usually 14-28 days). Isolation is not an effective measure to control outbreaks as the shedding of the virus is maximum during the early stages of illness when clinical illness may not have started and many patients are asymptomatic yet continue to shed the virus.

Clinical spectrum:

* The onset of jaundice is preceded by gastrointestinal symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, anorexia, and mild fever.

* Jaundice may appear within a few days of the prodromal period, but anicteric hepatitis is more common.

* Hepatitis A resolves completely in 98 percent of cases but relapse of symptoms is noted in 3-20 percent of cases

Diagnosis:

* Laboratory diagnosis of hepatitis A can be obtained by

* Demonstration of HAV particles or specific viral antigens in the feces, bile, and blood.

* Anti-HAV appears in the lgM fraction during the acute phase, peaking about 2 weeks after the elevation of liver enzymes. ELISA is the method of choice for measuring HAV antibodies.

Prevention and containment:

* Control of reservoir: Use of 0.5 percent sodium hypochlorite has been strongly recommended as an effective disinfectant

* Control of transmission: personal and community hygiene. Hand hygiene before food and after the toilet is highly recommended.

* 1 mg/L of free residual chlorine can cause the destruction of the virus in 30 minutes at pH values of 8.5 or less. Hence adequate chlorination can be helpful.

* Patients with chronic liver disease are at increased risk for fulminant hepatitis A and should be vaccinated. The use of the hepatitis A vaccine should be considered for pre-exposure(for travelers) and post-exposure(close contacts of affected individuals)prophylaxis.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: In a patient with CSOM, labyrinthine fistula most commonly involves
questions.explanation: Chronic Suppurative Otitis Media (CSOM), particularly the atticoantral type associated with cholesteatoma, can cause erosion of the bony labyrinth. The lateral (horizontal) semicircular canal (SCC) is the most common site for a labyrinthine fistula because it lies in the medial wall of the aditus and antrum, making it highly susceptible to pressure and osteolytic enzymes from a growing cholesteatoma. Option A (Superior SCC) and Option C (Posterior SCC) are involved much less frequently. Option D (Utricle) is deeper and better protected. Patients with a fistula often present with "fistula sign," where changes in ear canal pressure induce vertigo and nystagmus. Vertigo may also occur when cleaning the ear or with loud sounds (Tullio phenomenon). The presence of a fistula is a surgical priority during mastoidectomy. The surgeon must carefully remove the disease while preserving the underlying endosteum to prevent total sensorineural hearing loss (dead ear)

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient with a known marginal placenta presents for follow-up evaluation. Ultrasonography reveals a 4 × 4 cm placental mass extending beyond the uterus and invading the urinary bladder. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Placenta percreta is the most severe grade of the placenta accreta spectrum. It occurs when chorionic villi penetrate through the entire thickness of the myometrium and the uterine serosa, often invading adjacent pelvic organs such as the urinary bladder. Placenta previa (Option A) refers only to the location of the placenta near or over the internal os without invasion. Placenta accreta (Option C) involves adherence to the myometrium without penetration. Placenta increta (Option D) involves invasion deep into the myometrium but not through the serosa. Because the ultrasound explicitly identifies invasion into the bladder, the condition has progressed beyond the myometrium, confirming the diagnosis of percreta. This requires complex surgical management, often including a hysterectomy and partial cystectomy
questions.learning: Placenta percreta is the most severe grade of the placenta accreta spectrum. It occurs when chorionic villi penetrate through the entire thickness of the myometrium and the uterine serosa, often invading adjacent pelvic organs such as the urinary bladder.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with complaints of fatigue and is found to have a hemoglobin level of less than 9 g/dL. Peripheral blood smear examination reveals sickle-shaped red blood cells. What is the most appropriate management strategy for this patient?
questions.explanation: The presence of "sickle-shaped" red blood cells confirms the diagnosis of Sickle Cell Anemia. A hemoglobin level below 9 g/dL combined with clinical symptoms like fatigue indicates a severe anemic state. The most appropriate immediate management for symptomatic, severe anemia in this context is a blood transfusion (Option B). This quickly elevates the oxygen-carrying capacity and dilutes the concentration of sickled cells. IV antibiotics (Option A) would only be indicated if there were signs of concurrent infection. Deferoxamine (Option C) is an iron chelator used for chronic iron overload, not for acute anemia. "Wait and watch" (Option D) is dangerous when a patient is symptomatic with significantly low hemoglobin. For sickle cell patients, simple or exchange transfusions are critical interventions to prevent or treat complications such as acute chest syndrome or stroke during anemic crises
questions.learning: The presence of "sickle-shaped" red blood cells confirms the diagnosis of Sickle Cell Anemia. A hemoglobin level below 9 g/dL combined with clinical symptoms like fatigue indicates a severe anemic state.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presents with Kawasaki disease with multiple small coronary artery aneurysms. Treatment is?
questions.explanation: In patients with Kawasaki disease who develop small coronary artery aneurysms, low-dose aspirin therapy is typically continued for a duration of 6 to 8 weeks. This timeframe corresponds to the period of highest thrombotic risk during the vascular remodeling process, as these small aneurysms often regress over time. Lifelong aspirin (Option A) is generally reserved for patients with large or giant aneurysms where the risk of thrombosis remains permanently high. A 4-week course (Option B) is usually too short for cases with known coronary involvement. Dual antiplatelet therapy with clopidogrel (Option D) is reserved for more severe cases with higher risks of occlusion. Additionally, the administration of IVIG during the acute phase is crucial to reducing the overall risk of aneurysm formation. Therefore, a 6-week course of aspirin is the standard management for small aneurysms
questions.learning: In patients with Kawasaki disease who develop small coronary artery aneurysms, low-dose aspirin therapy is typically continued for a duration of 6 to 8 weeks.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The radiological imaging of choice for pheochromocytoma is ___
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. MRI

MRI is the investigation of choice for localizing the tumor in pheochromocytoma.

Pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting tumor derived from the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla.

Clinical features of pheochromocytoma are due to the autonomic effects of excess epinephrine and norepinephrine.

* Weight loss is due to the increase in catecholamines which increase basal metabolism.

* Pallor is due to alpha 1-mediated vasoconstriction.

* Abdominal pain with nausea and vomiting is commonly seen.

Diagnosis of pheochromocytoma requires biochemical testing followed by imaging.

* Urinary and plasma levels of catecholamines and metanephrines

* MRI is the investigation of choice for localizing the tumor

* MIBG Scintigraphy and PET Scans like Ga- DOTATE, DOPA- or FDG- PET can be used for extra-adrenal tumors and metastases

Treatment of pheochromocytoma:

Surgical resection of the tumor is the definitive treatment. Preoperatively, an alpha-receptor blocker (phenoxybenzamine) is given to control the effects produced by excess catecholamines. Beta-blockers are administered to manage tachycardia once sufficient alpha blockade has been established.This is to prevent unrestricted alpha-mediated vasoconstriction.

Following surgery, yearly follow-ups lifelong should be done.
questions.learning: MRI MRI is the investigation of choice for localizing the tumor in pheochromocytoma. Pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting tumor derived from the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which one of the following correctly describes the mode of inheritance of haemophilia B?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. X-linked recessive

Hemophilia B (Christmas disease) is an X-linked recessive bleeding disorder caused by factor IX deficiency. It primarily affects males, while females are usually carriers. Patients present with hemarthroses, deep muscle hematomas, and prolonged bleeding after trauma or surgery.

Why not the other options?

• A. Autosomal dominant: Incorrect. Hemophilia B is not inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.
• B. Autosomal recessive: Incorrect.
• C. X-linked dominant: Incorrect. Affected females would be common, which is not the case.
questions.learning: X-linked recessive Hemophilia B (Christmas disease) is an X-linked recessive bleeding disorder caused by factor IX deficiency. It primarily affects males, while females are usually carriers.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of these triggers apoptosis by activating cytochrome C?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. BAX

BAX triggers apoptosis by activating cytochrome C.

BAK and BAX are pro-apoptotic factors, whereas BCL2, BCL-XL, and MCL1 are anti-apoptotic proteins. Apoptosis, also known as programmed cell death, occurs due to the activation and release of certain proteases known as caspases. These enzymes are regulated by a balance between the actions of pro-apoptotic and anti-apoptotic proteins on the permeability of the mitochondrial membrane:

* Pro-apoptotic proteins increase membrane permeability, thereby causing leakage of proteins that initiate apoptosis, like cytochrome c.

* Anti-apoptotic proteins keep the membrane impermeable, preventing the release of cytochrome c.

There are two apoptotic pathways—

* The intrinsic or mitochondrial pathway

* Extrinsic or death-receptor initiated pathway

The intrinsic pathway is triggered by DNA damage, accumulation of misfolded proteins, and loss of survival signals. This leads to leakage of pro-apoptotic proteins like cytochrome c into the cytoplasm. Cytochrome c binds to APAF-1 (apoptosis-activating factor-1), forming an apoptosome. This complex activates caspase 9.

The extrinsic pathway is triggered by the engagement of death receptors on the plasma membrane. It activates caspases 8 and 10.

The active forms of these caspases activate executioner caspases (3 and 6), which act on various cell components to cause nuclear fragmentation, DNA degradation, etc. Cytoplasmic blebs and apoptotic bodies are then formed, which are ultimately phagocytosed.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Mycoplasma is inherently resistant to which of the following antibiotics?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Beta lactam antibiotics

Mycoplasma are inherently resistant to beta-lactam antibiotics.

Mycoplasma lack cell wall, and are therefore inherently resistant to antibiotics acting on the bacterial cell wall e.g. beta-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 50-year-old man presents with right-sided serous otitis media along with a history of cervical lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: In an adult, the clinical combination of unilateral serous otitis media (due to Eustachian tube obstruction) and cervical lymphadenopathy is highly suspicious for Nasopharyngeal cancer until proven otherwise. This malignancy typically originates in the fossa of Rosenmüller and can remain asymptomatic until it blocks the tube or metastasizes to the neck nodes. Angiofibroma (Option A) is a benign but aggressive vascular tumor seen almost exclusively in adolescent males, not 50-year-olds. Adenoid hypertrophy (Option C) is a common cause of serous otitis media in children but is rare in adults and does not typically present with significant cervical lymphadenopathy. A tonsillar abscess (Option D) presents with acute, severe throat pain, trismus, and fever, rather than chronic painless hearing loss and neck swelling. Any adult with persistent unilateral ear symptoms must have their nasopharynx examined using a fiberoptic endoscope to rule out this "silent" malignancy
questions.learning: In an adult, the clinical combination of unilateral serous otitis media (due to Eustachian tube obstruction) and cervical lymphadenopathy is highly suspicious for Nasopharyngeal cancer until proven otherwise.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which label is incorrectly marked in the basal ganglia diagram?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is (D) External capsule, as it is incorrectly marked in the diagram. The external capsule is a thin white matter tract located lateral to the putamen and medial to the claustrum. In the figure, label D does not point to this thin white band; instead, it appears to indicate a broader cortical or subcortical region, making the labeling incorrect. Other options are correctly marked: (A) Caudate nucleus is correctly identified. It lies adjacent to the lateral ventricle and appears as a curved gray matter structure along its margin, which matches the diagram. (B) Globus pallidus is also correctly labeled. It is situated medial to the putamen and forms the medial part of the lentiform nucleus, usually shown as a lighter shaded region. (C) Putamen is correctly marked as well. It lies lateral to the globus pallidus and is a major component of the basal ganglia, forming the outer part of the lentiform nucleus. Thus, only the external capsule is mislabeled, while all other structures are accurately represented
questions.learning: The correct answer is (D) External capsule, as it is incorrectly marked in the diagram. The external capsule is a thin white matter tract located lateral to the putamen and medial to the claustrum.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Mrs. Kumar, a 60-year-old woman, has been experiencing difficulty swallowing and a feeling of pressure in her chest. Her doctor orders an ultrasound, which reveals a retrosternal goiter. The commonest surgical approach to a retrosternal goiter is via:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Neck

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following does not classify as locally advanced breast cancer?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tumor more than 4 cm

A breast tumor of size > 5 cm (not 4 cm) is classified as locally advanced breast carcinoma (LABC).

Invasive breast carcinoma is of 3 types:

1. Early breast carcinoma (EBC) - TNM combination of T1 to T2, N0 to N1, and M0
2. Locally advanced breast carcinoma (LABC) - T4N0M0, T3N1M0, TanyN2-3M0
3. Advanced breast carcinoma (ABC) - TanyNanyM1

Locally advanced breast cancer (LABC) includes:

1. Breast tumors more than 5 cm in diameter
2. Cancers that involve the skin or the underlying muscles of the chest (T4 of TNM staging)
3. Cancers that involve multiple local lymph nodes (axillary or sub clavicular)
4. Inflammatory breast cancer - a rapidly growing type of cancer that makes the breast appear red and swollen

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the most common type of anorectal fistula?
questions.explanation: In the classification of anorectal fistulas (Parks classification), the inter-sphincteric type is the most common, accounting for approximately 45% to 70% of all cases. This type of fistula track begins at the dentate line and travels downward through the inter-sphincteric space (the plane between the internal and external anal sphincters) to open on the perianal skin. Trans-sphincteric fistulas (Option B) are the second most common (about 25-30%) and cross through both sphincteric layers into the ischiorectal fossa. Supra-sphincteric (Option C) and extra-sphincteric (Option D) fistulas are significantly rarer and often more complex to treat surgically due to their involvement of higher pelvic structures or the levator ani muscle. Accurate identification of the fistula type, often aided by Goodsall’s rule or MRI, is essential for surgical management. The high prevalence of the inter-sphincteric type makes it the standard expectation during clinical evaluation and surgical exploration for perianal fistula disease

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is unlikely to be seen as a side effect of lithium therapy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tardive dyskinesia

Tardive dyskinesia is not a known side effect of lithium therapy.

Tardive dyskinesia is involuntary movements of the tongue, lips, face, trunk, and extremities, usually seen in patients treated with typical antipsychotics (first generation) for more than a year. This may be reversible with early recognition and drug discontinuation. Treatment is with valbenazine, deutetrabenazine (VMAT2 inhibitors).

Known significant side effects of lithium therapy include

* Polyuria-polydipsia

* Dry mouth

* Leukocytosis

* Headache

* Hand tremors

* Confusion

* Decreased memory

* Muscle weakness

* Hyperreflexia

* Muscle twitch

* Vertigo

* ECG changes

* Nausea & vomiting

* Diarrhea

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text:
India is a country with different cultures and diverse languages. Which of the following steps should a physician take to address the patient for better outcomes?

1. Insist on good communication

2. Insist on communication only via an interpreter

3. Treat them regardless of their cultural perceptions

4. The physician should consider the patient's religion and cultural perception.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 4

The physician should have good communication and consider the patient's religious, and cultural perceptions for better outcomes (statements 1 and 4 are correct).

Statement 1 is true since the proper usage of vocabulary that is easy for the patient to understand is essential for the patient. The doctor should clarify the patient's interpretation of the words used. Thus insisting on good communication is essential for better health outcomes.

Statement 2 is not true. An interpreter is needed if the patient is not a native speaker of the language spoken in that region. The interpreter can be a family member above the age of 16 or an independent interpreter. Communication gets affected with open-ended questioning getting lost in the double translation. The answer returned might not be adequate for the doctor and the consultation as such becomes longer than usual. The doctor will have to change to a more direct style of questioning to prevent any misunderstanding.

Statement 3 is not true while statement 4 is true. Personality, culture, and beliefs are important in creating trust between the doctor and patient and are an important component in the medical interview for a better outcome. The doctor must listen to the patients' concerns, and preferences.

Health communication may fail if the message is not adequate. A good message should have the following:

• It should be in line with the objective
• It needs to be meaningful
• Based on the felt needs
• Clear and understandable
• Specific and accurate
• Culturally and socially appropriate.
questions.learning: 1, 4 The physician should have good communication and consider the patient's religious, and cultural perceptions for better outcomes (statements 1 and 4 are correct).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · Ascites Chronic Diarrhoea
questions.text: The ‘¹³C-urea breath test’ and the ‘faecal antigen test’ are non-invasive techniques to diagnose infection with which one of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Helicobacter pylori

The ¹³C-urea breath test and H. pylori stool antigen test are non-invasive methods used to detect Helicobacter pylori infection.

• ¹³C-urea breath test: H. pylori produces urease, which hydrolyzes urea into ammonia + CO₂. After ingestion of labeled ¹³C-urea, labeled CO₂ is detected in the patient’s breath.
• Faecal antigen test: Detects H. pylori antigens in stool and can be used both for initial diagnosis and to confirm eradication.

Why not the other options?

• A. Haemophilus influenzae: Diagnosed using respiratory cultures, antigen/PCR testing in appropriate settings—not urea breath testing.
• B. Leishmania donovani: Diagnosed by demonstrating amastigotes or using antigen/serological/molecular tests.
• C. Giardia lamblia: Diagnosed using stool antigen testing, microscopy, or molecular assays, but not the ¹³C-urea breath test.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 50-year-old woman with diabetes and a history of recurrent deep vein thrombosis, currently receiving anticoagulant therapy, presents with a rapidly progressive skin lesion. What began as a small lesion has quickly enlarged to involve the entire limb and abdomen. Based on the clinical history and the image provided, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: (Note: There is a significant discrepancy between the clinical description of a "rapidly enlarging skin lesion" and the provided options, which are all pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors. However, based on the classic "skin-tumor" association in medical exams...). The diagnosis is Glucagonoma (Option C). This rare tumor secretes excessive glucagon, which leads to a pathognomonic skin condition known as Necrolytic Migratory Erythema (NME). NME typically presents as an enlarging, painful rash with central clearing and necrosis that "migrates" or spreads across the abdomen and limbs. The patient’s history of DVT is also a classic component of the glucagonoma syndrome. Insulinoma (Option A) causes hypoglycemia. Gastrinoma (Option B) causes severe peptic ulcers. VIPoma (Option D) causes profuse watery diarrhea. Therefore, despite the vague description, the specific association between an extensive spreading skin lesion, DVT, and these neuroendocrine options confirms Glucagonoma as the intended answer

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is false regarding acute radiation syndrome?
options: GI manifestations occurs at a lower radiation dose than bone marrow depression
Bone marrow suppression appear at doses greater than 1 Gy
Bone marrow suppression occurs earlier than neurovascular effects
GI manifestations occur at a lower radiation dose than neurovascular effects
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. GI manifestations occurs at a lower radiation dose than bone marrow depression

GI manifestations do not occur at a lower radiation dose than bone marrow depression.

Stages of Acute Radiation Syndrome (ARS)

The prodromal phase manifests with non-specific symptoms like nausea, vomiting, anorexia. Early and persistent symptoms predict severity.

Latent phase: The patient looks and feels generally healthy for a few hours or even up to a few weeks. In severe cases, this phase may be absent.

Manifest illness phase: Symptoms are seen as per the radiation dose. Tissues with greater rates of cellular division are most radiosensitive, and hence the hematopoietic and gastrointestinal systems are the most affected.

Recovery phase or Death: The recovery phase will be seen after the manifest stage when the patient recovers from the acute exposure. The time taken for recovery will depend on the severity of the injury and the organ system affected.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman presents with dryness of the eyes requiring frequent use of artificial tears and dryness of the mouth requiring frequent sipping of water. She also reports pain and stiffness involving multiple joints of the hands. There is no history of skin tightening, Raynaud phenomenon, oral ulcers, or photosensitive rash. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Sjögren syndrome

Sjögren syndrome, an autoimmune exocrinopathy characterized by lymphocytic destruction of the lacrimal and salivary glands, leading to keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry eyes) and xerostomia (dry mouth). It may occur as a primary disorder or secondary to another autoimmune disease, most commonly rheumatoid arthritis.

• Autoantibodies: Anti-SSA (Ro) and Anti-SSB (La) are highly characteristic; ANA and RF are frequently positive.
• Diagnosis: Positive Schirmer test (↓ tear production), ocular surface staining, and minor salivary gland (lip) biopsy showing focal lymphocytic sialadenitis.
• Complications: Dental caries, oral candidiasis, parotid gland enlargement, corneal damage, and a markedly increased risk of MALT (marginal zone B-cell) lymphoma.
• Treatment: Artificial tears, saliva substitutes, muscarinic agonists (pilocarpine, cevimeline), and immunomodulatory therapy for systemic disease.

Why not the other options?

• A. SLE: Typically presents with photosensitive rash, oral ulcers, nephritis, serositis, and hematologic abnormalities; sicca symptoms may occur but are not the predominant feature.
• B. Systemic sclerosis: Characterized by skin thickening, Raynaud phenomenon, sclerodactyly, and internal organ fibrosis rather than isolated sicca symptoms.
• C. Rheumatoid arthritis: Causes symmetric inflammatory polyarthritis but does not cause prominent dry eyes and dry mouth unless associated with secondary Sjögren syndrome.
questions.learning: Sjögren syndrome Sjögren syndrome, an autoimmune exocrinopathy characterized by lymphocytic destruction of the lacrimal and salivary glands, leading to keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry eyes) and xerostomia (dry mouth).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A study was conducted in three states to measure the mean blood pressure in each community. Health workers visited every household in the three communities, and the mean blood pressures were then compared across communities. What type of study design does this represent?
questions.explanation: This study involves health workers visiting households and measuring blood pressure at a single point in time. The data is collected simultaneously from individuals in each community and then summarized (mean BP) for comparison. Since exposure/outcome (here BP levels) are measured at one time without follow-up, it fits the definition of a cross-sectional study. Although results are later compared between communities, the primary data collection is at the individual level, which is key. Therefore, it is not an ecological study, where only group-level data is used. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Case-control: Involves selecting cases and controls and looking back for exposure—not done here. (C) Cohort: Requires follow-up over time to assess outcomes—absent here. (D) Ecological study: Uses only group-level data, but here individual measurements were collected first. Hence, this is a cross-sectional study
questions.learning: This study involves health workers visiting households and measuring blood pressure at a single point in time. The data is collected simultaneously from individuals in each community and then summarized (mean BP) for comparison.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the FIGO stage of endometrial carcinoma when the disease has extended to involve the vagina?
questions.explanation: The FIGO staging for endometrial carcinoma defines Stage III as local and/or regional spread of the tumor. Specifically, Stage IIIb (Option B) refers to tumors that have spread to the vagina and/or the parametrium. Stage IIIa (Option A) involves the tumor spreading to the serosa of the corpus uteri and/or the adnexa (ovaries/tubes). Stage IIIc (Option C) indicates spread to the pelvic and/or para-aortic lymph nodes. Stage IVa (Option D) is more advanced and involves the invasion of the bladder and/or bowel mucosa . Accurate staging is essential for determining the prognosis and the need for adjuvant therapies such as radiation or chemotherapy. Because vaginal involvement is the specific criteria for the "b" sub-category of Stage III, Stage IIIb is the correct diagnostic stage. Management of Stage IIIb disease often requires a combination of surgery and radiation therapy

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: All of the following interactions between T cells and APC (Antigen-Presenting Cell) are required for T cell activation/differentiation except:
options: T cell receptor and MHC II
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. PD-PDL1

Signal 1: Antigen Recognition

• TCR (T-cell receptor) binds peptide + MHC (on APC)
• For CD4⁺ T cells → MHC II

Signal 2: Co-stimulation

• CD28 (T cell) binds CD80/CD86 (APC)
• Prevents anergy (non-responsiveness)

Signal 3: Cytokines

• APC secretes cytokines → directs differentiation:

• IL-12 → Th1
• IL-4 → Th2
• TGF-β + IL-6 → Th17

T-cell activation requires antigen recognition via T-cell receptor–MHC interaction and costimulatory signaling through CD28–CD80/86.

Cytokines from APCs provide signal 3, directing T-cell differentiation into specific subsets.

PD-1–PD-L1 interaction is an inhibitory immune checkpoint that downregulates T-cell activation.

Hence, PD-PDL1 is not required for activation but for immune tolerance and suppression.

| Signal | Interaction | Function

| ------ | ----------- | --------

| Signal 1 | TCR ↔ MHC-antigen | Recognition

| Signal 2 | CD28 ↔ CD80/86 | Co-stimulation

| Signal 3 | Cytokines | Differentiation

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following viruses can cause more severe disease and potentially serious complications upon reinfection?
questions.explanation: This question reinforces the critical clinical concept of Antibody-Dependent Enhancement (ADE) associated with the Dengue virus. As previously discussed (see Q.92), reinfection with a heterologous (different) serotype of Dengue often leads to a much more severe clinical course than the primary infection. This is due to non-neutralizing antibodies facilitating viral entry into host immune cells, potentially causing lethal hemorrhagic fever or shock. Rabies (Option B) is almost 100% fatal upon the first infection, so reinfection is not a clinical reality. Measles (Option C) and Mumps (Option D) are characterized by life-long, robust neutralizing immunity after a single natural infection or a complete vaccination series. Therefore, Dengue remains the definitive example of a virus where subsequent infections are statistically and physiologically more dangerous than the initial exposure

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient on antidepressants presented to you with hypotension. An ECG was done, which showed wide QRS complexes and right axis deviation. How will you manage this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. IV NaHCO3

The combination of:

• Antidepressant use
• Wide QRS complex
• Hypotension

strongly suggests: Tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) toxicity

The drug of choice for TCA toxicity is: IV Sodium Bicarbonate

Mechanism:

1️⃣ Alkalinizes blood

2️⃣ Reduces TCA binding to sodium channels

3️⃣ Increases sodium concentration

Result:

• Narrowing of QRS complex
• Improved cardiac conduction

Antidepressant overdose (classically tricyclic antidepressants) causes sodium channel blockade, leading to wide QRS complexes and hypotension.

IV sodium bicarbonate reverses Na⁺ channel blockade and corrects acidosis.

This narrows QRS and improves hemodynamics.

Antiarrhythmics, beta blockers, and phenytoin are contraindicated or ineffective in TCA toxicity.
